Freshwater Management—Water Quality
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his statement in relation to the Ruataniwha
Dam that “there’s quite a bit of debate about the science …”; if so, is the debate that he
is referring to being generated by other scientists or is the debate being generated by
Federated Farmers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, with regard to debating the science, does he agree with
the statements by Associate Professor Russell Death that “Mor e pollutants, lower water
quality, it’s not rocket science.”, or by Professor David Hamilton that “  ‘business as
usual’ will not get us over the line …” on water quality, or is it that he wishes to dispute
the statements of Dr Mike Joy that the “Impacts on  fresh water from dairying have
definitely got worse …” in the last 3 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, some of those statements have an element of truth in
them, but there is a range of particular views from the scientific community, and we will
see how the thing plays out.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, with regard to the range of views, when he said on the
BBC’s HARDtalk programme 3 years ago that he could find another scientist to state
that intensive agriculture is not polluting our rivers, how is that going, and can he tell us
the names of these other scientists?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can he tell us the names of those other scientists?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There would be a range of people who would indicate that you
can actually increase agriculture and do it in an environmentally balanced way.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Otago Regional
Council, which stated tha t his Government’s water -quality rules misapply the science
and would result in water bodies that are not only unsafe for swimming or for letting
your dog swim in but are potentially toxic and unsafe for stock to drink from?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the reason that his Government is repeatedly rejecting the
scientific evidence when it comes to Māui’s dolphins, polluted rivers, or climate change
that the scientific evidence conflicts with his economic agenda of more oil, more cows,
and more motorways?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the last part of the question, no.
19030 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014
State-owned Assets, Sales—Purpose and Use of Proceeds
2. JOHN HAYES (National —Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance : What
progress is the Government making in allocating proceeds from its share offer
programme to pay for new public assets through the Future Investment Fund?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government continues to make
good progress in investing almost $4.7 billion from its share offer programme into new
public assets. We are able to invest this money without having to borr ow more from
overseas lenders. At the weekend the Prime Minister and Minister Brownlee confirmed
that $212 million from the Future Investment Fund will be invested in 14 important
regional State highway projects around New Zealand. That is on top of the $3 60 million
that we have already proposed for regional roads across New Zealand. This investment
will continue to build on the Government’s extensive investment in vital infrastructure,
which includes ultra -fast broadband, schools, hospitals, roads, and rai l, and more of it
will be financed from the Future Investment Fund.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: How will the latest investment in regional roads meet the objectives set
for using capital raised from the Government’s share offer programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: This investment follows through on the logic of the sales,
where the Government sold shares to investors, the investors passed cash to the
Government, and now we have the opportunity to invest that cash. As the Prime
Minister said at the we ekend, the investment in regional roads is a perfect example of
money from the share floats being invested for the benefit of New Zealanders, the
economy, and their families. The 14 projects are spread across the country from Otago
to Northland, from the West Coast to the East Coast.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What other investments in new public assets has the Government
confirmed using proceeds from the share offer programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the House is now familiar with, there is $4.7 billion of
proceeds from the share offer programme. In Budget 2014 the Government confirmed a
further $1 billion of new investment. This included $200 million for health, including
$67 million for the new Grey Base Hospital on the West Coast. This too k health
spending from the Future Investment Fund to $684 million. It also allocated $172
million to education, including the upgrade and replacement of schools in Canterbury.
KiwiRail received another $198 million. All up, the $1 billion allocated from th e fund
in Budget 2014 brought the total allocated to almost $3 billion, which left nearly $1.7
billion in the fund for new public assets over the next couple of years without having to
borrow more money.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What reports has he seen su pporting the Government’s approach to
investing proceeds from the share offer programme in new public assets?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen reports from an unlikely source: an alternative
budget that was issued in the last week or two. Th e reports indicate that this alternative
approach to the Government’s finances will continue the current Government’s
approach of using proceeds from the share offer programme. The Opposition budget
includes the $4.7 billion proceeds from the asset sales b eing spent on public assets,
which was rather a surprise given that they had spent 4 years vigorously opposing the
policy.
Education Sector—Impact of Government Policies
3. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he have confidence in the Minister of Education and all of her decisions?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.
1 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19031

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Did the Prime Minister agree with the decision in 2011 to
increase class sizes, which was heavily criticised for cherry -picking research,
misinterpreting findings, and the Government deliberately ignoring conflicting studies?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: By definition, yes, because it went through Cabinet. The view
taken was that a small increase in class sizes with money used to lift professional
development at a time when the country was cash -strapped would deliver better results
for New Zealand children.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In light of that answer, when he announced his teacher bonuses
and part-time principals policy to try to recover lost ground in education, did he expect
it to be received as unworkable and lacking direct benefit for children, and so bad that
teachers and principals were actually willing to turn down pay rises of up to $40,000 a
year?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We all know that the member has been working with the New
Zealand Educational Institute and was very miffed when we came out with our
announcement prior to them getting a chance to announce theirs. But if we go back and
look at that announcement, it is $359 million aimed at keeping the very best teac hers in
the classroom, aimed very much at making sure that expert principals can go out there
and lend a hand to other organisations, and aimed at making sure that the very best
teachers can get greater progression in their careers. That is why the Post Pr imary
Teachers Association and other unions are supporting it. I might add that all of the
unions came with the ministry when it went on a number of tours to look at this in cities
where it has been very, very effective.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In light of that answer about the importance of quality, does he
agree with ACT leader, Jamie Whyte, that schools should be like supermarkets; and
what will be the special of the week at these expensive, State -subsidised, supermarket
shop-ins?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have absolutely no doubt what the special will be. It will be a
moa burger.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Has the Prime Minister sought adequate funding for education
when parental donations to schools have increas ed by 30 percent under his Government
so that parents are having to shell out tens of millions of dollars every year for the cost
of their kids’ education?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: This year the Government has allocated $10.1 billion for
education, a record in the history of New Zealand. I do not want to remind the member,
but the last time members opposite were in Government there were donations being
made by parents back then, just as there are today.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I a m sure he believes that if he looks after the pennies, the
pounds will look after themselves. Does he therefore stand by his decision to transfer
responsibility for the Novopay debacle from Hekia Parata to Steven Joyce given that
she could not fix it and he could not either?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I know what she did do and that was to inherit it from Labour.
Actually, I think we would all agree that Mr Joyce has done an outstanding job in a very
difficult situation, resolving those issues acros s the country. I guess that back in the
days when moas walked around New Zealand there were not computer systems to pay
teachers. Nowadays there are, and under a National Government we are fixing that up.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the P rime Minister stand by each of his Government’s
decisions in education over the last 6 years, including increasing class sizes, introducing
charter schools, the debacle over closing Christchurch schools, Novopay, and now
teacher bonuses?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think it is best summed up with a few stats. In 2008, 66.5
percent of young New Zealanders got National Certificate of Education Achievement
19032 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014
(NCEA). Today that is 76.8 percent. Back in 2012, even, the number of Māori students
with NCEA l evel 2 was 44.4 percent. Today it is 58.6 percent. If we look at Pasifika
students we see that back in 2008, 55.3 percent of them had NCEA level 2. Today it is
71.8 percent. We know it is the same in terms of participation in early childhood
education, and we certainly know, if we look at the results of students going through our
tertiary facilities, that they are doing extremely well. Also, if the member wanted to
spend a bit of time wandering around Christchurch, he might be surprised to find how
much sup port there is for the Government actually spending $1 billion on new
schools—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Oh, rubbish!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: —than half a billion dollars on old ones. The members
opposite say “Rubbish!”, so I welcome them  to go to Christchurch and say they will
build the old schools back, and not build the new ones. Good luck. I will see you down
there at the press debate.
Transport Infrastructure—Funding for Regional Projects
4. DAVID BENNETT (National —Hamilton East) to the Minister of Transport :
What recent announcements has the Prime Minister made regarding the Government’s
commitment to transport infrastructure in regional New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: On Sunday the Prime
Minister announced an accelerated regional roading package of $212 million, which fast
tracks 14 important regional projects throughout New Zealand. This is in addition to the
Government’s recently announced draft Government Policy Statement on Land
Transport 2015/16 - 2024/25, which includes a specific regional fund of up to $360
million over the first 4 years of that plan. Between the Government policy statement and
the accelerated regional roading package, the Government is making over $3.7 billion
available to local and regionally important roads in New Zealand over the next 4 years.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are some of the projects included in the package?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Although our opponents on the other side of the
House are determined that these projects should not go ahead, they are projects that
communities have been wanting for a very lon g time. One of these projects is the
Normanby Overbridge improvements, which will straighten the approach road and
create traffic underpasses below the rail track. Another is the Ōpawa and Wairau
bridges in Blenheim, where those two bridges will be replace d. Time does not allow me
to extol the virtues of all 14 projects, but what New Zealanders will know is that if they
want them, we are whom they will vote for, not that lot.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What has been the reaction to this announcement?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think we have seen much of the reaction expected
this afternoon in the House: crying and weeping from the Opposition, which is accusing
the Government of pork-barrel politics, but it is a surprise—and then they say we should
have funded all this out of the normal transport funding from the National Land
Transport Fund. Somehow, though, if someone goes out there and builds an electrified
railway network in Auckland or an electrified railway network in Wellington outside the
National Land Transport Fund, that is OK; it is not pork barrel.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he agree with Ken Shirley of the Road Transport Forum that the
lack of analysis of these projects points to “pork -barrelled politics and just throwing
money into marginal electorates. That’s the old days.”; if not, will he release the
benefit-cost ratios of each of those projects or at least the polling data that he based the
decision on?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I do not agree with Mr Sh irley and the statements he
has made, and I am quite sure he finds himself in disagreement with the people who pay
1 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19033
his salary. Frankly, if we want to talk about benefit -cost ratios, I will put the benefit -
cost ratios up for the rail loop, and if the member  agrees they are as bad as they are and
is so concerned about them, I expect Labour to change its policies.
Unemployment—Impact of Government Policies

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Is the Government—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: A living moa.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I am not a living kiore like that guy there.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I am just telling him —I am not like the living kiore
over there.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to invite the member to start his question again. I
hope there will not be the same level of interjection from my right-hand corner.
5. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Is the
Government “working for New Zealand”; if so, does that apply to all New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes; and yes, and that is why the
Government was smart enough to support a situation where we would allow Coasters to
be working, and where we would ensu re that wind -blown timber was actually
harvested. We are amazed that some political parties oppose that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If “working for New Zealand” applies to all New
Zealanders, then why has the unemployment figure in this country increased by almost
60,000 people under his leadership since 2008?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As the member will be aware, New Zealand went through the
global financial crisis and the like. But our unemployment rate is 6 percent, it is on track
to go down to 4.4 percent, and the participation rate is, I think, pretty much the highest
in the developed world at 69.3 percent. But if the member is worried about creating
jobs, then I would have thought his party would be out there supporting jobs  on the
West Coast of the South Island to process timber that was blown over in a natural
disaster.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How has the Government been working for New Zealand
and all New Zealanders when almost one in four young Māori  and Pasifika aged
between 15 and 24 years of age looking for work is still without a job?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am glad the member asked that question, because the
Government has been putting a huge—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No you’re not.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, no, I am actually delighted. The Government has been
putting a huge number of resources into Māori and Pacific trade training. Actually, only
last Friday I was out at WelTec visiting the Māori a nd Pacific trade training. What was
remarkable was how well it is doing. I think 100 of its students have just gone down to
Christchurch to be part of the rebuild. We are seeing an increase in the rates of Māori
and Pasifika success at school. The member m easures the small group of Māori
youngsters who are not actually in training or employment or other forms of work.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If the Government is working for New Zealand and if that
was a fact, why is the Government exp anding student visa work rights to 79,000
international students, in direct competition with Kiwi students desperately needing
work to keep their student loans down?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We know the member does not like foreigners, but I hate  to
point out to him that it is an industry that is worth about $2.5 billion or $2.6 billion a
year to New Zealanders. We get 28,000 people employed as a result of that. If the
19034 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014
member does not like foreigners, he should just get up and continue to talk abo ut it and
hark back.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If the Government is working for New Zealanders, then
why would National’s plan to spend over $2 million on election campaign propaganda
be needed to convince New Zealanders that that is what is going on?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We will obviously be running a campaign. I have got a feeling
that, actually, it is going to catch on, because every single question from New Zealand
First has been about our slogan —“Working for New Zeal and”. So I am happy to spend
a few moments talking about that if he likes—about the way the Government is working
for New Zealand in creating infrastructure, making sure our health system is working
efficiently, and making sure that New Zealand is deliveri ng for this country. But if the
member wants to talk about our campaign, we are happy to do that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If the Government is, as it claims, working for New
Zealand and New Zealanders, then can he explain how export education works when
79,000 international students get to pay for a New Zealand education with income from
the New Zealand economy? How does that work?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: For a start off, when people come to New Zealand as part of
export education, they actually pay to be here. That is why it is worth about $2.6 billion.
Secondly, there probably are a few students who come to New Zealand and who choose
to work in restaurants and bars and cafes and motels and all sorts of other things. That
just shows how industrious they are. But if the member would prefer that no one comes
to New Zealand, then he is harking back to a day when moa used to freely walk through
the forests of New Zealand. I know that is an era he looks back to with great—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!
Regional Economies—Development and Transport Infrastructure
6. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Economic Development
items.text: What does he consider are the core components of a regional
economic development plan?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I thank the
member for his excellent question. It may take a little bit of time, given he has asked for
the core components. In my view, a regional economic development plan needs a
number of elements. An important component is access to capital, encourag ing
companies to invest. That is why, for example, New Zealand Trade and Enterprise has
established a new regional investment attraction programme to help regions attract new
investment and take advantage of their opportunities. Another key area is skills.  Right
around the country the Government is investing in more closely matching the skill
levels of New Zealanders with jobs in regions through our universities and polytechs,
and apprenticeships and industry training. Of course, developing our natural resources is
also important. That is why we are focused on reforming the Resource Management Act
to make better decisions; developing our oil and gas resources; water storage and
irrigation; and reforming the Maori Land Act. Infrastructure is vital as well, wh ich is
why the Government is building the roads of national significance and investing heavily
in regional roading projects, as well as innovative technologies like ultra -fast broadband
and rural broadband. In fact, I would say there are many key areas of a regional
development plan, so, yet again, I invite the member to take a look at the Government’s
Business Growth Agenda, which contains 350 initiatives across six key areas to grow
jobs and growth in regions around New Zealand.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer around infrastructure, is clear planning an
important part of creating a regional economic development plan; if so, how does
spending hundreds of thousands of dollars doing an upgrade to the Motu Bridge near
1 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19035
Gisborne—an upgrade that is due to finish in the next fortnight —only to decide to fund
a project that will see the newly strengthened bridge knocked down a good use of
taxpayer money?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member makes an interesting point. That parti cular
bridge is going to have $100,000 spent on it, which is going to keep it in shape for the
next 4 years, and then the big one can be built. If the member is opposing the new
bridge at Motu or repairing the existing bridge, I think that is going to be v ery well
received in Gisborne. All of those projects that the member raises, which are a small but
significant part—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Loony economics!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Do not be talking loony economics; you have got “Mr Moa
Hunter” behind you. That is loony economics.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is Gisborne Mayor Meng Foon correct when he says about the
replacement of the Motu Bridge “Now they can throw that money in the drain and get a
new bridge.”, and does throwing money down the drain represent National’s great
regional economic plan?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I understand that that is not what the mayor said. I have
been advised—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It is!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: But again, the member needs to go to Gisborne and talk to
the people there, as Mr Brownlee and I did with Mrs Tolley not very long ago,
launching the East Coast Regional Economic Potential Study. They are very keen to see
those projects develop, and th is Government has invested significantly in roading
projects in the Gisborne region. I encourage the member to continue on with his
approach, because, once again, he is showing he knows nothing about economic
development.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In light of the Minister’s
answer, I seek leave to table the comments of Gisborne Mayor Meng Foon—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I simply need to know the source of that document.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: W ell, the source is a media report, but he has challenged my
word on this—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am not putting the leave. The member may have further
supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: When Gerry Brownlee said that the c urrent strengthening project
would pay “instant dividends” to the local economy, can he assure the House that there
will hundreds of thousands of dollars of “instant dividends” before the bridge just gets
pulled down?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Let me explain to the member. This is 2014. The new
bridge will be finished around 2017. So, yes, it needs to keep the existing bridge going
for a while, while the new bridge is built. If the member turns his mind to that, he can
see that that will be $100,000 well spent for Gisborne.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Would a core component of a regional economic development
plan include developing plans to support industries that are significant to a region; if so,
why has he ignored the pleas of the East  Coast region that if money is to be spent on
roads, it should be spent on upgrading forestry roads, as Labour has committed to in our
forestry upgrade package?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do believe that we should be encouraging the
development of industries in regions, which is why this Government supported the West
Coast Wind-blown Timber (Conservation Lands) Bill last week, which the Labour Party
did not support. It is why this Government is unambiguously in favour of oil and gas
exploration in the Taranaki Bight, where the Labour Party was like “Yeah, nah.” and
19036 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014
was not interested in that. This Government, as I have pointed out, has 350 separate
initiatives in regional economic development through the Business Growth Agenda, but
I have to admi t that we do not have the resuscitation of the moa project in this book at
this stage, but we will look into it for the members.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why is it that after 6 years National’s best effort on regional
development is a somersault while standing on a pork barrel, and where is the support
for regional initiatives that will actually grow sustainable jobs, like supporting the
Mayors Taskforce for Jobs, for instance?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member, I am sorry, is so out  of touch. This
Government has supported a huge range of projects in the regions.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Struggling!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, let me take you through some. Thank you —I will
take the extra time. We are supporting ultr a-fast and rural broadband around New
Zealand, the Primary Growth Partnerships for the agricultural industry, the research and
development funding for companies all over New Zealand, and New Zealand Trade and
Enterprise’s regional business partners program me, which works on developing
management and research and development capability in businesses around the regions.
We are encouraging oil and gas exploration. Dare I say it, we are encouraging water
storage and new irrigation projects, the national cycle t rails, export education, and so on
and so on. We have a range of projects. Mr Robertson has just platitudes.
Transport Infrastructure—Funding for Regional Projects
7. JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green)  to the Minister of Transport : Why are the
regional State highway projects announced at the weekend being funded from asset
sales rather than the transport budget?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Future Investment Fund
was created to ensure that New Zealand has high -quality productive infrastructure. The
Accelerated Regional Roading Package delivers, as announced on Sunday, high -quality
infrastructure that will be of benefit to New Zealand’s regions.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This was a question on
notice, and I think that the intent of the question is quite clearly to ask why the projects
are not being funded from the transport budget. The Min ister did not address that in his
answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the Minister did. You asked in your question about why it has
been funded by asset sales. The Minister then went on and said that the purpose was to
create this fund to be used to develo p quality infrastructure. The question was certainly
addressed.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Is not the reason that the $3 billion transport budget is not
enough to fund crucial regional transport projects that this Government has starved the
regions to pay for its low-value roads of national significance programme?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, that is not true. The Government has had a
considerable amount of funding going into the regions. The point that has been made
over the last  couple of days is that that will continue for the years to come. In actual

Housing, Affordable—Reports, Development Contributions, and Auckland Issues
9. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū) to the Minister of Housing : Does he
stand by his statement that the rate of new house builds in Auckland “is the highest it
has been in years, and it shows the progress we are making”, given the average number
19040 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014
of building consents issued for new dwellings in the last six years is 4,408 per year,
compared to an average of 9,055 from 1999-2008?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, because the 33 percent annual
increase in new house builds in Auckland to May 2014 is the highest annual growth
since records began in 1991. The member’s selective use of averages hides the fact that
the collapse in Auckland’s new house build rate oc curred between 2004, when there
were 12,000 houses built, and 2008, when there were only 4,000. It is significant to note
that the worst quarterly Auckland house build rates since records began in 1991 were at
the end of 2008. In December 2008 there were 2 33 building consents in Auckland. In
May, the latest figures, there was 611—i.e., treble the number last month.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Why is it, if his special housing areas are so successful, that not a
single new house has been built in them that anyone is living in, and why have

abysmal record?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member is hiding the fact that there was a massive
collapse in house build numbers from 12,000 a year back to 4,000 a year in Labour’s
last 5 years in Government. His colleague the Labour spokesperson on finance was
complaining in the House only last week that there was too big a growth in GDP and
residential house builds, that it was happening too fast, and that there were too many
new houses. I think that just illustrates the level of contradictions of members opposite.

items.text: What steps has the Government taken this week to further help

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yesterday Cabinet approved Orders in Council for 41

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he stand by his statement on becoming Minister of Housing

Māui’s Dolphin—Preservation

Māui’s dolphins be granted out to 20 nautical miles from Maunganui Bluff down to

items.text: New Zealand officials at the
International Whaling Commission argued against extending the area of protection on

the protected area in 809 independently observed fishing trips since.

Government representative at that International Whaling Commission meeting lodge a

Accident Compensation—Hearing Loss
11. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland) to the Minister for ACC: What changes
has the Government announced about the way ACC covers claims for hearing loss?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: From 1 July 2014 changes to the
hearing loss regulations will significantly improve access to treatment for ACC clients
with hearing loss. We are addressing cost barriers as well as improving competition in
the market, to ensure clients with hearing loss have better access to the help that they
are entitled to under the legislation. The changes include increasing choice for clients,
allowing multiple repairs to each hearing aid, and increasing ACC contributions to the
cost of the device. ACC will now pay s eparately for the hearing consultation, which
means that clients will be able to shop around for the best price in hearing aids rather
than having to buy where they had the initial test. It is important that clients have the
option to look for the best pri ce and service. Children will be removed from the adult
regime so that their special needs as they grow and enter school can be better catered
for. This is good news for people who have been injured at work, who have injury or
work-induced hearing loss.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Was the hearing loss sector consulted about these changes?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes. Members of the hearing loss sector were involved in
workshops with ACC and jointly worked on the update to the regulations. The
consulted parties include the New Zealand Audiological Society, the National
Foundation for the Deaf, and six other organ isations that represent providers to the
sector. There was also a further targeted consultation with the sector for 3 weeks, once
the proposed changes were determined. The hearing loss sector has supported the
changes.

items.speaker: Iain Lees -Galloway
items.text: Will people like railway worker Malcolm Stone, who lost
$6,000, which was 80 percent of the funding ACC had previously provided for hearing
aids, as a result of National Government cuts in 2010, have all of that funding restored
under the changes she has announced?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The changes are from today. They are not retrospective.

Vote Communications Security and Intelligence

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: New Zealanders have a lot
of unanswered questions about our intelligence and security community. Over the last
couple of years New Zealanders have been ve ry disturbed at the lack of assurance from
the current Government about the protection of their privacy online and in cyberspace.
They have had grave reservations about the Government Communications Security
Bureau (GCSB) legislation that was passed by this Government through this Parliament,
and the Telecommunications (Interception Capability and Security) Act, which provides
for the intercepts that support it. At the start of this debate I want to revive and reaffirm
Labour’s commitment to two things: fir stly, on our taking office, a thoroughgoing and
urgent review of our entire security establishment; and, secondly, an absolute,
comprehensive, and unshakeable commitment to the principle that no New Zealand
citizen will be subject to blanket surveillance o r any surveillance by a New Zealand
security service without a judge’s warrant—no ifs, no buts, no maybes. That review will
absolutely assure New Zealanders that there are no gaps, workarounds, or other
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19045
exceptions in the legislation that would ever allow s uch unwarranted surveillance to
occur.
There has been a great deal of discussion about New Zealand’s security
arrangements with other countries. This is a sensitive area. The Labour Party recognises
that we live in a complex and dangerous world. We recogn ise that there is a legitimate
and appropriate place for well-governed security services, but we do not accept that as a
member of an international agreement that governs these services we should or could
give a blank cheque to our partners to use New Zeal and - sourced intelligence in any
way they see fit. It is absolutely appropriate that this Government is transparent with
New Zealanders about the governance arrangements and policies, within limits and
within the need for operational sensitivity, that govern the use of New Zealand - sourced
intelligence.
New Zealanders are rightly concerned that our security establishment is not up to
snuff. Today the Government has released, and it is on the State Services Commission
website, the Performance Improvement Framework: Review of the agencies in the core
New Zealand Intelligence Community . For an unclassified document, it is a remarkably
interesting one. On the business strategy and operating model, the reviewers say that the
establishment needs to, first, clarify priorities and the scope of the role of the security
agencies. In other words, they are in a muddle. They do not know what their priorities
are and they are ineffective.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Who’s the Minister for that?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: And who is the Minister? The Prime Minister.
Second, it must ensure that the intelligence community works effectively together,
the conclusion being that currently it does not. Third, it is to establish customer -driven
priorities and practices. They make the point that if nobody uses their reports, they are
not worth producing, and note that there is a huge gap between the level of interaction
between community partners such as New Zealand companies and the agencies in New
Zealand and their analogous agencies in the UK or Australia. It says that basic business
systems are “weak and require attention. Financial and managerial control systems have
not been maintained”. For goodness’ sake! These are supposed to be some of the most
sophisticated agencies in the New Zealand Government and they can barely run their
own budgets—they can barely run their own budgets. They are to establish a common
workforce plan, and ensure continued legal compliance.
Well, there the rubber meets the road , because the GCSB could not even, in its last
annual report, get to within about 50 percent accuracy of the number of intercepts it has
actually done. It was out by a factor of two —unbelievable. The Auditor -General was
called in to explain why our spies c ould not count to 50. It is embarrassing, and the
Minister in charge of the NZ Security Intelligence Service should be able to take a call
right now and explain to the Committee why some of the most sophisticated agencies in
the country cannot count past t wo hands and two feet. It is not good enough, Mr
Chairman, and it is not good enough, Minister.
They are to improve the public mandate —well, there is an understatement. The
agencies concerned do not have one, because the Government’s policies are not clear,
robust, and transparent.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Prime Minister and Cabinet agreed to.
Vote Security Intelligence agreed to.
Vote Tourism

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: It gives me pleasure to
take a call on tourism in this part of the debate. The reason for that is that tourism is so
19046 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
very important to our country. Indeed, it is so important to our country that the Prime
Minister himself decided to give it the honour it deserves and take on the responsibility
for tourism. That is very good news for all those who are involved in tourism in New
Zealand. The Government’s commitment to tourism over the last 6 years has been
greater than any Government’s ever before in this country.
What does this mean for Kiwis on the ground in New Zealand? Well, it is very
simple. It means greater effort into the local economy and it means more jobs —that is
right; more jobs in tourism for New Zealanders. At the end of May th is year, almost 2.8
million visitors had come to New Zealand, an increase of some 6 percent. In part that is
because of the great work the sector has done and the very important work and
commitment on the part of the Government. But it is really about a ne w relationship
where the tourism sector businesses up and down New Zealand have joined with the
Government to put New Zealand’s best foot forward and to promote the great things
that we do here, to the rest of the world.
I asked earlier what this means to  the economy. Members opposite keep squealing
about jobs. They are disappointed that job growth in New Zealand is on the way up and
unemployment in New Zealand is on the way down. During that same period of time,
up to May 2014, there was an increase in sp ending of 9 percent on the part of those
visitors. That means more people are coming and they are spending more than they
were before. Again, in every part of New Zealand, from our largest cities to our
provinces, and certainly in regional and rural New Ze aland, that is really, really good
news.
A quick note shows that over the last 6 years the Government has committed and
spent $600 million on the promotion of tourism in New Zealand. That is very important
when one considers where those visitors are comin g from and why they choose to come
to New Zealand. We know it is a beautiful country. We know they have a great time
when they are here. We know it is a safe country to visit under this Government. But
here is where it gets really interesting. Do you remem ber those movies that were made
in New Zealand that members opposite did not want to be made?
An increasing number of visitors to New Zealand, when they get off the plane, say
that the reason they have decided to visit New Zealand with their families for a holiday,
and to spend money here, is that they have seen the Hobbit movies when they have been
sitting at home in their own countries. That is a great way that the Government has
leveraged the use of taxpayer funding to support up to 5,000 jobs being cre ated in New
Zealand as part of the film industry. Now more people are visiting New Zealand
because they have seen films that feature New Zealand and they are staying for longer
and spending money in all parts of our economy, which boosts jobs, grows jobs i n our
regions.
I want to pick on two parts as an example. The first is our traditional markets. The
Government in the Budget last year committed an extra $134 million to spend in a
number of areas of tourism. That certainly looked at where growth and pote ntial will
come from in the future. We committed $34 million to significantly expand focus on
international business events —very important for our cities particularly —and $44.5
million has been allocated to attract visitors from emerging markets like India ,
Indonesia, and Latin America.
Next year New Zealand will co-host with Australia some of the games of the Cricket
World Cup. That is one of the largest sporting events. It will be watched by people all
around the world. We have agreed with Australia on a  border policy whereby people
who come from India can, if they have a visa for Australia, travel to New Zealand
without getting another visa, to come and look at our country and to watch these great
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19047
games of cricket. That is going to be really very importa nt for us, and it shows that the
Government is focused on the future in terms of where demand will grow in some of
these countries that have a lot of interest in New Zealand.
But we are also spending time and effort focusing on the existing markets of the
USA, of the UK, and certainly of other parts of Europe. Here is a really interesting
statistic: growth over the last 12 months of visitors from the US was 9 percent, but their
spending was up by 55 percent. So 9 percent more of them came, and 55 percent m ore
was spent in our regions. The Government is committed to tourism. The Prime Minister
as the Minister of Tourism is doing more work in tourism than any other Minister has
done before. Our economic commitment is there. We have joined with the sector. It is
good news because it is about jobs, it is about the local economy, and it is about our
commitment to growing New Zealand.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Finance

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to take a call to talk in
the estimates debate on Vote Finance and related items. This was reviewed by the
Finance and Expenditure Committee. One of the things that some members of the
committee noted was that inequality in New Zealan d is increasing and many New
Zealanders are not benefiting from the growing economy. It was noted that some
measures indicate that 46 percent of workers have had no pay rise in the past year. It is
against that background that we need to judge whether the proposals that are brought
forward through Vote Finance for the country are right. I would like to contrast them
with some of the proposals that the Labour Opposition is making.
Last week we proposed our alternative budget. That alternative budget has gon e
down pretty well. There are a few headline messages there. First of all, everything is
paid for, and we are in surplus. So we can get down to a debate—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: 10th surplus.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: A 10th surplus; that is right. It would be the 10th surplus in a
row for Labour Governments, given that in the last Labour Government we ran nine
surpluses in a row, and reduced gross Government debt from 38 percent to 18 percent of
GDP and net debt down to zero —net debt down to zero. It is clear that whether it is
Labour in charge of the Treasury benches or National, you are unlikely to have a
fiscally irresponsible Government in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: I don’t know about that!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The Minister in the chair says he does not know about that,
but the truth of it is that we actually have not had a fiscally irresponsible Government
since Muldoon’s National Government in the 1980s left New Zeala nd with Government
debt that was amongst the highest in the world, which took subsequent Governments, be
they National or Labour, a generation to pay off. So we know the ills of unbalanced
Budgets. This Government has not yet run a surplus. It is true that some of those deficits
were a consequence of a global recession that affected New Zealand and also the cost of
the Canterbury rebuild. That is why we do not whack Government members around the
ears too much about the deficits that they have run, but we do  know that it is time to get
back to surplus, and we would too.
Our numbers show how it would be done. The commentators who have been through
those numbers —produced not 3 weeks before an election but 3 months before an
election—have given them the tick. They said: “Clean bill of health here. It is obviously
clear that you’re not going to be fiscally irresponsible, that you are going to run Budget
surpluses, and that you are going to pay down debt.” In a fair society, everyone should
19048 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
get their fair share an d everyone should pay their fair share. One of the provisions that
we have got in this alternative budget is to shift the economy away from speculative
activity towards the productive economy. There is no doubt that one of the reasons that
we over-invest in property-based assets is that the tax system encourages it. Just about
everyone now accepts that, except for the Government. The OECD says it, the IMF says
it, Treasury says it, the Reserve Bank says it, the Labour Party says it, the Greens say it,
and j ust about every other developed country in the world says it. We need to have
people investing in the productive parts of our economy, not chasing tax advantages in
the speculative economy.
That is why if there is one policy that should be looked at really carefully this
coming election—and I think the people of New Zealand are up for it—it is the question
of whether we should change our tax system and tax capital gains excluding the family
home.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: How is this relevant?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: How is this relevant? You could take a call. You can see
that one of the issues that was raised in the financial review by the Finance and
Expenditure Committee was that the absence of a capital gains tax means that we have
got an economy that is out of shape, that invests too much in the speculative sector and
not enough in the productive sector. We have got higher house prices as a consequence
of the i nvestors in rental housing piling in, particularly in Auckland, where
homeownership rates are the lowest they have been in 50 years and still dropping.
Our alternative budget makes it clear that we are fiscally responsible, that we are not
going to be wri ting cheques that we cannot cash, and that we will be back into surplus.
You know, National has racked up $60 billion worth of debt, just about —$60 billion
worth of debt. It made it worse through tax cuts, where 40 percent of its income tax cuts
went to the top 10 percent. It quotes tax figures excluding the burden of GST.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I think you
can hear with that  speech by David Parker the problem that Labour has. It has got a
finance spokesperson, someone who wants to be the Minister of Finance, who cannot
finish a speech on time, cannot articulate an argument, and cannot get a key point
across. It is a big problem. What he did say was that whoever gets into Government will
be a fiscally responsible Government. Well, I can tell you that we have a 6 -year record
showing that we are fiscally responsible.
What he did not actually tell you was that if these people wer e part of the
Government, they would be there with Russel Norman pulling the strings. The big
question is whether the tax rates that Labour would impose would be high enough for
Russel Norman. Would the punishment of hard -working Kiwis be tough enough?
Would Russel Norman be laying into the people he does not like hard enough? He
would be putting a lot of pressure on David Parker. So, in the end, all that stuff that
David Parker is saying is absolutely and completely irrelevant. If, as Chris Finlayson
says, the multi-headed Hydra gets into Government, I do not know whether there would
be room for even old Clayton Cosgrove in Cabinet. He would probably find his place
taken by the American lady from Mount Eden, who would suddenly become the
spokesperson on small business.
Russel Norman could take David Parker’s place. Old Annette King there —well, I
mean it will probably be the bald -headed guy from the West Coast. He would end up
being the Minister of Health. So you start to see the picture of a very different -looking
Cabinet if these people got in.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What a nasty thing to say.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: It might be nasty, but it is true.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Stop all the personal attacks.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19049

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Phil Goff would actually finally want to retire.
The problem is that these guys have not come up with a single bit of policy. Do you
know what their economic development idea for this week is? It is to bring  back the
moa—to bring back the moa from extinction. I think it would be far better if they
worked on something like bringing back David Lange or maybe bringing back Michael
Joseph Savage, because, frankly, without someone inspirational from the past
chromosomally re-engineered, these guys have absolutely no hope at the next election.
If they ever got the Treasury benches, I can tell you that the Budgets would be bad, bad
news for New Zealand.
And then if you look at what we have, basically we have nearly 4 percent economic
growth over the past year, the third -highest rate in the OECD, and 1,500 people every
week moving off welfare and into work —1,500 people. So, actually, we are getting the
country moving ahead. There were 84,000 new jobs in the last year.  That is growth.
That is economic development. That is responsible fiscal management. There is a very
coherent plan there. But look at the Budget —through tight economic times, what have
we done? We have preserved the entitlements for the most vulnerable Ne w Zealanders.
We have a $500 million package there for families, with free general practitioner visits
for under-sixes, paid parental leave—
Simon O’Connor: Under-13s, now.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Sorry, under -13s—even better news. So, you
know, we are focusing on getting the country ahead at the same time as protecting the
most vulnerable.
Gerry Brownlee’s $220 million regional roads package was announced at the
weekend. That is infrastructure that, I can tell you, the Green Cabinet would stop,
because the Greens do not like roads. They do not like the regions. They do not come
from the regions, most of those people, except for the bald guy from the West Coast.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a poin t of order, Mr Chairperson. I would have thought
you would stop that sort of behaviour. Naming a member of Parliament in that way is
just not acceptable.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I thank the member. It is not nece ssary.
[Interruption] I am on my feet. I would ask the Minister to confine his comments to the
estimates. I remind members of pages 128 and 129 of Speakers’ Rulings . That is the
debate that we are on. Although some latitude is allowed, I will ask the Minister to
bring his focus back to the estimates debate.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I know you would not have been so sensitive,
Mr Chair, about that sort of matter—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! [Interruption] I am on my fee t. The
member will apologise for those comments.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I apologise, Mr Chair.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: You cannot comment on anything that the
presiding officer says, which you did do.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: So when you look at this, you see that it is a
carefully thought-out package, focused on the needs of New Zealanders. I can tell you
that when you look at what these guys have come up with,  the one idea that David
Parker has personally come up with, is something called “the big tool”. What you do is
you use people’s KiwiSaver to control inflation. Well, how is that going to appeal to
Labour’s core base out there? In the end, what it means is  its core voter will be told:
“Sorry, inflation is going up. You are going to have less money in the pocket to spend
each week.” It is absolutely nuts. David Parker is the architect of that. You can tell how
agitated these guys are getting over there, beca use they are under real pressure. It is
falling apart in their caucus. They have got no plan. They are deeply frustrated—
19050 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Back on the estimates.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Oh, come on! This is—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, no. The member will sit. Earlier I
mentioned relevancy and com ing back to the estimates debate. You are in the final few
seconds, and this is a peroration of your 5 -minute speech to bring together those points
that you want to make relevant on the estimates. I would ask the member, in the last few
seconds, to confine his comments to that.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The point I am making is that you should look
at the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance managing the economy very soundly
for 6 years. It is a very sound economic plan, which  has delivered for New Zealanders.
These people can shout as much abuse as they like, but out there we are connecting with
the electorate. The National Party is objective—

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: On behalf of the Green Party, I
want to make a few comments about the estimates with regard to finance. The thing
about the finance estimates is that they do not just include the issues of economics and
the fiscal position of the Government, they also impact on the environment and society
more generally. The Green Party has a view that what we need in New Zealand is a
cleaner environment, a fairer society, and a smarter economy. For those reasons, we
think that we need to change direction. Unfortunately, this Government—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry. The member will sit.
Members—[Interruption] I am on my feet, and when the presiding officer is on their
feet, that is it. I will ask the member to apologise for that comment.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Which one?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The very unparliamentary comment you
interjected with that called the Minister Jonathan Coleman a word that should not be
used in this House. The member will withdraw and apologise for those comments.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Unfortunately, we have heard from Associate Minister of
Finance Coleman a long, personal attack on various people instead of debating the real
issues that are before the country, such as the issue that we have got a Government that
continues to rack up massive amounts of debt and continues to criticise the previous
Government, yet it was the previous Government that paid down debt. That is the
reality. The previous Government, with  the support of the Greens, voted for Budgets
that reduced debt, and National, at that point, told us time and time again to not pay
down debt but give tax cuts to the wealthy. But, of course, Labour, with the support of
the Greens, New Zealand First, and others, said: “No, no. We are responsible about this.
We intend to pay down debt.”
So in 2008 when National came in, it inherited a position of very low Government
debt. Since then it has increased debt dramatically and has not run a single Budget
surplus. Except for the last one, in the 2014 -15 year, where there was a wafer -thin
surplus, every other Budget that this Government has run has been a deficit Budget. It
has built up nearly $60 billion worth of debt —$60 billion worth of debt —under the
watch of J ohn Key and Bill English. They tell us that they are great fiscal managers.
These are the people who have built up nearly $60 billion worth of debt and who,
through the course of all of the previous Government, time and again, through nine
Budgets, opposed  the attempts to reduce Government debt, because it said: “No,
surpluses should not be used to pay down debt; surpluses should be used to give tax cuts
to the wealthy.” That was the argument of the National Party during those 9 years.
Fortunately, everyone ignored the National Party, because it does not know anything
about fiscal management. When the global financial crisis happened in 2008, there was
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19051
very low Government debt and the Government we have now was lucky enough to
inherit that very low Governme nt debt as a result of the very good fiscal management
of, actually, the Labour Government. We have been critical of Labour on many things
on various occasions, but you would have to say that when it comes down to looking at
the Government’s debt position and fiscal management, when you compare the record
of Clark and Cullen versus Key and English, it is miles apart. Clark and Cullen paid
down massive amounts of debt. Key and English have built up $60 billion in debt. Sure,
some of that debt was unavoidable —no question about it —but let us look at which bits
were avoidable.
How about the $5 billion that the National Government gave to the top 10 percent of
income earners? Was that avoidable debt? Remember, it had racked up $5 billion worth
of debt in order to give tax cuts to the top 10 percent. That seems to me not a very good
reason to rack up $5 billion worth of debt —to give tax cuts to the wealthiest people in
the country—yet that is what the National Government is proudest of. It tells us time
and again that it is very proud when it looks at its fiscal position. It says: “We added $5
billion of debt to the Government books in order to give $5 billion in tax cuts to the
wealthiest 10 percent in New Zealand.”
This is at a time when most ordinary families, h alf of all workers, have not had a pay
increase in the last 12 months. This is at a time when housing affordability is going
backwards. Housing affordability is going backwards not just because houses are
getting more expensive under National but also beca use wages are flat-lining under this
Government. Ordinary working families’ wages are flat -lining under John Key and Bill
English, house prices are going up, and the Government says this is a sign of success.
Well, talk to ordinary people. It is no sign of  success. Their household budgets are
under enormous pressure because electricity bills keep going up, housing bills keep
going up, and their wages are flat under this Government. There is no increase for
ordinary families. That is at a time when we are no t dealing with some of the great
issues facing the country—for example, climate change.
The Green Party put forward a plan of a climate tax cut. We put a price on carbon
and returned it in the form of income tax cuts and company tax cuts. That deals with
environmental issues and economic issues at the same time. That is a much more
sensible direction than the one in which this Government is going, which is more debt—
environmental and fiscal.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSO N
items.text: I call Andrew Little. Oh, sorry —I
apologise. Sorry to the member. I made that mistake the other day when I called
Andrew Little Andrew Williams. Andrew Williams, you have the floor.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: That is right. I take a call on behalf of New
Zealand First on the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill in regard to the finance
debate. It is most disappointing, as a New Zealander, to have to look at the figures that
this Government puts up, because much of it is a litany of lies. The reason I say that is
that New Zealanders have been robbed for the last 5 years of Government contributions
to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. This National Government has not
contributed 1 cent to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund for the last 5 years, and
this Budget and the estimates going forward also do not provide for any contributions
for the next 5 years. For a whole decade under this Government, New Zealanders are
being robbed of their future retirement fund.
That retirement fund, to the year ended 31 May 2014, is currently worth $26.14
billion. The average return of the fund, since its inception under Dr Cullen, when he
was Minister of Finance, has average 9.74 percent. The  last 12 months the fund has
returned a 17.2 percent return to the fund after costs. And in the last 5 years the New
Zealand Superannuation Fund has returned a 16.8 percent average over those 5 years.
19052 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
These are incredible figures. In the 1 month alone of M ay 2014, when the finance
Minister was issuing his Budget, the fund made 2.57 percent return —for that 1 month.
Yet the Minister of Finance tells us that it is poor fiscal management to borrow any
money to put into the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. When the Government can
borrow funds in the order of 3 or 4 percent per annum and when a fund is returning 17.2
percent in the last year, basically, this Government is robbing the people of New
Zealand in order to falsify the books and make sure that the Budget looks OK.
At the same time during that same period when the Government sold the State -
owned assets, it promised the people of New Zealand that it would get between $5
billion and $7 billion for those assets. That is what it sold the promise on. It ended up
with a miserable $4.5 billion from the sales —some $2 billion to $2.5 billion less than
what it promised the people of New Zealand. It said originally that it would use the
funds to pay down debt, but what did it do? In the meantime the debt carried on
mounting. It took on a debt 5 or 6 years ago of about $6 billion, when it left the
Opposition benches and became Government. That has now gone up tenfold to $60
billion under this National Government. At the same time, it said that it would put that
$4.5 billion into new projects, such as 21 st century schools. It said it would put it into
21st century schools. But what is it actually doing? It is putting the money into fixing
leaky schools—hundreds and hundreds of leaky school buildings. There are over 300
leaky school buildings around New Zealand. That is where the money is going —again,
to make up for an error of the National Government from the 1990s, when it allowed the
leaky building programme to get under way.
At the same time, where has the rest of the $4.5 billion gone? Well, $120 million
went to the sharebrokers who sold the shares in the first place. So this whole Budget and
estimates have come out showing that the Government has a $372 million surplus, and
showing how wonderfully it is doing as managers of the economy, but $120 million -
odd in the last year has just gone to the sharebr okers—the friends of Mr Key and Mr
English—just to sell the shares. At the same time another $40 million went to pay for
free bonus shares for those who bought into State assets. Is that not incredible? The
Government gave away another $40 million to the 2 .5 percent of New Zealanders who
bought into the shares. Previously the shares were 100 percent owned by you, me,
everybody else in this room, and everybody else around this country, and now 2.5
percent of New Zealanders own those shares and $40 million wa s given to the asset
buyers to help pay for free bonus shares in the coming year.
At the same time another $100 million went into shoring up stricken Solid Energy,
another State -owned enterprise —another $100 million. Most of these figures are just
absolute nonsense. This is an absolute smoke and mirrors Budget. The estimates going
forward are absolute hogwash. This Government makes out that it is running a surplus,
but, in actual fact, if the media was to jolly well do some proper research —some proper
investigative research —and show how the Government is not putting any money into
the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and how most of the money—
PAUL GOLDSMITH (Chairperson of the Finance and Expendit ure
Committee): Well, we have certainly seen a vision of the proposed new Government.
First, we had David Parker saying that there is no problem in the world that cannot be
solved by a capital gains tax. Then we had Russel Norman, who wants higher wages,
but who has no solution other than higher taxes, and somehow that that is going to lead
to higher wages. And then we had Mr Williams, who gave us a lecture on economics
and said that we should be borrowing more in order to invest in the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund. So why do you not just go out and borrow $100 billion and put it
all in the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, if that is such a sensible idea? I do not
think many households go out borrowing money to put it on to the stock exchange. It is
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19053
not very sensible. I only wonder what Hone Harawira and Kim Dotcom would add to
this mix in a proposed new Government.
This has been a successful Budget that has seen the finances of the country restored.
It has seen 3.8 percent growth in the year to March, wh ich is the third -highest among
the OECD countries. It has seen average wages rising faster than inflation. It has seen
84,000 new jobs being created, and this is a result of 6 years of working for New
Zealand. The question that New Zealanders will ask is: “Well, what is next? Who do
you trust best to carry on the good work?”. I expect from National —if we are fortunate
enough to get more time in Government —an extension of the strong, stable, predictable
Government that has generated confidence in this economy over the past few years. It is
confidence that leads to investment, it is investment that leads to jobs, and it is jobs that
lead to higher living standards for all New Zealand families. That is what we want to
see.
So what we will continue to see is mo re disciplined spending, such as we have seen
over the last few years and in this Budget. We will see a continued effort to build a
stronger and more competitive economy that underscores the living standards that we
all hope to enjoy —and the Business Growt h Agenda is the core source of direction in
that area—investment in infrastructure, such as in regional roads, which is opposed all
the time by the Greens; and investment in skills. There is no better way to solve worries
about inequality than by ensuring that everybody has access to a quality education
system, and that involves good quality teachers and investment in good quality teachers.
It involves trade access, and it amazes me that the Greens are opposed to free -trade
agreements all the time. New Zeal and has benefited enormously from the free -trade
agreement with China, and I was glad that Labour stood for that back then. Nobody is
quite sure where it stands now.
Capital markets —increasing the depth and variety of capital markets in New
Zealand, and t hat has been greatly assisted through the share programme that we have
had in the past 3 years. Natural resources —it was amazing to see that all the Opposition
parties were opposed even to collecting the dead trees from the forests that had been
blown over in the wind. That seems to epitomise their attitude towards making use of
natural resources in this country. Finally, the sixth area of the Business Growth Agenda
is innovation, where this Government has been pouring huge resources into ensuring
that New Zealand companies have access to skilled and innovative people and that we
support them in their work in research and development to grow their businesses, to
employ more New Zealanders, and to create more wealthy New Zealand families.
The other thing that we have been focusing on, and that I expect we will continue to
work on, is getting better results from the investment that the Government makes in
public services. We have seen that through much higher immunisation rates. We have
seen a massive reductio n in teen pregnancy, which will see much reduced costs, over
the length of time, in the area of welfare, and it will also see many New Zealand
families avoiding the problems that have been created through unwanted teen
pregnancies. In the welfare area, thr ough the investment approach, when we see what
the expectations were around the cost of welfare back in 2008, we have lowered that by
more than $1 billion, and that has led to more New Zealand families seeing the benefit
of work and being encouraged into work.
Another area, which I have heard about for as long as I can remember, is the need to
ensure that prisoners who are suffering from drug or alcohol addictions are getting
access to programmes to improve that situation. This Government, again, has massi vely
increased the number of programmes available for prisoners.
So it is about doing the job of Government well, working out what the key drivers—
19054 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: You know that the
Government has run out of ideas when the Minister in the chair, the Minister of
Defence, just takes to insulting members of the Opposition from the Greens and the
Labour Party, rather than addressing the issues. It is also somew hat ironic to hear the
Minister in the chair criticising potential coalition parties, when his own coalition is in
disarray, with the ACT member having resigned for election -related fraud, and United
Future’s Peter Dunne having had to resign because he lea ked a Government document,
and now they are trying to shoehorn Colin Craig in —a man who believes in chemtrails,
who does not believe in evolution, and who is not sure whether a man landed on the
moon.
One of the reasons why our alternative budget went down  pretty well was that
journalists believed it. They believed it on the basis of the numbers that were presented
and our record when last in Government. The Dominion Post  said: “The party’s
approach is moderate and centrist, and so there is no reason why it  should frighten off
middle-of-the-road voters. … Perhaps, however, policy will … become a serious part of
this election campaign. At that point, the voters might see that Labour offers a wide
range of genuine policy alternatives to National. And then perh aps there will be a
serious debate about what really matters for New Zealand and its future. At that point
clichés and outdated slogans might give way to actual debate.”
That is what we are trying to do through our alternative budget: get through to a
debate where we can talk about the widening gaps in New Zealand. It is not just the
Labour Party saying that; the head of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research,
its chief economist, said that the gaps are widening between rich and poor suburbs in
Auckland, between the regions and the large cities. We have got the lowest rate of
homeownership in 50 years. We have had a trebling of luxury car sales. We have got
increasing income gaps between wealthy suburbs and poor suburbs, which have shown
up in the c ensus figures, and we have got more children than ever living in poverty.
Against that background we should be having a debate at this election as to whether the
policies of the current Government are making those gaps larger or reducing them. And
the real ity is that we know that they are making them larger. That is why Labour’s
economic plan, which we can now talk about because we have got past this tax and
spend nonsense from National —that accusation has been laid out for the public to see
that it is just a hoax.
We can talk about what we need to grow the depth of capital markets. We need to
have everyone in a universal KiwiSaver scheme, like they have in Australia. Of course,
today is the seventh birthday of KiwiSaver. If you go back 7 years, who voted a gainst
it? The National Party. Who voted against the Cullen fund, which National members
now say is one—the National Party. National called it a dog. It gets these big questions
wrong all the time. Who voted against the surpluses that we ran when in Govern ment to
reduce Government debt? National members wanted tax cuts weighted to the wealthy,
as they always do.
Having built pools of capital in the same way that they do in Australia, through
universal work-based savings, you then need to get it going into the right part of the
economy. Under National too much of it goes into land speculation, and that is one of
the reasons why we have the highest -ever houses prices on average in Auckland. A
capital gains tax helps push that money that is currently chasing a tax advantage—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Rubbish. Hasn’t worked in Australia.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Look, Dr Smith, you are so, so wrong. That is why the
IMF, the OECD, the Reserve Bank, Treasury, and other countries disagree with you.
You also need to have some more money spent on innovation. So we say that we
should recycle some of that money through a research and development tax credit.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19055
Bring forward more investment in productivity, and improve equipment in the likes of
the forest processing industry so that we do not export as many raw logs but, instead,
cut up timber and make finished products. Those are the sorts of policies that the
Labour Party is promoting for this election. Indeed, following our forestry upgrade
launch, one of the forest processors has said: “Oh, give us this policy package and we’ll
invest another $100 million in an expansion, a very significant expansion, in our
factory.” That would, of course, bring more export earnings and higher-paid jobs.
The gaps are widening under the current Government. There is no doubt about that.
Seventy-five percent of New Zealanders think that that is true, and those New
Zealanders do not like it. They want a fair society. They know that these sorts of
widening gaps do not  make any one better off; they make us all poorer because the
economy does not go as well. National is conservative. All it does is trim expenditure. It
never makes any significant changes to economic settings. That is why, when the cycle
turns, it is up to Labour and our allies to make the changes our country needs.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): Well, it is fascinating that we have just
heard from the Labour member David Parker that sam e sort of empty rhetoric that
Labour has been accusing the National Party of—and it finished, in fact, on the idea that
the National Party, because it is conservative, does not spend money. This Government
has spent over $500 million extra in this Budget t o support Kiwi families, particularly
children and parents—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: The most vulnerable.
SIMON O’CONNOR : The most vulnerable. This is one of the fundamental
differences between a left -wing and a right -wing Government: the left wing is great at
talking but never walking the walk that is required.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: We target the expenditure.
SIMON O’CONNOR: We target the expenditure, but we actually do it. We have
heard for weeks members on  the other side say: “Oh, let’s put together a whole lot of
measures on child poverty, let’s put a whole lot of reports together, let’s just make
numbers stack together.” The National Party, through the likes of Vote Finance, has
walked out and actually wa lked the talk. There is $500 million more for families, and
the most vulnerable are targeted.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Free GP visits.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Absolutely—National has funded, as my colleague has just
noted, free general prac titioner visits until the age of 13. It is about actually doing
things.
But what about members on the other side? They were talking about wood just a
little bit earlier. This seems to be the great solution. I remember being at a social justice
talk with L abour and the Greens, which was hilarious —they have no idea of what it
means to be social or just, but, anyway, there they were. Their great solution to the
economy, just like we heard before, was logs. Logs are the solution. Of course, last
week this Government was passing the West Coast Wind -blown Timber (Conservation
Lands) Bill—under urgency, rightly —to take native timber that had been downed and
felled by nature. You would think the Greens would love that. But only this side of the
Chamber moved that b ill and supported it. All these others —oh yes, they say logs are
our future—voted against it. There we go, New Zealand—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Just slugs and bugs.
SIMON O’CONNOR : Absolutely. This is the side that actually makes the
difference, and you know you are making a difference when you talk in this Chamber
and they start getting fired up. Again, they talk but they do absolutely nothing.
