We are very proud of what we are do ing. I found over the past few weeks
campaigning around my electorate of Tāmaki, including last night at an excellent public
19056 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
meeting, that people are grateful for what this Government has done in the financial
spaces. We have an incredibly well -performing economy, which is growing at 3.8
percent. We had average wages increase by $3,000 in the past 2 years and 84,000 new
jobs have been created.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much was that?
SIMON O’CONNOR : That was 84,000 new jobs created . These are real things.
These are measurable statistics that you can bring out. Not just measurable; what I am
finding from people in my electorate is that they are experiencing it. In fact, a number of
people in my electorate are some of the top earning people. And do you know what?
They are happy to pay their taxes and their fair share, and they are paying even more
than their fair share now. Through National’s comprehensive tax cuts right across the
board, those top income earners —and there are a good n umber in my electorate —are
now paying more taxes. Do you know why they are prepared to pay them and they are
happy to pay them? Because they are with a party that cares about and tries to help
people.
Once again we have seen those moneys given to the most  vulnerable. I keep talking,
rightly, about the parental tax credits, the extension of paid parental leave, the general
practitioner visits for under -13-year-olds that are now free, and more money into
schools. Unlike the member from New Zealand First, And rew Williams, who
complained that it is just about repairs to leaky schools, we are actually investing in
new—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Did he say that?
SIMON O’CONNOR : He did —it is shocking that that member of all members
would talk  about leaks. But that member forgets that we are pumping hundreds of
millions of dollars into new classrooms, like the ones at St Thomas’s School. Look at
something like Stonefields School in my electorate, which is now a green school. The
way it has been  designed under the governance of this Government is as a school of
sustainable quality. That is a new school, with new innovations, new technologies,
which this Government has championed.
In Vote Finance National walks the talk. We walk the talk. We actu ally make a
difference. That is why we poll the numbers that we do, and that is why we see that
others are not seen as relevant. Coming back to my electorate, it understands day by day
that the changes that have been made are making a difference. I think e ven of an area
like Glen Innes. For me, that is a wonderful community in my electorate. They are
experiencing this change. Hundreds of new homes are being built, a number of those
State houses. They are warm and modern, created—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Healthier and drier.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Healthier and drier, absolutely. They are raising the options
for people, and that is moving right across the sector. There is an enormous amount of
positivity happening here.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Canterbury Earthquake Recovery

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Thanks very much for the opportunity
to take a call in the estimates debate for Vote Canterbury Earthquake Recovery.
Nowhere in New Zealand, in my view, is it more needed than in Canterbury for people
to have a bit of support, a bit of a vision, and something positive to look forward to. We
have been through a lot, and where that vision, that support, and that hope for the f uture
could have been provided, there is a big empty space. People are looking for local jobs
for local people. They want to have training opportunities for young people in our city
so that they can go on with a passion and stay in our communities.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19057
We want  homes that are affordable. I have watched the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery wash his hands of any concern at all about the situation that
people are finding themselves in. I have said to the Minister that I do not care what he
calls it. He argues about whether or not it is a crisis. I do not care about the description.
The fact is that people in our communities cannot find an affordable home to rent. From
my perspective, that is a crisis, and the Government has done nothing.
I see that the Hon Dr Nick Smith is about to make a major housing announcement in
Canterbury over the coming week. I look forward to something positive. Do you think
anyone will be a little bit suspicious that 3½ years since the February quake, after
constant denials from  the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, suddenly —
what a coincidence, we are 80 days from an election —we have the Minister of Housing
giving a toss about our housing situation? I think that would be greeted with the
cynicism that it deserves.
The National Government has walked away from the hardest part of the Canterbury
earthquake recovery. That is what I have previously found so frustrating, but that
frustration has now been trumped, because what we learnt during the estimates was that
Minister Brownlee and Minister English have used the Canterbury earthquake recovery
as a way of fiddling the books and putting on the table a Budget surplus. It is not a true
surplus. We will not know the true figures involved in the central government
contribution to the earthquake recovery until —when? Ah, the end of the year. It is a
deliberate decision by the Hon Gerry Brownlee that there would be no auditing of the
costs until after the election. This is a cheap and nasty way of producing a Budget
surplus on the back of tragedy. On behalf of my constituents, I resent that.
The Minister debated this —not very strongly, admittedly —at the select committee
with my colleague David Parker, my other colleague Clayton Cosgrove, and me during
the estimates consideration. But we produced a document that is a minute of a meeting
between Tony Marryatt and Bob Parker —the former chief executive and the former
mayor—and the current Minister. It said this: “Following discussions with the Minister,
it was felt that due to the poss ible negative impact on the cost of borrowing for the
Government following an audit opinion that highlighted the uncertainty of the
Government’s share of the response and recovery cost, a long -term plan process should
not be undertaken by the council.” The  Hon Gerry Brownlee said to the Christchurch

items.speaker: City Council
items.text: “Do not get your books audited before the end of 2014.”, and Bob Parker
and Tony Marryatt went along with that direction from Minister Brownlee. No wonder
Minister Brownlee got so upset when the cu rrent council commissioned the
KordaMentha report, which gave robust figures about the council’s need and the
ratepayers’ need for contribution towards our recovery.
We know that it is not all good news in Canterbury —we do not expect it to be —but
we deser ve the truth. We do not deserve having Ministers poncing around our city,
going to the opening of an envelope, and misleading us about the costs that our
contribution will require, let alone using shonky figures to put on the table a Budget
surplus that is  made up. I think that people all over the country should resent that
happening. The estimates on the Canterbury earthquake recovery show a shallow
Minister and a shallow department with huge expenses —nearly $100 million to run the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority to produce well-being surveys—and, on the
back of the recovery costs, it was denied a robust audit, having shonky Budget figures. I
do not think that is good enough.
Hon NICKY WAGNER (Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery): I am very pleased to be speaking on this Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates)
Bill. I want to start by thanking the Prime Minister and the National G overnment for
their consistent, ongoing, and future support for the recovery and rebuild of greater
19058 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
Christchurch. The appropriations for 2014-15 are $570.4 million, as part of a multi -year
appropriation of over $15 billion, with the total expenditure on th e Canterbury rebuild,
including insurance payouts, private sector investment, and local government
expenditure, being $40 billion. That sort of investment in our community over the next
few years underpins a very positive future for Christchurch and the Canterbury region.
After the earthquakes there were some very dire predictions about Christchurch —
that people would leave the city in droves, that businesses would close, that insurers
would pull out, and that the city would die. Thanks to some very careful  and hard work
by this Government, 3 years later it is a very different story. The population of greater
Christchurch is growing, there are 11,000 new businesses registered, GDP growth is
more than 6 percent, and unemployment is just about 3 percent. The r ebuild is well
under way—in fact, the city is pumping.
Just before I talk about the tangible signs of restoration and rebuild in Christchurch, I
want to look at the human dimension —to look at the restoration and the rebuilding of
individual and community well-being. Christchurch people have supported each other
throughout the earthquakes, and on into the recovery period. Funded by the Ministry of
Social Development —and I want to thank the Hon Paula Bennett —local and central
government, community organisati ons, and neighbourhood groups have collaborated
and worked hard together to support anyone and everyone who needed it. This is set to
continue, with the new Community in Mind Strategy and $13.5 million for ongoing
services to make sure that all those peopl e who are still adversely affected by the
earthquakes are supported as they recover.
Let us get back to bricks and mortar. The number of homes that have been repaired
and rebuilt has accelerated recently. The Earthquake Commission has rebuilt 60,000
homes, and that is nearly 80 percent of the claims. Families are moving into their new
homes every day. I just want to make the point that although there has been pressure for
temporary housing, the Government has built four temporary villages and introduced—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. I advise members on my left to have a look at Speaker’s ruling
60/5. Interjections are to be rare and reasonable and, if at all possible, witty.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Just to reinforce, for temporary accommodation, four
villages have been built, and we are entering into a housing accord with the city council
for 200 more units.
Let us look at SCIRT —the Stronger Christchurch Infrastructure Rebuild Team. That
has been a very innovative and successful project. It works on the city’s underground
infrastructure and the roads above it. Almost 50 percent of its work has been completed,
and the rest is well under way. That is good news because we all know that the long -
term prosperity of Canterbury, and of the South Island around that, is based on the
rebuild of Christchurch, as it is the tourist gateway and the export shipping hub for the
whole South Island. But right now t he central business district is full of cranes, diggers,
hard hats, and high-vis vests. Over 200 building projects are complete or are under way
within the four avenues. The publicly funded Avon Ōtākaro River Project is almost
completed, and that will prov ide a people-friendly public space and a waterfront for the
central business district.

items.speaker: The Re
items.text: START Mall, which has actually become world -renowned as a symbol of
Christchurch coming back, has for the last 3 years provided the retail anchor for the city
and ensured that people have come back into our city. Now it has been relocated
because new construction dominates the three blocks round that area. The future for
retail looks very bright in the central city. Thank you.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call the honourable member Denis
O’Rourke.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19059
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First): A good choice, Mr Chairman, thank you. There is
now a very large question over whether the Government resources allocated in the
Canterbury recovery are anywhere near adequate. The member Nicky Wagner, who has
just spoken, constantly looks at the Christch urch recovery through rose -coloured
glasses, seeing only some of the good things —and, yes, there are good things —but
never acknowledging the problems, the many problems, that are still with us in
Christchurch.
We all know that billions more will be needed  for the recovery—the Prime Minister
himself has said so —but there is nothing to indicate that in what the Government has
allocated currently for the rebuild. It has been 3½ years since the February 2011
earthquake. We are now in a fourth winter. Thousands  of homes in fact are still
unrepaired. Bare-section and self-insured landowners are taking the Government to the
Supreme Court over the illegal offers made to them, and the legality of the red -zoning
itself is in question. Dozens of homes are still expect ed to be flooded yet again before
the winter is over. Port Hills residents are still in limbo awaiting a decision, living in
rented accommodation while their own homes rot. A massive housing crisis, in which
people simply cannot find an affordable home to buy, is getting worse by the day. For
those who need to rent —well, that is a nightmare. Even if they can find a home to rent,
they would have to spend something like $1,000 a week for an average three -bedroom
house. If that is not a housing crisis, then I do not know what is.
But I especially want to talk about the Earthquake Commission and its treatment of
the owners of units and multi -unit dwellings. No Minister could be satisfied with the
progress of the commission in the settlement or disposition of th e claims made in
respect of multi -unit dwellings. Where the units and multi -unit dwellings are assessed
by the commission as being under the $100,000 cap per unit but the damage claimed is
greater than this, and when the cost to repair the building as a wh ole would exceed the
total of the Earthquake Commission - assessed damage for all individual units together,
then that situation is currently in an absolute shambles. In far too many cases the
Earthquake Commission is resisting a realistic sum for repairs of whole buildings where
they are multi-unit buildings.
Only yesterday in my office there was a case where the Earthquake Commission had
failed to assess adequately the cost of repairs to all of the units in one small, six -unit
building in the central city. It had failed to offer nearly enough for the repairs to obvious
damage to each unit, but it had also failed to assess the building properly as a whole,
leaving the owners to take legal action. In that case the total assessment was only
$350,000, which i s clearly grossly insufficient to repair all six units, so the total for
Earthquake Commission purposes had to go under the $600,000 cap for all six together.
And that did not take into account repairs that needed to be made to the building as a
whole to make it leak-proof again, or to the land and driveways and many other issues.
The inadequate assessment by the Earthquake Commission in those cases means that
the private insurer takes no part and, therefore, the owners are left to battle the
Earthquake Commission on their own.
Private insurers would be much better taking over the process in those cases for the
full repair or replacement of the whole building, but this is prevented by the Earthquake
Commission’s intransigence and inadequate technical assess ment. Its only interest
appears to be to find a way to justify keeping the costs under the cap. The Minister for
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, as well as the Earthquake Commission, seems
careless about the people who are caught in this trap of an inadequ ate offer by the
commission for repairs. The commission insists that units are under cap when they are
clearly not, leaving the owners to pay tens of thousands of dollars to engineers and
assessors to do the commission’s job for it as well as to pay lawyers’ fees.
19060 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: One of the ways you measure recovery is
by looking at the number of people who are settling claims. I will concede one thing in
Nicky Wagner’s spe ech—although after that speech I have to say I have got a bit of
sympathy for Gerry Brownlee having to work with her —which is that the Stronger
Christchurch Infrastructure Rebuild Team is going well. I think the team is quite an
outstanding example of comm unity engagement and communication, despite the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority’s intransigence. I think it is a good
example, and it is a pity that the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery did not
follow the same pattern with his own department.
Mr Brownlee is fond of making statements, and he has claimed from time to time, of
course, that—in fact, I will read his quote—“Only a small fraction of outstanding claims
are in dispute and there are a range of appropriate channels to deal with co mplex or
disputed insurance claims.” Well, one of them is the court, and we propose —and we
will implement it when in Government—an earthquake court. It will be a division of the
District Court —a lean, mean, fighting machine to get claims through. Mr Brownl ee’s
response to that was to say, basically, that he believed that “lawyers would have a field
day at taxpayers’ expense.” That is what he said. The point I would make to Mr

items.speaker: Brownlee is
items.text: what about the insurers having a field day at the claimants’ expense, which
has been going on for 4 years?
If the insurance industry, which he is very fond of, sucks up to, and puts his arms
round, is doing such a great job, then why is it that only 44 percent —44 percent—of
claims are settled? That is on the authority’s ow n website. There are 10,000 outstanding
claims, and the census tells us that there are two and a half people per household on
average, so that is equivalent to the size of Timaru —25,000 families and households in
dispute. They have still not settled their claims with those wonderful people from the
insurance industry nearly 4 years down the track, so we say it is time to do something
about it.
What we should not keep hearing from this Government is how well these guys are
doing, because every insurance com pany in this country has let down its claimants.
Every insurance company in this country is in breach of its contract because insurance
policies say that claims should be settled in a reasonable time —not 1 year later; not 4
years later. Mr Brownlee’s answe r is that his department says it is all OK, there is no
problem, there is a bit of an advisory service here, and if you have got enough money,
over and above all the other things that you are grappling with, you can toddle off to
court. He also says, of co urse, that most claims do not get to court. Well, that is true,
because people cannot afford to go to court, and in another 2 years’ time the Limitation
Act says that if they are still in dispute with the insurer, they then lose all their rights if
they have not lodged a court case. So Mr Brownlee does not connect the dots. He says
that very few cases end up in court —that is correct —but they do not end up in court
because people cannot afford the means to get there.
So what is their alternative? Oh, a bit of disputes resolution, a bit of mediation —sit
there and wait, 4 years later. We say that we will set up the Earthquake Court. The
Crown will hit the bill and then pass it on to the Earthquake Commission and the
insurance industry. There will be compensation payments to the claimants if the
insurance companies delay. Mr Brownlee, I am sure, will get up and say: “Oh, we don’t
need more lawyers. We need more plumbers, we need more sparkies, we need more
carpenters working on these houses.” He is right, but the only way you will get more
plumbers and sparkies and carpenters is if the people have the money from their
insurance claim and the Earthquake Commission to then rebuild or build their houses
and employ those sparkies and carpenters and plumbers.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19061
If they cannot get the money out of the Earthquake Commission and they cannot get
the money out of their insurance company and they cannot afford to go to court on their
own volition—and under our policy it will not cost th em a dime —then how on earth
does this Minister expect people to get ahead? What are the other appropriate avenues
for people, as he says, to actually get ahead, get their claims sorted, and get it done and
dusted? The truth is that there are none, Mr Brownlee—there are none.
All we hear from this Minister is that his officials —the Earthquake Commission
officials—and the insurance industry are working tirelessly, as he said on 31 August last
year, to get these claims settled. Well, here is the problem: 44 p ercent—that is it. There
are 10,000 outstanding big claims, not to mention some of the other ones. Then we have
the privacy breaches, the obfuscation by the Earthquake Commission, the lack of
information, and the inconsistent information, and people still languish. So I say to Mr
Brownlee, let us hear your solution for the person who has no money, whom the
advisory service cannot do a lot for, who cannot go to court, and who has nowhere to
go—
This afternoon the Committee has been regaled with a number of terribly inaccurate
statements from members of the Opposition, and I am going to deal wit h them back to
front. The first point is that the Government has been deeply involved in the recovery in
Christchurch since the outset. There was a comment made by the Hon Ruth Dyson in
which she claimed that I had instructed the Christchurch City Council not to have an
audit of its books, because it might affect the Government. Well, any analysis of the
documentation that Ms Dyson has will show that it was, in fact, the council itself that
was facing significant uncertainty about the interest rates that it  might have to pay on
lending that existed pre -earthquake, and it knew that it had some expenses that were
coming. It has been long established that there is a cooperative arrangement between the
Government and local bodies. It is roughly a 60:40 split on horizontal infrastructure, but
no one knew exactly what the problem was.
So I am pleased that the Opposition has said that the Stronger Christchurch
Infrastructure Rebuild Team is doing a good job. I believe that it is.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Always has.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I believe that it is—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: It’s nothing to do with you.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: —and I am very pleased that I was the Minister who
negotiated that particular body’s coming together. Actually, under the structure, Mr
Cosgrove, for your information —which you should have known because it has been
provided to you—there is an alliance board, there is a governance group, and, over and
above that, there is the Minister, quite simply. So what we have is an Opposition—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: That’s why they’re getting things done and you’re not.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: —and, particularly, Opposition MPs who know t hat
they are not going to win their seats back and are now trying to create an environment
that, essentially, is based on mistruths. It was unreasonable for the city council to have
to go through an audit process in the uncertain environment that it was in , and the
council unanimously voted to take that particular course of action. There was no
direction from the Crown for it to do so.
The next point was the suggestion that the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority itself is an organisation that is taki ng up too much of the Government
resource and that it should, in fact, start to pare itself back. So there you have a totally
contradictory argument right from the start: “It is not doing enough. Let’s not make it
do any more.” But can I point out that its  current budget is about three -quarters of 1
percent of the Government’s total spend in Christchurch and it is about one -quarter of 1
19062 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
percent of the expected cost of Christchurch across all sectors. So I think it is doing a
very good job through the manage ment of recovery programmes, of community
engagement, of working through the council where it has got difficulties, etc., etc.
Then there was this issue about housing, raised by our friend Mr O’Rourke. I note
that if you do not want to know the truth in a ny circumstance, do not hang around to
listen to it, and that would be a doctrine that is clearly taken up by the last two speakers
in this debate. It is unfortunate that when we get to factual information, it gets in the
road of the story, so they take off. Well, right now, in this instant, in this Chamber, I am
able to show that there are 1,182 houses in Christchurch City for rent, and that half of
those—half of those—are being rented out for less than half the rent that Mr O’Rourke
was talking about a fe w minutes ago. So there you have another construct, a mistruth,
being thrown into the Committee, etc., etc.
The Government has engaged in quite a significant amount of activity in trying to
alleviate some housing issues in Christchurch. In the end it will  be the build that gets
there. Part of that is the Land Use Recovery Plan, but a huge part of it is the work that
the Earthquake Commission is doing to get people back in their houses, and then there
is the work that the Hon Dr Nick Smith has undertaken wi th the housing accord; the
temporary villages at New Brighton and Linwood and in Kaiapoi; the temporary
accommodation at Rangers Park, which will eventually come on to the market for sale;
and the opportunities that he is currently pursuing out at Awatea, where there will also
be several hundred affordable houses built. But, in addition to that, 700 new State
houses will be built in Christchurch over the next 2 years, and 5,000 State houses will
be reoccupied as Housing New Zealand brings them back up to a much higher standard
than they were before for the occupants.
In addition, of course, there is the problem of the Christchurch City Council always
railing against housing issues, with the Labour members on that council, particularly,
getting on their high  horse, but, in fact, the Labour chairman of the housing committee
is doing absolutely nothing. A mere five houses have been repaired, I understand, over
the last 4 years out of the 250 that the council has got. It is unbelievable.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Where’s the EQC money?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Of course, the Earthquake Commission has paid out.
The commission has paid the council nearly $30 million so far —$30 million for five
repairs. That is a really, really good result! It is one that Labour would, of course, be
impressed by, but I think it is utterly pathetic.
Mr O’Rourke talked about the thousands of people living in Christchurch in broken
homes in cold circumstances. Over the last few winters we have partnered with NGOs
and we have had our own programmes running where we look for people who might be
in difficult circumstances where that has not been reported. This year there has been,
with the Wider Earthquake Communities Action Network, what I think is a very good
programme. It calls them the lost 900. It went out to see who they were. It thought that
there might be 900 houses out there in trouble. It found a much, much lesser number,
where there were some instances of trouble, and so all of those are being dealt with.
Across the whole time, around 20,000 heat appliances have been put into Christchurch
homes, no questions asked —“If you are cold, you get warm with this new heating
appliance.”
Then the issue of flooding was raised by Mr O’Rourke —“Mr Doom and Gloom” —
over her e. Unbelievable comments were made about that. Well, I can say to this
Committee that on 5 March this year the Government was in town —the Prime Minister,
other Ministers like Nicky Wagner, etc., and I were saying to the council: “We want to
help. What do we do?”. And, I have to say, we are still waiting for the full details. Last
week we got the papers asking us to extend the temporary accommodation assistance
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19063
available to these people. We have done it. And that really also gives the lie to a lot of
what Mr  O’Rourke was saying because we do have temporary accommodation
assistance at very, very good levels available to everybody, regardless of income.
Then there is the Canterbury Earthquake Temporary Accommodation Service —
CETAS. There is the residential serv ice, etc., etc. It goes on and on —good things
happening as Canterbury works itself to get itself out of a difficult circumstance.
Then we come to the beauty of them all. Clayton Cosgrove, having railed for the last
4 years about all sorts of things—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: “The beauty”? I wouldn’t call Clayton a beauty.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, I am the only one who sees it—I am the only one
who sees it. But it is, let me say, exceptionally ironic in my expression. He has railed for
the last 4 years on all sorts of issues. He has never once come to my office with a
constituent issue that bore any resemblance to the public position that he was taking —
not one in 4 years. Then we come to the issues. He is saying that there are 10,000
people out —[Interruption] See? Those members do not like it. I tell you what, when
you are losing, you struggle —when you are losing, you struggle. He is saying that
10,000 people want to go to court because, I think his term was, they had outstanding
claims. Well, a claim is outstanding until the keys are handed over to the occupant —a
claim is outstanding until the keys are handed to an occupant.
I have got some figures in my pocket here that come from some of the houses that
are being built in Christchur ch at the moment, and there are hundreds that are in that
category—almost ready to hand over—there are thousands in the process of being built,
and there are thousands where people are making choices about what they have in their
plans. It is not unusual w here someone is getting a new house built that they might say:
“Well, hold on. You’re up for this much. If we put this extra in, can we have an extra
bedroom? Can we have an en suite? Can we have a flasher kitchen?”, or whatever. Why
would they not? I thin k it is a good thing. To say that there are 10,000 people out there
who have outstanding claims and who are waiting to go to court is a gross exaggeration.
The numbers of people who are going to the courts are exceptionally low, and it is not
because they do not get a hearing; the courts have bent over backwards to create a
bench. There have, in fact, been only 270 cases out of all those thousands —170,000
damaged homes—that have gone to court with some application. Many of those have
been settled.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Transport
DAVID BENNETT (Chairperson of the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee): It is a pleasure to speak on Vote Transport. This is one of the good news
stories that we will be promoting during the campaign. Last weekend the Minister made
another announcement in regard to transport around regional State highway projects.
That is something of interest to many New Zealanders and something that will continue
to build a stronger economy for our country going forward. It is all about working for
New Zealand. It is a good news story in transport for our communities. Not only have
we got th e roads of national significance, which are in the predominantly urban
environments, but they are very successful roads. I know in the Waikato that we look
forward to the roads of national significance continuing. Our danger is that if there is a
change of Government those roads will not progress. I see the Greens smiling over there
because they know that they do not want to build those roads in Hamilton. That would
be a great shame for our region, which has waited 30 years to get the opportunity to
build that road.
19064 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
We all know that in transport the Greens lead the policy of the Opposition. The
Labour Party is a little puppy dog really —just coming along and doing what the Green
Party says. Whatever Labour members say in this area is to be taken with a grain  of salt
because they cannot deliver on it. If they ever did get near the Treasury benches with,
say, 30 percent of the vote and the Greens at 15 percent, then we know who would be
the Minister of Transport and we know who would be running the transport portfolio.
When we look at the roads of national significance, they are huge projects and they
are delivering major economic benefits for New Zealand going forward. But we also
often hear of regional funding and we often hear of arguments that there is not enough
spent in the regions. That is simply not the case. The regions get a huge amount of the
transport budget that is spent each year. Not only is there investment in local road
maintenance, which translates to between about $550 million to $595 million per year
over the next 4 years, there are also those local road improvements, which go from $190
million to $250 million over those 4 years. Then we have the R funds, which is the $360
million that has already been announced, and then the accelerated regio nal roading
programme that was announced this weekend of another $212 million for our regions.
Those projects that were identified in the $212 million were significant projects in
different parts of the country. I am going to leave it to my good colleague  from the
north to explain some of those. I know that he has been advocating hard for some of
those projects. It is good to see that they have come forward for the two members from
up north who have done such a great job in advocating for transport projects.
We also have significant funding in walking and cycling and public transport. We
will hear from the Labour and Green parties that there is no money going into public
transport and all of these things —simply incorrect again. There is huge money going
into public transport —$350 million in the Government policy statement for the year
coming, and going forward into 2017 -18, and that rises to $410 million. That is a
significant investment in public transport, contrary to what those other parties will say.
We have a balanced approach to transport spending. We take into account the needs
of the communities around road, rail, and other infrastructure. We look at what is in the
essence of building economic growth and something that will deliver on a day -to-day
basis as well. We do not go out there and promise pie -in-the-sky events, which the
Green Party will do. It has now been overtaken by New Zealand First, which wants
passenger rail from every town or city in New Zealand basically, and by the Labour
Party, which is stagnant in its transport policy and has no idea what is going on.
We give real and constructive policy that delivers real and constructive results to our
communities. It is not false promises. It is not leading people down garden paths that
have no sense of reality or sense of being able to be delivered. We deliver real promises
in real time for real New Zealanders. That is the difference when it comes to transport
funding that New Zealanders will see as we go through this election process. Just to
recap: this is a Government that has invested heavily in transport. It has invested in a
balanced way that has taken into account all the different modes of transport and
delivered for them. Through rail with our KiwiRail—

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Today the Government raised the petrol tax yet
again. The reason it has had to raise the petrol tax is that there has been a deficit in the
money that is coming into the National Land Transport Fund b ecause New Zealanders
are actually driving less. They have been driving less for 7 consecutive years now.
There is not enough money coming in to spend on what the National Government
wanted to make a priority.
When the National Government came in, I rememb er it very clearly, because I was
working as a transportation consultant for the New Zealand Transport Agency. I
remember being there in 2008 when the people working at the New Zealand Transport
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19065
Agency, who are experts in this, were saying it was very, ver y disturbing because the
National Government was coming in and wanting to prioritise a few very expensive
motorways that simply did not make economic sense. They had not been funded for
precisely that reason. So the National Party went ahead —it was in Government—and it
decided to try to build a few of these big expensive motorway projects that carry a very
small percentage of daily vehicle trips, at great expense. It is spending the largest share
of the transport budget over 10 years on these motorway proje cts. It is going to be $12
billion to $14 billion on just a few projects that carry less than 4 percent of daily vehicle
trips. So the motorways are not going to improve the commute of the vast majority of
New Zealanders. They are not even going to affect most of the freight that is being
moved around the country.
At the same time, road use has been declining. It has been declining for a number of
reasons, around all the rich countries. One of the reasons is higher petrol prices. As
petrol prices go up, peo ple look for alternatives. Of course, in New Zealand they do not
have many alternatives because successive Governments have built a very unbalanced
transport system. Unlike comparable rich countries, we do not have the same good
public transport options —good buses and trains —and safe walking and cycling that
they have in other countries.
As petrol prices go up—and now the Government is putting up the petrol tax, so that
will mean petrol is even more expensive —road use does decline. It has been declining
for 7 years now. So the Government had the option of perhaps revisiting its transport
projects, which it did not. Because there was not enough money in the transport budget
to pay for the Government’s crazy motorway promises, and to also do the standard
upkeep that was needed on our regional roads, the maintenance that was needed around
the country, the Government was then forced to put up the petrol tax, firstly, and that is
what it is doing. It is also now using the money from asset sales to pay for projects  in
the regions. Some of these road projects in the regions might be of very high value. I do
not know because the economic assessment is not available, really, on the website. I did
see one project that has a benefit-cost ratio of 0.5, which means that it  is not worth even
half the cost of building it. Hopefully, some of the other ones are very good projects that
are going to improve road safety. The Green Party absolutely supports spending on our
regional roads and putting more money into road maintenance , in particular, and safety
upgrades.
Now the Government has announced this regional package, which apparently has
been chosen —just like the roads of national significance —entirely by focus groups.
That is simply not a responsible way to handle the transpo rt budget. It is not one that is
going to have long-term economic benefits for New Zealand. Although the Green Party
does support looking after our regional roads, and in fact getting better use out of our
existing roads —and we can do that at low cost —we d o not support this irrational,
irresponsible, pork barrel politics approach to prioritising transport projects. That is
clearly what the National Government has done.
It is the perfect time to be investing in smart alternatives. That is what New Zealand
is missing. All across the country it makes sense to invest in safe walking and cycling
facilities so our kids can walk and cycle to school. That reduces congestion, reduces the
transport bill, and it frees up the roads for those who need to drive. In our la rger cities it
makes sense to invest in better buses and trains so that more New Zealanders have the
option of getting to work without having to pay a high petrol bill and so they can talk on
the phone and get some work done, instead of just sitting there behind the wheel stuck
in traffic. That is the best way to deal with congestion. That is a smart, modern, green
approach that countries all across the world have successfully implemented. We want to
see more choices for New Zealanders here. That is what the Green Party is campaigning
19066 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
for. It is not unrealistic, is it entirely achievable, and it is really a shame that National is
wasting this opportunity.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am very  pleased to take a call in this
particular debate on Vote Transport. I wonder whether the member Julie Anne Genter
can explain to the children in Te Kao how they will make it to school in Kaitāia. It is
about a 1 -hour one-way trip. So what are we going to do with them? I would hazard a
guess that if the member actually went—I do not know—outside the city, she might find
that the rest of New Zealand has a contrary view about what is important in terms of
roading infrastructure. This Government actually under stands that, and that is why this
Government has made a substantial and significant contribution to roading and transport
throughout its entire term.
Another point that was raised by the Green speaker was the fact that there is less
revenue being gathered  in terms of petrol excise, and so on and so forth. There are a
number of reasons for that, of course, and a couple of good ones are that this
Government has invested in substantial improvements in roads, and therefore the roads
are improved and fuel efficiencies are established as a result of that. So what we are also
seeing is the benefit of the very thing that the Greens would knock back —that there is
greater efficiency in the roading network. After decades of underspend, what we are
now doing is actually catching up on a lot of that.
A good example of how successful this Government’s approach has been is the very
area that the Opposition members like to beat up against, and that is the regions. They
are saying: “Oh, the regions have been left out. They’ ve been forgotten.” Well, I will
speak to you from a region that is growing at 7.4 percent year -on-year growth, from a
region that has had six successive quarters —and thank you, Mr Mitchell from Rodney,
my partnering MP. He is just south of me—“South Northland”, I like to sometimes refer
to it as. There are six successive quarters of growth. We have business confidence up
and unemployment down. Although Hone and “Sideshow Bob” up there are sort of—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! The member must use a
member’s full name or title, not just their first name.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Certainly, Mr Chairman. Hone Harawira from the Mana —well, I am
not sure whether it is the Mana -Internet-German party. I am not su re what it is called.
Anyway, that is the sideshow that is the far north. The fact is that people like them will
stand up there and protest against the idea of —I do not know —the gas and oil
exploration and the billions of dollars of revenue that will make its way into New
Zealand, into the community, as a result of that. But, although they will stand there and
vote against every initiative of this Government that looks to grow the economy, to
invest in roading infrastructure, to invest in ultra -fast broadba nd, and to invest in the
things that make an economy worth engaging in and worth investing in from a business
perspective, this Government is getting on with business.
Let us just have a look at what that looks like in terms of Northland. We have a
primary growth initiative under way. We have a regional growth study under way. We
have that gas and oil exploration, but also we have onshore mineral exploration under
way. We have a Primary Growth Partnership in avocadoes in the far north, looking to
quadruple returns in that particular area, and an aquaculture strategy that will see $300
million added to the New Zealand economy and 700 jobs in the region over the next 10
to 15 years. We are working on the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act / Maori Land Act to
ensure that the productivity of that land can be better realised, to return productivity and
jobs to those who most need it in these more vulnerable communities.
Look at the work that is going on with Treaty settlements. This Government has
actually got on with the  job that the former Labour Government spent about 9 years
talking about and doing not much with.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19067

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Oh, all that member’s own work—all that member’s own work.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, if the member David Clark would like to come to the far north,
I would be very, very pleased to host him in the far north. Perhaps we could go around
and have a talk to a few of those —what spokesmanship does he have? He has small
business or something, does he not? Actually, that would be a great area. Let us book
that in. Let us make that a bit of a bromance date sort of situation there, Mr Clark. Come
on up and see what is happening at the other end of the country, where, of course, the
sun shines for about 18 hours of the day. I would be pleased to host the member.
But, in all seriousness, in the draft Government policy statement that was recently
announced we are looking at $360 million of additional contestable funding, $212
million going into 14 specific projects, and almost $1 billio n a year of investment in
regional roads. That is a substantial investment, and the Pūhoi to Wellsford motorway,
the fast tracking of that, has said to everyone in Northland that Labour and the Greens
would get rid of it but that this Government believes i n Northland and believes in the
economy, and invests in it and continues to invest in it.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: As the
Associate Minister of Transport I think it is really important for us to understand that
the building of infrastructure certainly has an issue from an economic development and
a movement of people perspective. I think it is also very important to understand th at
good roads mean better road safety. The delegation I have as Associate Minister of
Transport is for road safety, and it is with that in mind that I want to talk about some of
the announcements that have been made both through the Budget and, in particul ar, a
most recent announcement by the Government that it intends to improve the regional
roading network with extra funds from the Future Investment Fund.
When we came to office, it is fair to say that after some reductions in the 1980s and
1990s the road  toll effectively flat -lined. It was stubbornly stuck at around 400 per
annum. It is true that road vehicle kilometres travelled increased in that period, but we
were making no significant inroads into the road toll. I do not think there is a family in
this country that has not been affected by the trauma of serious injury or death on our
roads. So it was very pleasing to see that when the Safer Journeys Action Plan was
introduced and the 2 -year safety strategy under the previous transport Minister, Steven
Joyce, was implemented, the effect was nearly immediate.
Last year, I am pleased to report, we had the lowest road toll in this country since
1950. If one uses the measure of vehicle kilometres travelled, it would have been one -
sixth of the road toll of 6 3 years ago. So we are making progress, but I think it is
important to reflect on what happens next. The 2 -year action plan has an engineering
aspect to it, recognising that human beings, as we are, will make mistakes on the road,
and the important thing t hrough Budget 2014 is to ensure that the engineering of those
roads is as good as we can afford and that drivers purchase vehicles that are as safe as
we can afford.
I think we have a bit of a mind -set issue in this country around road safety in that we
tend to tolerate or accept that there is going to be a level of death or injury on our roads,
and the idea is to try to minimise that. I want to challenge that view. I think that we can,
through good roading engineering, good technology with our cars, and i ntelligent
transport systems—which are not just things of the future but are available today, in our
lifetime—set a goal of zero for car-to-car road collisions. There are already technologies
available that will prevent drift from one lane to another, and there is adaptive cruise
control that will slow a car down automatically if the car in front is slowing down. I am
about to make some announcements around electronic stability control, or ESC, to
ensure that over the next few years it becomes mandatory for all cars to have it.
19068 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
The Minister of Transport, Gerry Brownlee, has taken a test drive in California in a
virtual driverless car. He, of course, released the intelligent transport systems map,
which sets out what those technologies could be both now and in the future. I think
there is a very, very real likelihood that in the not too distant future we will be able to
say that on our roads in New Zealand the goal is zero for car-to-car collisions.
It is a different thing when one introduces the issue of cycle, motorcycle, and tr uck
safety into the discussion, but I am also pleased to report that the Ministry of Transport
is looking at, and investing in —thanks to Budget 2014 —significant investments in safe
walking, safe cycling, and strategies in combination with ACC to improve mo torcycle
safety. There has been plenty of work going on, including in the technology area, to
improve truck safety. Of course, the introduction of very large trucks has reduced the
number of truck journeys taken and made our economic performance more productive. I
think there are very good strategies at work, but I am disappointed to note that in the
first 6 months of this year we have backslid slightly on our road toll. I hope we are able
to make that up before the end of this year.
The mistakes we are ma king on our roads are the same: distraction, fatigue, not
wearing seatbelts, speed, drugs, and alcohol. We know what causes death and injury on
our roads, and we need to continue to redouble our efforts. I think the engineering, cycle
safety, and road tran sport safety elements of this Budget go a significant way toward
achieving that goal.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I just briefly want to take a call to say that
it is telling in this Par liament that we have a situation where transport was the most
talked about topic of the weekend, and one of the big funding boosts in the Budget, and
there has been not a single call from the Labour Party on it. The Minister of Transport,
Gerry Brownlee, a nd Associate Minister of Transport, Michael Woodhouse, know that
this country requires investment in transport, and this Government is doing that.
As an Auckland member of the National Party, I am very proud of the fact that this
Government has legislated for significant funds towards boosting and speeding up some
important projects in our region. You would know very well, in fact, Mr Chairman, that
the southern motorway in Auckland is in desperate need of widening. This Government
is delivering on that. Th e Committee will also know that State Highway 20A to the
airport needs to be upgraded.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Your constituents are wanting public transport, and they’re not
getting any.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Guess what, Mr Twyford —this Gov ernment is delivering.
Aucklanders also know that where State Highway 18 meets State Highway 1,
significant works are going on and are very much required. Labour never delivered;
National is delivering.
At the weekend Gerry Brownlee and the Prime Minister announced significant
funding for the rest of New Zealand as well —much-needed funding to progress
important transport projects that New Zealanders in the regions know are required and
know that National is delivering. We are working for New Zealanders. Lab our has had
nothing to say on transport. I am very keen to hear from the transport Minister, Gerry
Brownlee, so I will let him have a go now.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Economic Development and Employment

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: When we were looking
at the estimates for Vote Economic Development and Employment, we learnt a very
interesting piece of information: that to keep the wheels whirring, in the mind of the
Minister for Economic Development, it requires 56 spin doctors —56 s pin doctors.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19069
Twenty of them are devoted to Mr Joyce alone —20 of them are devoted to Mr Joyce
alone, making sure that the spin keeps on going. My assessment is that it took the best
and the brightest of the 56 spin doctors at the Ministry of Business, Innov ation and
Employment to come up with the lines to try to explain why it was that hundreds of
thousands of dollars were to be spent on the Motu Bridge, only for the dynamite to
come along and for it to be blown sky -high within a couple of years to build ano ther
road and another bridge across there. That is what they came up with. So here is the
line. The line from Gerry Brownlee is that it was OK to build a bridge and then blow it
up a couple of years later because it would deliver “instant dividends”. That was the
line—56 spin doctors at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, and
they came up with “instant dividends”.
Well, I challenge the Minister for Economic Development to tell me in the
Committee today whether or not he could assure New Zea landers that the instant
dividends made up for the hundreds of thousands of dollars that have been spent on the
“Bridge to Obsolescence” —the Motu Bridge. He cannot guarantee that, because it is a
terrible, terrible mess that the National Party has made, tr ying to indulge in a bit of
election year pork-barrel politics and bringing up these ideas that, remember, had been
rejected by the Government. The Government had sent them away. It had said: “No,
that’s not part of it.” But it comes back to New Zealanders  and says this is the regional
economic plan. This is the turbocharging of the regions: a bridge that has already been
built and that Meng Foon, the Mayor of Gisborne, said was pouring money down the
drain. Steven Joyce challenged me on that quote today. I t is right there in black and
white from Meng Foon—pouring money down the drain.
Bear in mind that this is the hallmark of this Government’s approach to regional
economic development. This decision about a bridge to be blown up and replaced by
another bridge came in the middle of a consultation process between the New Zealand
Transport Agency and the Gisborne District Council about what the important roading
developments for economic development were. What is the point, Minister, in
consulting with a regio n about its economic development when you come to your
National Party conference and you just make the announcement anyway? That is the
hallmark of this National Government when it comes to regional economic
development—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Arrogant.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: —arrogant and out of touch. It is not actually engaging
with the regions. It is wandering around claiming there are silver bullets for the
economy in oil and gas: “That will be the answer. Everyone get on board, every region .
It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t suit you.” That is not an approach to regional economic
development that is going to work. An approach to regional economic development that
is going to work is actually getting alongside regions and industries to help the m grow
sustainable jobs. That is the Labour Party’s plan in regional economic development. We
have already put out our economic upgrade, and it is based around the three i’s:
innovation, industry, and investment. They will be the core: investing in these r egions
and investing in those industries to make sure they can thrive.
We have already talked about forestry. Forestry is a good example of where this
Government has taken its eye off the ball. There have been hundreds and hundreds of
job losses in the fo restry sector under this Minister’s watch, and there is no plan to deal
with that. Forestry needs an upgrade. It needs some certainty about the development of
skills. It needs the infrastructure from forestry roads. That is what the Gisborne District

items.speaker: Council wanted to talk to the Government about
items.text: how it was going to upgrade the
forestry roads. But, no, instead Steven Joyce knows best —Steven Joyce knows best.
That is the National Government’s economic development strategy: one man who
19070 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
knows better than anybody else and who can dictate to regions. Well, that is simply not
good enough.
This vote we are looking at today covers both economic development and
employment. I want to mention something about employment and, in particular, the
complacency of the Natio nal Government when it comes to unemployment in certain
communities. We have this great slogan of “working for New Zealand”. Well, it is not
working for New Zealand when nearly a third of young Pasifika women are
unemployed. It is not working for New Zeala nd when 75,000 15 to 24-year-olds are not
in education, employment, or training. That is the future of New Zealand. I can
guarantee this to New Zealanders: the next Labour Government will make it an absolute
priority that every person who leaves school is going into work or further education and
training. That is our absolute, cast -iron commitment, and it is where this Government is
letting down the next generation of New Zealanders.
It is all very well to stand up in the House, as Mr English and Mr Joyce do, and
trumpet the great economic indicators that are going to show that the economy is
improving. Well, it is pretty hard to argue with somebody who has made 100 job
applications—like the person who came into my office the other day —and cannot get a
job that the latest GDP statistics are something great for them. It is quite hard to argue
with a family that is struggling to pay its bills that there is a new economic indicator that
is going to be good for them. A new economic indicator will not pay a new b ill for the
car when it comes in and you have not got the money to pay the mechanic. That is the
reality for many New Zealanders —that they are struggling to make ends meet and that
wages are not keeping up with their increasing cost of living, whatever sta tistics the
Minister might want to throw around.
When we look at those communities —Pasifika, Māori, young people, and certain
regions of New Zealand —this Government is not working for them. This National
Government is working for its mates. It is focused on the economic indicators, and not
on the outcomes in the regions or the outcomes for young people across New Zealand.
The Labour Party will have a comprehensive plan that we will be taking to the people of
New Zealand to ensure that every young person ge ts those opportunities and that we
encourage development in our regions.
I want to pay tribute to my colleague Dr David Clark, the MP for Dunedin North, for
the campaign that he has run on the Invermay Agricultural Centre, because that sums up
a major issue for this Government. It stands by and it washes its hands of the problems
that are happening in the regions. For Dunedin and for Otago, that region has been
struggling with a loss of manufacturing capability. That is another result of the
Government taki ng its eye off the ball when it comes to procurement policy. So jobs
went at Hillside, and the economy in the Otago region has struggled and those jobs have
been lost. But the one thing that those people in the Otago region said to me when I
went down ther e was that they have got that commitment around research —they have
got the university. They can leverage off that; that is where a Crown research institute
comes in. Steven Joyce sits there and lets the jobs at Invermay disappear, despite the
fact that all the evidence shows that that kind of work will flourish and the New Zealand
economy will flourish with the kind of work taking place at Invermay. We need proper
regional development that builds on the strengths of regions like Otago, and builds on
something like the Invermay programme.
Instead, what we have from the National Government is a belief that the recovery
from the earthquake in Christchurch is enough to sustain those statistics. It looks good.
Unemployment is down in the South Island, says Mr Jo yce. Well, of course it is,
because we are recovering from one of the largest disasters of all time, but that is not a
sustainable economic development plan. A sustainable economic development plan
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19071
should be about creating good and decent jobs right across  New Zealand by working
with industries like forestry, like manufacturing, and like information and
communications technology to help create those jobs. The Government must be a
partner in that, not a bystander, and not sitting there coming up with silly p ork-barrel
politics 3 months out from an election to try to make itself feel better. That is not an
economic plan.
In these estimates we went looking for the National Government’s plan. Steven
Joyce will get up in a moment and he will talk about the nice glossy document that he
has. Well, Mr Joyce, it is not good enough. The people in the regions of New Zealand
are not impressed by a glossy Business Growth Agenda document. What they are
looking for is the commitment of the party in Government to help creat e jobs, to be a
partner in their community, to support the industries that need support, and to provide
infrastructure that will actually add to jobs—not to come up with silly roading projects.
This particular piece of the estimates, Vote Economic Develop ment and
Employment, is a huge, huge disappointment. It does not address the issue of creating
jobs. This complacent Government leaves 75,000 young people not in work,
employment, or training and more than 157,000 people out of work. New Zealand needs
a Government with a policy for full employment, and that is the Labour Party’s policy.
John Key thinks it is too difficult to get to. He says we will have to wait for 4 percent
further down the track. That is not good enough. If New Zealanders can work, they
should be able to work. We need to ensure that we are providing the skills and the
training to give people the opportunity to take up jobs in the new economy. We have not
seen that from this Government; we will see that from a Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: With the greatest
respect to Mr Grant Robertson, his argument is, as always, a mile wide and an inch
deep. He actually does  not do any work. He criticises the Government for not working
for New Zealand, yet he still has not actually got off his chuff and read the Business
Growth Agenda at all, which could never be described as a Labour Party - like glossy
document, because it is written in a font that is too small for Grant to be able to read.
That is the challenge for him. He has not done any work and his party has not done any
work over the last 5 years, and now they are turning up with some platitudes.
He says that Labour wi ll have a full employment plan. Well, let us go back a little
bit. Just at the beginning of the global financial crisis, Labour’s numbers were already
worse than the numbers that we have got now, as the recovery continues. He brings up
Dunedin. Well, with the greatest respect, Dunedin’s unemployment rate —currently, the
Otago unemployment rate is 4.6 percent. It is apparently a disaster —4.6 percent is a
disaster, according to Mr Robertson. Well, he should go down there. He should go back
to where he came from. I think the last time he went back there, he tried to run a student
protest when I was there, and he was heard to lament that the students did not turn up —
the students did not turn up. The world has moved on since Grant was there. Well, I tell
you, Mr R obertson, the world has moved on from your view of economics. The world
has moved on to understand that things do change over time.
In the case of Otago University and Otago research, the good news is that there is a
lot more money going in. The Health Res earch Council has just given the university the
biggest amount of research money that it has ever had in one year. We have introduced
two new centres of research excellence in Dunedin. There is lots of additional
investment going into that region.
The difficulty I have with Mr Robertson’s approach —in fact, with the whole Labour
Party’s approach—is that his view is that nothing should change. It is completely what
could be described only as preservational economics, which is that nothing should ever
change—no matter whether the world has changed and things need to be done, nothing
19072 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
should change. Labour members have actually taken it even further. They have gone to
resuscitation economics, where they now propose, as their big economic proposal, to
bring back the moa. I think that is at least innovative, which is more than we can say for
the last 6 years of Labour Party policy. It at least has the merit of being something that
is new and not being tired rhetoric. But I hate to refer to that particular ex ample too
much because I think I need to point out to the member who raised it that Jurassic Park
was a movie, not a documentary. It was a movie and not a documentary, so, sadly for
the member’s idea, I think it falls apart about there. Nevertheless, he sh ould at least be
rewarded for coming up with it. I imagine he will get a promotion back to the front
bench on the strength of the moa resuscitation plan, but maybe it is something he will
have to wait for until after a certain election event coming up.
The other thing that Mr Robertson raised was the performance of young Māori and
Pasifika. I personally believe that this Government has a lot to be proud of in terms of
improving the training outcomes and study outcomes of young Māori and Pasifika.
Today bet ween 3,000 and 4,000 more young Māori people a year are studying at
university than when those guys were in Government in 2007, and there are 3,000 or
4,000 more young Pasifika. Their completion rates are improving dramatically —they
are not there yet, but improving dramatically —from where they were when that lot
disgracefully left them when they left office. Also, we have many more initiatives like
the Youth Guarantee, like the Māori and Pasifika trades training initiatives, and like the
trades academies, which are lifting the skill levels of young people of all ethnicities and
ensuring they have the opportunity to participate in this recovery. The recovery, by the
way, has generated 84,000 more jobs in the last 12 months —84,000 more jobs. What is
going on there?
The other thing that Mr Robertson was talking about was that somehow the roading
projects announced at the weekend constituted the whole regional development strategy
of the Government. Well, it is one of those things where you create a straw person  and
then you knock it over. In Mr Robertson’s case, that is something he does all too
regularly. He does it all too regularly, and yet it is all rubbish.
Actually, this Government has a comprehensive economic development strategy. I
went through some of i t in the House this afternoon. The limitation of time stopped me
going through all the rest of it. I am happy to add a little bit more for members at the
moment because it is really important. Our strategy is around providing opportunities
for New Zealand companies to be more competitive, wherever they are and in
whichever region. Different regions need different things. This Government is working
with every region, and that is being well received by the local councils, including in
Gisborne. With the great est respect to Mr Robertson, if he wants to make the case that
the Motu Bridge should stay that way for ever, then I invite him to go to Gisborne and
say that. Actually, nobody believes that. It is a one-lane bridge. It is a one-lane bridge—

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: They’ll never see him again.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: They would never see him again —that would be the reality
of it. Anyway, there is a whole range of things.
In the innovation space, there is the Primary Growth Partnership a nd research and
development funding through Callaghan Innovation —miles more than was ever done
under Labour. Now Labour members are saying they will have an innovation plan, and
that it is part of their economic upgrade. Well, first they have to explain wh y they did
not do very much at all during all the time they were in Government. They also have to
explain why the only policy they have announced in the last 6 years —nine separate
times—is their research and development tax credits, which have been well ov ertaken
by time. They need something new.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19073
Also, in the skills space, they are going to do all these things about skills, but so far
the only thing they have said in that space —the only thing they have said —is that they
are going to bring back some of the adult and community education funding that was
withdrawn in 2010, which was the stuff that could be described as hobby courses. So
the big innovation for Labour is that it is going to bring back the hobby courses. Good
on Labour—that is the skills space.
Meanwhile, we are doing the Youth Guarantee, the New Zealand Apprenticeships,
the Māori and Pasifika trades training, the trades academies —all these innovations,
including working with the Mayors Taskforce for Jobs and all these things —and the
Labour Party is stuck in 2008, once again not having done the work. But it is worse than
that. It is worse than that because Labour says it will get alongside the regions. Well,
explain to me, New Zealand Labour Party and your mates in the Greens, how a carbon
price a t five times the world price would ever constitute getting alongside New
Zealand’s regions. I hope you promote that strongly, both of you, in the election
campaign. I know Labour has been very quiet so far —neither confirm nor deny —but
that is the Green Party’s policy and Labour has not backed away from it. Labour has not
come out and said it will not support that, and the regions are noticing.
The second one is having a capital gains tax on every productive business and farm
in this country, supported by b oth of those parties. They say it is all about discouraging
investment in property and encouraging investment in businesses. Well, how do they
explain the fact that it is a tax on 100 percent of businesses and only about a third of
housing? How does that s imple explanation work? That is the second area that the
regions will be looking at and going: “I don’t think so.”
Then there is the small matter of trade, which, of course, is hugely important to our
export-focused regions and one of the reasons they are  doing well at the moment. Well,
in the trade space, the Labour Party says: “Oh, we’re not sure about the TPP. Don’t
know whether we’ll do that.” The Greens are flat out against it. The regions notice that
too.
And then there is the small matter of the da iry industry and oil and gas. They are not
the whole story of our regions, but they are significant in some regions, so let us have a
look at them. Anti - irrigation and water storage; anti -dairy, in fact; anti - oil and gas;
and anti any form of internati onal investment. Apart from that, they are really in favour
of the regions. So apart from the capital gains tax, the carbon price, the wind -blown
timber on the West Coast, the rolling back of the Resource Management Act reforms,
trade, investment, oil and gas—I think that is everything, but there might be more.
Apart from all of those things, they are well behind the regions. They are all supporting
the regions apart from all of those reasonably crucial things that most of regional New
Zealand is noticing.

items.speaker: Here is the good news
items.text: this Government is not going to do any of those things. Oh,
there is another one: the high water -resource levies that are being promoted by the
Greens and the Labour Party. They are also not on the policy list for this Government.
This Government has 350 separate initiatives in innovation, in skills, in opening up
markets for our exporters, in providing capital, and, yes, in infrastructure, which is very,
very important.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: As we look
at the economic development estimates for this Government, I think we can be very
encouraged to see a very proactive plan that is going to make a huge difference for this
country and, in particular, the regions. We know, as the Minister for Economic
Development has reported today, that the regions have led New Zealand out of the
global financial crisis and into a very strong recovery. We want to see that continue. We
want to see a sustainable growth path for New Zealand’s economies and our regions.
19074 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment is tasked with that sort of
work. Since its formation in July 2012 it has, according to its statement of intent for
2013 to 2016, “con solidated related business -facing functions and created new
opportunities for delivering policies and services to advance New Zealand’s prosperity
and wellbeing.” I believe that it is doing a great job on that, and I believe that this
Budget is investing n ot only money but the right sort of thinking into enhancing New
Zealand’s success not only domestically but globally.
We all understand that we live in a global environment that is highly competitive,
where innovation is absolutely essential. This Governm ent has been building the
innovative base, the work base, of this country very, very significantly. It is critical to
our country’s competitiveness in a global economy that is crowded with goods and
services. If we are going to enjoy the First World lifest yle that we have been used to in
decades past and that we feel is our right as New Zealanders, then it is very obvious that
we have to continue to earn that First World income. That does not come about by just
doing the same thing year after year after yea r. We have to keep that edge. We have to
keep innovating. We have to develop businesses that are looking all the time at how we
can improve our productivity, how we can improve the products that we do sell
internationally, and how we can improve our market place and space.
Callaghan Innovation gives businesses a single front door to the innovation system. It
works in partnership with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, economic development
agencies, business incubators, universities, polytechnics, Crown rese arch institutes, the
venture capital community, and, of course, industry associations right throughout this
country. Callaghan Innovation, named after one of our leading scientific innovators, is
critical in the success of this nation, and it is something that I know that the Minister has
spent a huge amount of thinking time and work on in terms of developing. It connects
businesses with research organisations across the innovation system. It manages more
than $140 million a year in Government funding and g rants to support this innovation
and capability-building.
Innovation is a central driver of economic growth and development. Firms rely on
innovation and related investments to improve their competitive edge in a globalising
world with shorter product lif e cycles. Innovation has the potential to mitigate some of
the emerging problems related to health, energy, and the environment that are faced by
both richer and poorer countries. We have got to see that innovation is critical to the
modern way of life and  that through it we can not only improve the health and lifestyle
of people and bring people out of poverty and into production and employment but we
can receive premium prices for the products we sell on the international stage. It is all of
these things that I believe are very, very important to our country.
The previous Government seemed to think that a research and development tax credit
was going to do it all —that that was all that was needed, and that it was going to be the
biggest driver for innovat ion in the New Zealand economy. What we were concerned
about with that sort of thinking was that that tax credit could have been paid out on
standard operating expenditure that was recharacterised as research and development -
related expenditure —essentially being a cost to the Government for a research and
development purpose without any significant added research or development actually
occurring. So we would just be treading water without anything being achieved, with
the Government giving a benefit to companies that was essentially a handout.
Our approach has not been that. We have ensured that, especially in this Budget, we
are freeing up cash flow for innovation in a far more effective manner. Our goal is to
see research and development spend or investment be 1 percent of our GDP.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak in the current debate. It has been interesting to listen to t he Opposition
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19075
spokespeople speak about what they will do for provincial development. Let us just start
at the beginning and look at some of the facts. Something like 72 percent of the
country’s gross export earnings comes from our primary sector. It will c ome as a
surprise, I know, to the likes of Grant Robertson that these businesses and industries are
based out in the rural provinces and the small-town areas of New Zealand.
It will also come as a big surprise to the likes of Mr Robertson that those sector s,
particularly in areas such as Taranaki - King Country, where I come from, represent
about 95 percent of what the economic activity is in those areas. Let us just look at
Taranaki in terms of GDP per capita by region. Taranaki produces, per person, about
$560,000 in export earnings. Compared with most other areas of New Zealand, that is
substantially ahead. I will just ask the simple question: why is that? Well, it is because
over the last 7 or 8 years, particularly in the time of this Government, there h as been
massive development in the sector that produces the wealth —that is, obviously, the
dairy industry and also the oil and gas industry. Those are the areas, ironically, that our
colleagues on the other side of the Chamber, particularly in the Green Pa rty, have a
great aversion to. They are constantly saying that we need cleaner, smarter, and more
sustainable activities in the area.
Let us just look at what —[Interruption]. Well, OK, if that is a fact, why do we not
use some facts, and measure against th at? What the Green members are saying is that
industry that grows in non -rural areas is cleaner and smarter, yet, actually, our
agricultural sector, particularly our dairy industry, has the lowest carbon production of
