any dairy industry in the world. We ha ve the lowest carbon production of any industry.
In Taranaki, we have the cleanest water of any other agricultural sector in the world
where that activity takes place, and we have 22,000 kilometres of fencing and planting,
which the Green Party never touches on.
We have some of the smartest technology innovation —companies like Tru-Test and
C-Dax, which has invented a machine for measuring grass growth and the metabolisable
energy of the grass, so you know what you are growing and how much nutrient it uses
to grow it. We are world leaders in this area. At our processing end, we have some of
the most sophisticated, some of the largest, and some of the most efficient processes in
the world, which produce sophisticated, smart products like nutraceuticals and
pharmaceuticals.
Here is a question for the Greens and their Labour colleagues. Apparently, the
American company New Holland has developed a tractor that will run on hydrogen.
When did the Green Party last promote that? Yet we have a forecast of something lik e
200 billion extra people in the world who will need feeding by the year 2050, who are
going to have to have smart technology to feed them. What is the Green Party saying
about that? When did I hear about that innovation recently? When did they promote
that? They would not know about it. The real irony of those members’ debate is that
they have never been there, they do not know, they live in cities, but they throw stones
at those who are out there doing it.
So what is the alternative? The Minister in the chair, the Hon Steven Joyce, touched
on some of the alternatives that the Opposition has put up. It intends to introduce a
capital gains tax. It is going to introduce a methane tax on methane emissions from
animals. It is going to lift income tax. It is go ing to have a higher company tax. It is
going to put limits on livestock numbers. It is going to limit nitrate use. It is going to do
away with the 90 -day trial period in employment. It is going to do away with the
reforms that we have made to the Resource  Management Act. It is going to bring in
higher ACC charges. All of these things, according to Grant Robertson, are standing
alongside industry, helping industry to grow. Well, it will come as a big surprise to
someone like Mr Robertson, who lives entirely  within the beltway and never sets foot
19076 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
outside it, that industries require innovative, focused Government policy that allows
industry to get on. In fact, what industries want more than anything else is for the
Government to get out of their way, and to st and back and let them grow and do what
they are good at—and they are the best in the world—not put up further hurdles in front
of them. The Government has invested a lot of money.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call during the
Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill debate. I just want to focus on the fine job that
is being done by this Government around education and skills training. It is not an easy
part to get ri ght. When you look at the transitions between our compulsory education
and our tertiary education, it has always been a challenge. However, it would have to be
said that the National Government is a far better and far more trustworthy steward of the
nation’s economy and of managing this very, very challenging situation and location
within the education system.
Our Youth Guarantee scheme has proved to be very successful. It has been a difficult
area because some people learn far better in the workplace or i n the tertiary education
sector than they do in the compulsory education sector, and that is what this
Government has done. Any individual between the ages of 16 and 19 who wishes to
avail themselves of the opportunity can get tertiary education to level 3  for free. That is
a great step forward. Vocational pathways have been structured with the—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. We have a vote specifically on skills and employme nt, which comes under
Vote Tertiary Education, and the member is actually moving into that area now, when
this vote that we are discussing is economic development and employment. So I do not
know whether the member was intending to focus on the whole area of skills and
employment, which will come up shortly, or whether he has something else to say on
economic development. So I am just inviting the member to come back to the
substantive matter of Vote Economic Development and Employment.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: When we look at the development of 84,000 jobs in 2013, one does
certainly see how the Government’s agenda around training for skills and employment
is very appropriate. When you think about what contributes the most to the economy of
a country, it is very important that those people who come through our education system
present themselves to our employers as ready and fit for employment.
When you think of a country that is 4.5 million people in size, with a workforce to
support a First World economy, it is very important that those who are going through
our education system are fit for purpose. We have got to not just look at those people
who are fit for employment but also find ways to improve outcomes for all of our young
ones as they leave school, w hether they are European, Asian, Pasifika, or Māori. It is a
piece of work that has been done very successfully by this Government, and Budget
2014 keeps building on the progressions that have been made. It is with great pride and
confidence that we see that trades and skills are being promoted in such a way now that
they are truly recognised as contributing to economic development. It is so very, very
important.
When you look at what the Government has done, it has incentivised training in five
specific areas, and those specific areas are to do with economic development, especially
in construction, infrastructure, manufacturing, technology, and primary industries. It is
also very interesting to see that the Government is going one step further with a six -part
vocational pathway into employment, which is going to further contribute to the
nation’s economy, and that is in the creative industries. Effectively we can see that the
Government is very focused on ensuring that everybody lives up to their potential and
that economic development encompasses not just building bridges, building primary
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19077
industries, or increasing technology, but that it is also directly linked back to our
education system, whether it be early childhood education, the compulsory sector, or
our tertiary education. It will ensure that we do have the right number of engineers
coming forward and that we do have those skills appropriately anchored back into our
education system, so that we can build an economy that will not only take us forward in
economic development terms into the future but well beyond that.
When we stop and really analyse the whole question of economic development, it is
tied back into the nation. It is a very fundamental and basic principle that you have got
to have the qua lifications and skills to be able to carry that on with a passion, and that
those people whom you put up for employment have the various opportunities that
should be available to them.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Science and Innovation

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am pleased to take the time to make a few
comments about science and innovation, in part to reflect on the importance of science
and innovation historically, in the present, and, all being well, into the  future. We know
that the New Zealand economy —the Pākehā or European economy —was first
established on an extraction model, which was a very basic extractive economy, and we
know that the member for Tauranga, Simon Bridges, might choose to return us to that
unhappy situation. Most of us, though, would like to see the future development of a
modern economy.
New Zealand’s pastoral economy, our manufacturing, and the wealth we have as a
country have to a large extent been built on a very positive collaboration between public
sector science and private sector innovation, entrepreneurship, and capital, and that has
served us very well historically. Institutions like the Department of Scientific and
Industrial Research and the old MAF, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries,
contributed a great deal to the creation and the success of the pastoral industry. We have
had some extraordinary innovation like the HamiltonJet, the electric fence —all of these
remarkable, New Zealand - based innovations and creations. And, more recently, Fisher
and Paykel, with its medical appliances, and companies like Buckley Systems have
relied on good, basic science, good engineering, and some entrepreneurship in selling
into a very difficult market.
It is important that we continue t o base our economy on science and innovation —
more so than ever, perhaps, because we know that despite the protestations of some, we
cannot and will not build a rich and prosperous economy by trying to increase the
export of high -volume, low -value goods. In evitably, we will hit very solid
environmental constraints and physical constraints. We will not become a rich country
by selling more and more milk powder or more and more pine logs. We do need to
move to a knowledge -based economy, a much smarter economy that relies on niche
manufacturing, on the provision of services, and on weightless exports. We want, in this
way, to create sustainable, long -term employment, not simply short -term jobs
endeavouring, at great risk to life and limb, to rip out logs from th e conservation estate
or to cut down more pine trees. This is not the way forward for a modern, prosperous
economy. We have a very low -productivity economy, a low -wage economy. The smart
application of good scientific research, innovative thinking, and cre ative thinking can
break us out of that downward spiral, which we have been on for several decades, it has
to be said.
I am sure that very few people in the Chamber would, for the most part, disagree
with my comments that we need to move towards a much mo re sophisticated, high -
value economy that is based on knowledge, based on science, and based on innovation.
19078 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
Unfortunately, what we have seen of late is that we are in fact moving away from that,
and that we are doing very little to support the development or the future of such an
economy. In all sorts of ways large and small, we are not enhancing the probability that
we will enjoy a good economy, a cleaner economy, and a smarter economy based on
science and innovation.
One has only to look at some of the p rimary providers of science in New Zealand,
the Crown research institutes, which, it must be said, are in something of a muddle. The
model has never been particularly robust. We know that Crown research institutes since
day one have had to commit far too much of their time and energy to chasing short-term
funding. You cannot do long-term strategic science if your funding is for only 1 year or,
at best, 3 years. We have seen the shambles that has evolved from the proposed
restructuring of AgResearch, the los s of a significant part of the scientific capacity. We
have seen objections from the farming community, which knows that the science that is
being done on behalf of farmers has to be done close to where they live.
Despite a number of comments from some of  our National commentators this
afternoon, I actually live in a provincial area, as does my colleague here, Catherine
Delahunty, from the buzzing, bustling metropolis of the Kauaēranga Valley. We
understand very well the challenges in the primary sector. A dvances in that sector will
not be about volume; they will be about adding value and smart processing, and we do
have some very good examples. We think of what Barker’s has done in Canterbury. It
has created some really high -value products based on researc h and development, some
very hard work, and local, high-quality product.
The Crown research institutes are not in good shape. Morale at the universities is as
low as I have ever seen it in 20-odd years of association with the tertiary sector.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I just wanted to
make a few comments on the matters the member David Clendon has raised. Firstly, he
finished, I think, by having a swipe at university morale. My view —and I think you can
see it in the universities—is that actually they have worked very hard and done well out
of Government funding over the last few years despite the global financial crisis. The
reality is that the university sector is probably more positive about its funding than it has
been for a significantly long time.
I can agree with the member on some things in terms of the importance of
innovation, and that is something that this Government is investin g hugely in. In fact,
the example he raises of Barker’s is just another of the companies that benefits from the
research and development co -funding of Callaghan Innovation. Hundreds of companies
around New Zealand benefit from that support as a result of this Government’s work.
Where I cannot agree with him is the suggestion that somehow New Zealand is
getting less innovative and that innovation has been downgraded in the last several
years. There is no evidence to support that rhetoric at all. He needs to  go across to the
Fieldays in the last couple of weeks, where there was amazing innovation on display. In
fact, if you talk about the productivity of the agricultural sector, it is a story of a history
of innovation. If they had taken the view a hundred ye ars ago that he is taking today,
which is that there is no further innovation in the primary sector, then we would be a lot
poorer now, because they have had a trajectory of innovation and productivity
improvement over that time.
He also raised productivity and said we are a continually low -productivity economy.
Well, I bring good news for him. Our productivity in the 12 months to March 2013 has
improved. It had a 2 percent in front of it —one of the highest numbers for a
significantly long period of time. So it is very encouraging that we are making good
progress in the productivity space as well, because we are very focused on this
innovation.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19079
And I bring good news to him as well on the information and communications
technology sector and the high -tech manufacturing sector, which are continuing under
this Government to grow from strength to strength and which now represent something
like 8 percent of our total goods and services exports. That actually has them already up
to numbers that are significant alo ngside some of our primary sector exports. We have
wonderful companies like Xero and others that are succeeding under this Government
with the support alongside them from New Zealand Trade and Enterprise and Callaghan
Innovation but also, importantly, an e nvironment that allows them to be competitive on
the world stage, with the sorts of economic settings that ensure that we have a sensible
policy that delivers lower interest rates over the cycle, more opportunities in the skill
space and in hiring people, and so on. That is what is occurring under this Government.
But I also wanted to touch base briefly, if I could, on the National Science
Challenges because they are an important part of the Government’s programme. They
are on a range of research areas suc h as the deep south, high -value nutrition, resilience
to nature’s challenges, ageing well, and a better start. I was looking down the list earlier
and I thought to myself that there is one there —New Zealand’s biological heritage —
that is a very topical subj ect today. I can report to the Committee that we have had a
very recent additional application in regard to New Zealand’s biological heritage, where
we have had a proposal from a gentleman to actually reinstate New Zealand’s biological
heritage in a sort o f Jurassic Park model. His intention is to recreate the moa. Look, I
think that is a very aspirational target, but I say to the member: why stop there? If you
are going to start bringing back animals and people from the past, why not bring back
some people as well? Why not get the DNA of some New Zealanders and perhaps some
Labour Prime Ministers from the past who have passed away; you could bring them—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —back to life so that there is—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —this is very important science —more talent on the
Labour benches. I think that would be quite excitin g, and I am prepared to support that
sort of innovation. I know Labour needs it and I would be happy to help. So I invite a
proposal from the Labour Party in that regard, alongside everything else we are doing in
science and innovation.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Tertiary Education

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Kia
ora tātou katoa i tēnei ahiahi. On behalf of the Māori Party, I am pleased to take a call
on the 2014-15 estimates for tertiary education to respond to the report of the Education
and Science Committee. It would not be too much of a surprise that the Māori Party
believes that if you put the learner first, everything else will fall into place f or
achievement for the nation and for generations to follow. If it is important to have an
educated population as a precursor to economic prosperity, we say that we must address
student debt at the core. Since 2012 any domestic student, after earning above  $19,084,
must make compulsory repayments of 12c in the dollar on their student loan. The 12
percent repayment rate makes our student loan scheme one of the most regressive in the
world. This compares negatively with our Australian neighbours. Their studen t loan
repayment scheme starts at 4 percent after a graduate earns over $53,345. It is nearly
three times our level. By freezing the repayment rate in New Zealand at a level below
the full-time minimum wage, payments are imposed on those people who have th e least
ability to repay. That, for us, is a real concern.
19080 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
The Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment announced that he
expects to save another $72.6 million over the next 4 years because of additional
funding freed up from reduced demand and the suspension of inflation adjustments. If
effective, Minister Joyce, you will have to cut, according to our estimates, $144.2
million, and in that regard the word “effective” is questionable, we suggest, as your cuts
basically have cut potential stud ents out of the tertiary education sector. The total
student debt in Aotearoa is over $13 billion and climbing, and Māori students take up
over 22 percent of that total. They are also more likely to take longer to complete study,
more likely to staircase from lower level to higher level qualifications over a number of
years, and more likely to be parents when they return to study, plus have relatives from
their extended family living at home with them. They are more likely to access the
student loan scheme,  loans, allowances, course -related costs, and bank overdrafts, and
more likely to be older, mature students, who are limited in their ability to access loans
and allowances.
Looking at the tertiary sector, we support a student voice by and for students. W e
would say that they are the No. 1 stakeholder in education, and the passing of the
Education (Freedom of Association) Amendment Act 2011 has further compounded the
loss of voice, the loss of infrastructure, and the loss of important services that serve t he
student body. In fact, for Te Roopuu Māori, Ngā Tauira Māori, and other Māori
students associations, this action breaches Te Tiriti o Waitangi. From the Māori Party
perspective, we would say that we will repeal this Act if we are given the chance.
We s upport he tauira mō ake —for ever learning —because we acknowledge that
many students choose to study as adults, as parents, or as grandparents. The system
needs to accommodate the demand from mature students generally, and learner -centric
policy to protect the mana of each student. We support professional development
opportunities for staff in education and certainly in the tertiary sector to attend local and
international forums, to increase research opportunities, and to have for learner -centric
development in teaching and learning. We support the implementation and resourcing
of Te Kaupapa Whaioranga: the Blueprint for Tertiary Education . We support equal
outcomes for all students to achieve in education.
To end on a positive note, the Education and Science Committee also draws attention
to centres of research excellence. A fund was established in 2001 to encourage the
development of excellent tertiary education research. Budget 2014 includes an
additional $53 million over 4 years for existing centres. The  Government intends to
fund four additional centres from 2016, towards an eventual total of around 10. Three of
the new centres will be funded from new funding, with the fourth being funded from
existing allocations. One of the new centres will be dedicate d to Māori developmental
research. This was a huge win for the Māori Party —$12.45 million over 4 years to
enable a Māori -focused centre of research excellence that will produce research
beneficial to whānau, hapū, and iwi.
It is appropriate to be talking about this today, 1 July, as this is the day that Associate
Professor Tracey McIntosh has officially commenced her role as Director of Ngā Pae o
Te Māramatanga, New Zealand’s indigenous centre of research excellence. She is
taking over the role from Professor Te Ahukaramu Charles Royal. We acknowledge her
for that achievement. Ngā Pae o Te Māramatanga consists of 12 contributing and
participating research entities, and it conducts research of relevance to Māori
communities as well as contributing to global indigenous research and affairs. Since
2010 its research has focused on Māori economic development, fostering health and
prosperous whānau, and enhancing Māori distinctiveness, particularly mātauranga
Māori. Research priorities have included models for edu cational success, traditional
child-rearing practices, Māori language revitalisation, resilience of whānau following
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19081
the Christchurch earthquakes, the restoration of the marine environment following the
Rena grounding in Tauranga, Māori men’s health, marke rs and models of flourishing
whānau, and much, much more. This type of research is really important for growing
our knowledge economy.
I want to finish by also using the opportunity of the date of 1 July to note that today
is the first official day of oper ation of the Whānau Ora commissioning agencies Te Pou
Matakana for the North Island, Te Pūtahitanga o Te Waipounamu, and Pasifika Futures.
This is yet again another key milestone achieved in the relationship accord we
negotiated with the National Governmen t to support the evolving focus and ongoing
implementation of Whānau Ora. Today marks the day that its annual investment plans
become operational. This is about ensuring Whānau Ora continues its amazing
momentum throughout whānau, hapū, and iwi. We believe  that the Māori centre of
research excellence could be a key player in enabling the stories and the successes of
Whānau Ora to be available to a much broader audience. That is why we paid so much
attention to ensuring that particular Ngā Pae o Te Māramatan ga was included in our
Budget allocation, and we are pleased to support that outcome.
Vote agreed to.
Vote ACC
DAVID BENNETT (Chairperson of the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee): It is a pleasure to take this call on Vote ACC. I know that other members
of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee will also take a call on this vote —
and very fine members they are, as well, with a special interest in ACC —so they may
be able to delve into a little more detail and go through some of the further issues.
Essentially, one of the big things we need to look at is the indication that there is
further room for ACC levy cuts. That is something that Budget 2014 indicated. The
Accident Compensation Corporation is on track to provide further levy cuts for New
Zealanders of around $480 million in 2015 -16. That is because of the great results that
ACC has had, but it is also a result of the Minister for ACC and the Government
sticking to the funding package that could have been thrown away 3 or 4 years ago if we
had listened to what the Green Party and the Labour Party said, which was to have a
non - fully funded Accident Compensation Corporation and one that was paid for by
taxpayers’ funding. That is what the Greens and Labour have promoted in the last term
or so of this Government. Imagine if that had been the case. Not only would you not be
able to deliver levy reductions but you would have put New Zealand in a situation
where it would be constantly funding accident compensation through its tax funding. It
would have led to higher taxes on New Zealanders if this Government had followed the
approach taken by the Opposition parties.
The Labour Party, to be fair, was actually quite reas onable about that for a certain
period of time, but then it gave in to the Greens, as we normally see it do, and decided
that it would follow the Green Party policy of not seeking the full funding. This was a
disappointment from the Labour Party, but reall y shows that it is not willing to be
constructive and take into account the New Zealand industry going forward.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The biggest lies told about ACC.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Did you have something to say there, Ms King?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, I’ve plenty to say. Just wait—give me a chance.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, OK, all right. Eventually there will be another turn -round
from that member because I am sure that she will be coming in here  and saying:
“Although we were all in favour of fully funding and all those things”—which is not the
case, because they gave in to the Green Party. Just remember that. Just remember your
press release when you gave in to the Green Party.
19082 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Who’s “you”, Mr Assistant Speaker?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: You see, the member has to go to technicalities because she
cannot handle the pressure of it, but that is the nature of that member.
OK, when we look at it, that $480 milli on is a lot of money, and it is money going
into New Zealanders’ pockets from the good economic management of this country by
this Government. If we remember what we came into when we came into Government
and see the checklist of things that this Governmen t had to deal with —look at the way
that New Zealand was in recession before the rest of the world when Labour was in
control.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Because we had a drought.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It was not because of the drought. We have h ad two droughts
since then and we have not had a recession of that nature, have we? So that member
there would have no idea. We were in recession because of poor economic
management. That is the reality of it. Food prices were up 10.9 percent in the last y ear
under Labour, and were up 1.5 percent under this Government. House prices went up 96
percent over the 9 years of Labour, and went up 28 percent under this Government.
Electricity prices went up 72 percent under Labour—
Simon O’Connor: How much?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: —72 percent, under Labour. That is how much electricity
prices went up. The current account deficit —this is the Greens’ mantra of economic
management. They keep on referring to the current account deficit. It was  at 7.9
percent—7.9 percent—and it is at 3.4 percent under this Government. Maybe the most
telling of those signs was the number of New Zealanders leaving to go to Australia. We
in this Government turned round those economic indicators, and by turning roun d those
economic indicators, organisations like ACC were able to deliver these levy cuts going
forward.
That is the nature of good economic management. It is making the right decisions at
the right time and building a strong economy so that we can go forw ard and deliver
those results. The decision on how that $480 million will be attributed is going through
a process at the moment, but you can anticipate that the bulk of it will be in motor
vehicle levies, along with possibly a levy reduction for employers  and the self -
employed.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call Simon O’Connor.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Oh God!
SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): Do not be so disappointed across the
other side. It is amazing how hearing works quite well for some members, particularly
on this side of the Chamber. We hear the needs of New Zealanders, which is very
pleasing. But hearing the small talk from the Opposition, you learn quite a bit.
I will get back to hearing in a moment, because I want to continue the contrast noted
by my colleague from Hamilton, David Bennett, the very fine chair of the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee, which has consid ered Vote ACC. What we have seen,
really, is an ACC scheme under National that is working very, very well, a board that is
working well, and the staff and wider teams of ACC working very well. If I can, I will
just say thank you to those staff, particularl y those on the front line at ACC who are
working through those claims day after day —that can be very difficult. I acknowledge
too, though, that there are often Kiwis who still find it difficult engaging. That is always
a challenge, but it is something that  the National Party hears and this Government hears
and continues to work positively towards.
We have turned ACC round. Before we took over the Treasury benches, it was pretty
clear under the previous Government that ACC had lost its focus. In many ways i t had
just become about pouring in more money but not actually getting claimants back to
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19083
their independence. That is analogous, of course, with the approach of previous left -
leaning Governments—to actually keep people dependent, rather than independent, in
this false belief that if you just throw enough money at people, everything will be
solved and fixed. Whereas on this side we understand —and it is our approach to ACC
as well—that the absolute key is to get someone back into work and to give them that
opportunity to re -engage with themselves, their family, their community, and their
workforce.
Just to illustrate that, the cost of claims under Labour increased by 57 percent in 4
years—the cost of claims went up 57 percent. Again, we have had it analogously  across
a number of portfolios in this House where a Labour Government and a Labour -Greens
Government believed that more money would make a difference. What we saw in
portfolio after portfolio—and ACC is no exemption —was that more money went in but
there were fewer results.
This Government is proud to have turned that round. It has turned that round. We
have seen enormous changes and about $387 million less in ACC levies. Since 1 April
2014, so only a few months ago, New Zealand households have been keeping over $200
a year, and businesses are about $180 better off —that is, small businesses, because
larger ones are about $6,000 better off on average. That is substantial money back in
Kiwis’ pockets, which enables them to continue to make their decisions wit h their
money. We are very mindful that although we are proud of ACC and the work that it
does—a scheme that is in some ways the envy of the world—and we want it to be there,
we also understand that it is funded by Kiwis for Kiwis, and so we do not want to  have
to levy them any more than required.
The really good news is that as we approach this new Budget year we are expecting
further reductions in ACC levies. In fact, one of the ways you will find it directly
manifest will be actually within your private  motor vehicle costs, which could drop up
to about $130.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: How much?
SIMON O’CONNOR: It is $130, I say to my fine colleague Paul Foster -Bell, who
is working here in Wellington Central and across the count ry. So this is great news. We
will actually directly experience that, and that is fantastic.
But we are also focused on getting people back into work, so there has been a lot of
action in the rehabilitation space. I have got some statistics in front of me , and we can
see that long -term outcomes for clients here in New Zealand are 5 percent higher than
those of our Australian counterparts and that more people who have been off work for
more than a year have returned to independence. This is absolutely critical.
One of the things that we have manifested through ACC and other areas was for
under-6-year-olds. This was one of our first steps. If you were under 6 years of age, you
could get free care at the general practitioner or free after -hours accident care.  Of
course, we have now extended free care from general practitioners and free
prescriptions for those up to 13 years of age.
I mentioned at the start about hearing and that the Government has heard, and I think
we just want to note the excellent announce ment today by the Minister for ACC around
hearing loss and the extra money and support we are putting in.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Justice

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: I am delighted to be able to take a call in this
debate on the Vote Justice estimates for the 2014 -15 financial year. I would like to
begin by paying tribute to the Ministers who have led this sector so effectively and so
19084 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
capably over the past term of Par liament. They have truly been working for New
Zealand and working very hard indeed to achieve such positive outcomes.
I would like to acknowledge hard -working colleagues on the Justice and Electoral
Committee—our chairman, Mr Scott Simpson, MP for Coroman del; the Hon Kate
Wilkinson, MP for Waimakariri; and Alfred Ngaro and Jo Hayes, National list MPs —
for their dedication in scrutinising and fine -tuning the legislation that underpins and
implements this Government’s policies in the justice sector.
Crime rates have dropped to 30 -year lows, court waiting times have plummeted, and
reoffending rates have been slashed, thanks both to innovative approaches in
rehabilitation and also to some simple, common -sense measures like boosting drug and
alcohol treatment an d rehabilitation, literacy courses, and work in prison programmes.
There is no doubt that Budget 2014 and the funding voted to the justice sector
programmes contained therein further advance this good work.
But this is not a Government that rests on its l aurels, and this year’s estimates
promise that we will be working even harder for New Zealanders in the year to come.
This may be a concept that some on the Opposition benches struggle to grasp, but
modern Budgets are about more than just spending money; t hey are about more than
just inputs into the departments; they are even more than just about the outputs achieved
by the departments. They are about achieving real outcomes for New Zealanders.
Paramount is the real-world results that Kiwis—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. The time has come for me to leave the Chair for the dinner break.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER -BELL
items.text: I was sayin g just before the dinner break that I was
absolutely delighted to see that in spite of the efficiencies and savings in some areas and
falling crime rates, the number of real Kiwis who are benefiting from our policies in the
area of victim support is growin g. After providing support to 32,000 victims in the last
financial year, provision has been made this year for 35,000 victims to receive that level
of support. I am, of course, referring to page 112 of the Estimates, justice sector, B5,
volume 7, for the members opposite who may not be keeping up with this speech.
Of course we hope that there are fewer victims of crime, and thanks to proactive
policing and a Prevention First strategy, that is proving to be the case. But having
widened the definition of who can receive victim support and extending it to, for
instance, children who are witnesses to domestic violence in the family home, it is right
and proper that we are making budgetary provision to support this wider group.
Similarly, there is more provision for the victims of sexual assaults and abuse, domestic
violence, murder, and other serious crimes.
It is great to see that having achieved a 100 percent success rate in delivering crucial
services in a timely fashion in the last financial year —for instance, processing victims’
assistance scheme grant applications within the 10-day period of their submission —we
are resourcing, once again, a 100 percent timeliness standard this year. That is outlined
on page 111 of the Estimates. This is yet another example of how we are a practical
Government that is working for New  Zealand and putting real -world concerns ahead of
the political dogma, ideology, and out-of-touch theories so favoured by our opponents.
Finally, I would like to touch on the Hutt Valley mobile community office trial,
which has been deemed so successful t hat Budget 2014 provides funding for it to be
rolled out more widely throughout the country. I know it is something that our candidate
for Hutt South, Chris Bishop, will be referring to on the hustings. The mobile
community office is a wonderful example of how, by working together and hunting as a
pack, agencies can achieve much better results than if they were to do their own thing.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19085
One just wishes that members opposite from the Hutt Valley paid more attention to
these excellent projects as contained in th e 2014 -15 Estimates than they do to
reincarnating extinct ratites. This is a Government that is achieving results, and I am
very proud to be part of team Key, which is working for New Zealand every day.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I would like to draw
attention to a number of initiatives within the courts space that we on this side of the
Chamber are very proud of, and also to the excellent work of the team at the Ministry of
Justice, building on changes made within legislation over recent times. Under this
Government the Ministry of Justice has turned round rising court waiting times. In
2013, for instance, we cut the age of cases before the c ourt. For all court cases the
averages are down 8.9 percent. For criminal cases the average is down a staggering 18.3
percent, and disputes tribunal cases are down an average of 21.2 percent. Over the
course of the last few years we have introduced audiovi sual links into prisons and 11
courts, and with crime at historic lows, there were 86,000 fewer court cases last year
than in 2011.
Today is the anniversary of the introduction of the Criminal Procedure Act, and after
a year’s implementation there have been 176,000 new charging documents issued under
this new legislation. We are getting better at enforcing court fines as well, with $250
million less owed in fines since National came into office. When we came in, the
number of outstanding fines was over $800 million and now it is just over $500 million,
and that is good news for the taxpayers of New Zealand because that is money we can
spend in other ways, particularly around the social sector. Specialist courts have brought
down their number of days in cons ideration and waiting times. Coroner’s court cases
are down 54 days. We all know the devastating effect that dragging out coroner’s court
cases has on the families of those who have passed away. Employment Court matters
are down 85 days, and the Environmen t Court is down 64 days. Māori Land Court
matters are down 69 days. Time waiting to get in front of a court is dead time, and it is a
huge frustration.
Within the youth justice space we have applied a number of initiatives introduced
with the Fresh Start policies in 2008. They were quite contentious as they traversed
through the Social Services Committee, but based on court data from June 2011 to June
2013, youth crime, as measured by Youth Court prosecutions, has dropped 27 percent,
from 3,345 cases down to 2,490. These are young people for whom their appearance
before the court is delayed or does not occur. The best way, as we know, to keep young
people away from a career in crime is to prevent them going to court the first time.
So there is excellent work by Police for Alternative Action and the excellent work by
Child, Youth and Family in dealing more appropriately with young people as they come
before the court. The result of a family group conference review found that family
group conferences had a num ber of improvements that they could make in terms of the
timing of those family group conferences; the venue where they were held in regard to
being off Child, Youth and Family premises and into the neighbourhoods and
communities; the use of lay advocates to assist families to come to good resolutions in
their decisions as to what should happen to their young people who were offending; and
the encouragement of bringing complainants before the family group conference to
enter into the restorative justice process. This has seen far better resolutions.
When I was in Opposition, attending, for instance, the youth justice residence at
Rolleston, the very sad thing that we found there was that most of the vast majority of
young people incarcerated were there on th eir fourth or fifth stint of 2 months. Fresh
Start applications—which allowed people to be sent to the youth justice residence or to
have supervision with activity for slightly longer periods but also to add on to the back
of those sentences drug and alcoh ol therapy and intensive supervision —means that
19086 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
those people are not coming back, and in the meantime are not creating further victims
for which they are incarcerated.
It gives young people significant hope. It gives their families help through mentoring
and parenting programmes. We are very pleased with the results that we are seeing
there, with 27 percent fewer young people appearing before the Youth Court. Thank
you.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call the honourable member—what
is Scott’s name—Scott Simpson.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.role: Chairperson of the Justice and Electoral Committee
items.text: It is
almost the end of the 50 th Parliament and it is nice to be so readily recognised by such
an esteemed and long -serving Chair as yourself. It is a delight and a pleasure for me to
stand and rise and speak in the debate on the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill,
because as chair of the Justice and Electoral Committee I have been able to see firsthand
the very good work that team justice in this National -led Government has been
achieving under the leadership of the Hon Judith Collins. The Hon Chester Borrows has
been playing a role, of course; the Attorney -General has been doing a particularly good
job; and then, of course, in corrections and in police the Hon Anne Tolley is doing a
very good job.
It is part of National’s role to build a safer New Zealand for all New Zealanders. It is
an important part of our plan to provide better public services. Under National recorded
crime has reduced to the lowest level in 33 years.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: How long?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Thirty-three years. Recorded crime is at the lowest level, Mr
Foster-Bell, that it has been in 33 years. Unlike members in the Opposition we are tough
on crime and we are tough on criminals. We make absolutely no apology for putting
victims at the centre of our criminal justice system, because they are the victims of
crime and they are the ones who are in our justice system through no fault of their own.
They are there as reluctant participants in a system that sometimes in the past has not
treated them as well as it perhaps could.
I want to spend a minute or two just going over some of the methods and some of the
pieces of legislation —some of the things that team justice under John Key’s National
administration has been able to achieve. We want to continue to reduce crime and the
harmful effects that it has on citizens of the nation.
What have been some of the key issues and what are some of the key shifts? Right
from when this Government took office back in 2008 it has been a priority to focus on
the things that matter for all New Zealand. Justice has been an important ar ea for us. It
has meant that harsher penalties for the worst offenders have been introduced. It means
that we have been focusing on the underlying drivers of crime and better rehabilitation
of offenders. We have also been ensuring that the justice system b etter helps those
people who are victims of crime. As I said earlier, we make absolutely no apology for
placing the victims of crime at the centre of all we do in the criminal justice area.
Labour remains, to its shame, soft on crime and soft on criminals.
There has been a vast amount of legislation and legislative change. We have, for
example, strengthened the bail laws. We have given police greater powers to take on
and tackle serious crime. We have brought in alcohol reforms that give local
communities the option of having a tailored alcohol regulatory environment that tackles
alcohol-related issues in their local communities.
There has been just as much practical, operational, and even attitudinal change
within the ministries. This National Government introduced Better Public Services, or
the BPS, targets in 2012 for key public services that would make a real difference for all
New Zealanders. In the justice sector, the main agencies are the Ministry of Justice,
New Zealand Police, and the Department of  Corrections. They were all set ambitious
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19087
targets for reducing the rates of total crime, violent crime, youth crime, and reoffending
I am pleased to report that all of our initiatives, however, have been about reducing
crime and improving front-line results, and the results are very, very good. I am pleased
to report that our target for the reduction in overall crime was 15 percent by 2017, and
as at December 2013 it was down by 14 percent. So we are well on the way to achieving
that. As well as th at, the violent crime rate was down by a full 10 percent and overall
reoffending was down by 11.7 percent.
These are just a few of the measures that team justice under the John Key National
administration has been able to bring about on behalf of all New Zealand, in order to
make New Zealand a better, safer environment for all of us. We aim to continue to
ensure that New Zealand is a safe environment for all our citizens. Under the very
capable leadership of Judith Collins in the justice sector, I think we  are going to see an
awful lot more of it. It is a key role of the Government to protect its citizens, and in
justice we have.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Health

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Can I first of all say how much I
enjoyed Scott Simpson’s speech, because he did talk to the estimates and he did talk to
achievement, and he did not go into a mad rant and rave of personal abuse of the
Opposition. That man should be a M inister. But he made one mistake. It is not “Team
Key” or “Team Justice”; it is “Team Toadies”. That is what they are —“Team Toadies”.
They are a whole lot of toadies all bowing and scraping to Mr Key.
I want to talk about the health estimates 2014/15. I wa nt to talk in these estimates
about the health workforce. The cost of our health system is made up by our health
workforce. About 80 percent of the costs of health come from our health workforce,
those who provide our health services. Just recently, health  workers in New Zealand
were offered a 0.7 percent pay increase.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: It was a 0.7 percent pay increase. They are rather upset
about that, because our health workforce believes it is competent, it is quality, it is
professional, and it is providing incredibly good health services to the people of New
Zealand. I agree with it.
But you have to ask why such a small increase is being offered to our health
workforce. It is because the tr uth is the health budget has been reduced in real terms.
The members do not like to hear this, but before they say I am wrong I suggest they
read the Budget documents. The health budget was reduced in real terms by 2.3 percent.
They are Treasury figures. T hey are in the Budget documents. But worse than that, go
and look at the graphs in the Budget documents. Treasury is saying that in 2015/16
health will be reduced by 3.7 percent in real terms, in 2016/17 it will be reduced by 3.6
percent in real terms, and  in the 2017/18 financial year by 3.1 percent. So we have a
pathway for health under a National Government of year-on-year cuts, in real terms.
So I am saying to the health workforce in New Zealand that it is going to be a rocky
road, should this Governmen t be re-elected, and it is going to be a rocky road for New
Zealanders receiving health services. We are facing some huge health workforce
shortages. I draw the attention of members opposite to the Ministry of Health’s report
that it put out just last week . It is warning that there will be a serious shortage of cancer
specialists looming in this country. It has said that over the next decade cancer in New
Zealand is going to increase by almost a third, and by 2022 there will be a shortfall of
seven radiatio n oncologists, 30 medical physicists, and 25 radiation therapists. It said
19088 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
that there were only three trained in New Zealand, but we would need six in every year
to cope with the demand over the next 10 years. It said that since 2009, six of the 13
medical physicist graduates had gone straight overseas. It said it had been warning of
this problem since 2012. What we do know about a health workforce is it takes times to
train them —you just cannot pluck them out of the air —and there is an international
shortage of a cancer health workforce.
What I say to the Minister of Health is can we not learn from the past? I have had to
listen to the Minister of Health say how under a Labour Government cancer patients had
to be sent to Australia. I tell the members opposite that one of the first decisions I had to
make as Minister of Health was to approve sending patients to Australia in early 2000.
Why? Not because of anything a Labour Government had done but because report after
report on the health workforce had been pr ovided in the 1990s to the previous
Government about the shortage of radiation therapists —that we were not training
enough, that we had ageing linear accelerators, and that we needed to take this issue
seriously. We did not.
It was not until 2000, when we increased the number of radiation therapists, who
take 3 years to train, and we started to buy new linear accelerators, that we were able to
start to cope with our own treatment of cancer. I am asking why we have not learnt.
Why did we not look ahead and s ee what was happening? We are now told that we are
facing a serious nursing shortage in New Zealand —a serious nursing shortage —not a
serious doctor shortage. There is a shortage of general practitioners, yes, but there is not
a shortage of doctors overall,  and there is going to be a surplus out of Australia,
anyway. But we face a serious nursing shortage, and we are told that we should have
started providing for that in 2012.
I have to say that I am really disappointed in Health Workforce New Zealand. We
were told that it was going to be the organisation that would solve all our problems for
our health workforce. I have to say that it has come up, pretty much, with a lemon,
because there have been no serious decisions made around our nursing workforce. It is
still deciding on that. There have been no serious decisions made about how we are
going to be able to offer cancer services going forward. I have to tell you: this is an
organisation that is costing taxpayers an awful lot of money for a few pieces of pap er
and some ideas about physician assistance, some American idea that it wanted to try,
when we ought to be building our health workforce, training them, and upskilling them
here in New Zealand.
I was staggered to read that over the last 5 years the chair of Health Workforce New
Zealand has been paid $743,138 —$743,138—in fees and in reimbursements. The chair
of Health Workforce New Zealand is paid $13,000 a month. Our senior citizens, single
superannuitants, or old veterans are paid $19,000 a year. So we ar e paying all this
money for an executive chairman of an organisation that is not addressing the health
workforce issues this country faces —serious issues. I have not even talked about what
is called the unregulated workforce, the place where most of our he alth care is
provided—in the home and in the community for our older people. Almost no work has
been done by Healthcare Workforce New Zealand on that issue. It is not good enough. I
think it is time that we took health workforce issues seriously, because w e do have
highly competent, highly trained, and quality health care workers in New Zealand
whom we need to value. But we will not if we underpay them and if we do not value
them. They are overworked and stressed because there are not enough of them.
Unfortunately, that is the picture that is emerging under Minister Ryall, so I would
like to put to rest, once and for all, this nonsense that a Labour Government left a
shortage of a workforce. We were the first Government in living memory to try to
address the health workforce by increasing the number of doctors. The first increase in
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19089
the number of doctors training was in 1981, until we became the Government. We
increased the number of radiation therapists, nurses, nurse practitioners, and many
others, includin g dental therapists, my own old profession. We took the health
workforce seriously. That has not been what has happened under this Government. So if
we are facing, according to Treasury, year -on-year cuts in the health budget under a
National Government, t he ability to pay and hold that health workforce will diminish
year on year. Once again, we will be forced to send people to another country.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I am very pleased to tak e a call on behalf of
New Zealand First in the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill. Each year in the
estimates debate on the health budget, we anticipate that it might focus on some
preventative health measures. In this Committee we all know that preven tion is far
better than cure. We need that vision. We know that the health budget is reducing in real
terms year on year, and the Hon Annette King also spelt that out very clearly. Spending
on prevention is logical. It will work towards preventing an incre asing burden on our
already strained health budget. Yet these estimates hold very few thoughts for
preventative strategies, which is a shame. We were expecting this. Why are there not
any plans? We know that there is an obesity and diabetes tsunami actuall y coming to
our country—just about to pass, I would say. We must praise the Government in one
area, and that is for the free doctors visits for under -13s. That is a preventative measure.
We are very pleased that National is looking at New Zealand First pol icy and starting to
implement some of our health policy.
We would also have liked to see in the estimates an attempt to reduce the hospital
waiting lists, perhaps by having additional staff to help out. We see the media
highlighting the plight of people w ho require surgery but who do not qualify for the
waiting list. Effectively, they are waiting to get on the waiting list. Every member of
this Parliament receives letters from people saying they have been waiting for months
and months, and some even for ye ars. In the end they have to revert to living with pain
or borrowing money to pay for the surgery that they need —some are lucky enough to
go to a charity hospital to get the operation that they need.
It is really disheartening that the Government has set a test for the level of need for
surgery, when clearly many thousands of people are actually left off the waiting list and
yet are in dire need. The people who do not win this game of roulette often end up
loaded up with painkillers and other drugs that th ey need. While they are waiting to go
on the waiting list, their health will deteriorate and their quality of life will be
compromised. By the time they finally get to have the surgery, the toll on the health
system’s dollars will be vastly more than if th e surgery had been done earlier or when it
was initially dated for them to have it.
The number of people waiting to get on the waiting list is a ticking time bomb and it
really requires urgent action by the Minister of Health. The sad part of this is that
nobody really knows the extent of this hidden list. Even the medical profession is
speaking out and questioning the management of the health system, pointing out that
there is a hidden waiting list and saying that doctors themselves are very frustrated by
the constraints imposed by the Government’s targets, which looks at outputs rather than
outcomes. This is a problem that disproportionately affects seniors, which is particularly
concerning, given that we have an ageing population here in New Zealand.
New Zealand First would rather see an ailment checked out with a general
practitioner at an early stage before hospitalisation becomes necessary. It is far less
expensive. The rising costs associated with this costlier health care will drive the district
health boards’ books persistently into the red unless further action and fiscally neutral
health plans are actually actioned. We know this is going to happen, we have all the
evidence, and yet there is nothing on the books to try to sort this problem out. We pride
19090 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
ourselves on being a First World country, so this level of Government disassociation
around our health system is not good enough. Nothing appears to be planned, either, to
ensure that we have a workforce for aged care. There does need to be parity be tween
those who are working in private rest homes and those who are working in district
health board rest homes. We all know that caregivers are absolutely essential in rest
homes.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is indeed a
great pleasure to speak on these estimates in Vote Health because this year the National
Government has committed to an investment in Vote Health of $15.6 billion, an all-time
record. Nat ional has indeed managed to achieve an increase in productivity and an
increase in outputs over the last 5 years.
What is really important to realise in health is that right around the world there is
almost infinite demand and finite resources. And in sta rk contrast to the National
Government’s achievements, the previous Government failed on all accounts. It
doubled the health expenditure, decreased outputs, and, indeed, decreased productivity.
If, indeed, Labour’s spending record had continued at year -on-year 8 percent increases,
in a few decades’ time Vote Health would have made up 60 percent of the entire
Government spend. It was absolutely, absolutely unsustainable along that trajectory.
So it is a great worry when I hear Annette King once again shroud -waving about the
achievements of the previous Labour Government in this area. Just to remind you, they
were to double the expenditure, decrease productivity, and decrease outputs.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s just untrue.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Yes, she was. She was saying that Labour had achieved a
lot. She was saying that it was not the Labour Government’s fault that women were
heading to Australia for radiation therapy. Once again, she showed the absolute inability
of the previous Labour Government to be realistic about sustaining a value -for-dollar
health system.
But the record of the National Government over the last 5 years has been 40,000
more elective surgery outputs per year since 2008, and I would like Barbara St ewart to
take note of that. There have been 1,000 more doctors and 3,000 more nurses. We have
heard Annette King talking about her health workforce, but for the first time in the
history of New Zealand there have been more medical graduates available than there are
jobs in the resident hospital training programmes available in New Zealand. This is an
incredible achievement. But the reality is that workforce planning is extremely difficult
because international conditions change. Australia has, indeed, trained a great deal more
doctors, and now New Zealand doctors are wanting to stay here. There is still a great
attraction for doctors from Britain, Canada, and South Africa to come to New Zealand.
One of the clear focuses of the National Government has been t he introduction of
taxpayer-funded free access for children under 13 to general practitioner care. It was
good to hear Barbara Stewart saying what a great National Government this is for
introducing this policy. At the beginning of this year David Cunliffe , with a blare of
trumpets and sirens, announced a $1 billion package of unmitigated baby bribes —a
non-directed, untargeted baby bonus. This was a clear example of a party and a leader
that have no cognisance whatsoever of making sure that every health dol lar counts. In
contrast, in this Budget the National Government announced a very well -directed and
very practical family and children package. Amongst it, of course, were the free access
and the $90 million that will go towards ensuring that children right  around New
Zealand will be able to access primary care, keeping them out of hospitals.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call the honourable member Jian
Yang. Ni hao ma?
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19091

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Wo hen hao xie xie. It is a pleasure to take a call in this
estimates debate. Again, congratulations to the Minister of Finance, the Hon Bill
English, and our Prime Minister, John Key, on delivering a great Budget 2014, and also
on 6 years of strong and stable leadership.
New Zealanders want a Government they can trust. Our Prime Minister, John Key,
has led the country from recession to sustained growth. The National -led Government
has delivered for New Zealand, an d our hard work is paying off for New Zealanders.
Our books are now back to surplus—a $372 million surplus next year, growing larger in
the coming years—and there will be 2 percent to 4 percent economic growth in the next
4 years. In the past year alone, 8 4,000 new jobs were created, and Budget 2014
forecasts an additional 170,000 new jobs by mid-2018.
The feedback from the Chinese community has been very positive. The Chinese
community is confident that our National -led Government is delivering on issues that
matter to them. Indeed, in Budget 2014 we focus on the issues that matter to ordinary
New Zealanders and that will make a difference to their lives. This Government has
been looking after and supporting New Zealanders from day one. It is also about
growing the economy to the benefit of New Zealanders, and that is why in Budget 2014
we are investing $500 million in a package of practical support for young families and
vulnerable children most in need. This includes free general practitioner visits and f ree
prescriptions for all children under 13.
I am particularly pleased to see increased spending in health. I would like to take this
opportunity to thank our Minister of Health, the Hon Tony Ryall, and also the chair of
the Health Committee, Dr Paul Hutc hison, for their wonderful work. It has been a great
privilege to work with them. Unfortunately, they will be retiring from politics. I wish
them all the best.
National is spending more on health than any other Government in New Zealand’s
history—$1.8 billion of extra investment over 4 years. That takes health spending next
year to a record $15.6 billion. This includes $90 million for free general practitioner
visits and free prescriptions for all children under 13, which I just mentioned; $112.1
million for disability support; $96 million for increased home -based support services;
$40 million for additional support for the elderly; and $33 million for faster cancer
treatment. There is also $20 million for the rheumatic fever prevention programme; $6.3
million for bilateral cochlear implants for children; and $40 million over 4 years for the
new Healthy Families NZ anti -obesity initiative, which is expected to reach around
900,000 New Zealanders.
Also, the Government will spend $110 million of new money over the next 4 years to
provide even more New Zealanders with elective surgery, including hip and knee
replacements. The National -led Government has provided record numbers of New
Zealanders with the operations they need and has provided them faster than bef ore.
Over the past 5 years the number of patients receiving elective surgery has lifted, from
118,000 in 2008 to 158,000 in 2013 —40,000 more patients are now receiving elective
surgery each year. As I am on the Health Committee I have been particularly int erested
in people’s stories about the health system.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Education

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I am looking forward to speaking on
Vote Education tonight. It is one of  the most important votes in this year’s Budget, as it
is in any Budget, because it is where we think about the future, and we think about the
legacy that we will leave for future generations of New Zealanders. I have to say that in
19092 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
that regard this curren t Government’s priorities in education have been woefully
inadequate and completely wrong.
The education portfolio starts in early childhood education. In fact, if we want to
ensure that every young New Zealander gets the best chance in life through educa tion,
that starts with a quality early childhood education. That means investing in quality:
investing in making sure that we have really good teachers in early childhood education,
really good centres, and that all of those centres are well supported. Thi s Government
has not been doing that. If there is one area that is the clearest example of how
Government funding is not keeping up with increased demand, is not keeping up with
the cost pressures that centres are facing, it is early childhood education.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Government funding simply is not keeping up. Every early
childhood centre will tell Tim Macindoe, who has got his head in the sand, that on a per
child basis early childhood education fu nding is declining under this Government. It is
declining under this Government, and those members have their heads buried in the
sand. They simply do not want to know.
Parents are having to pay more for early childhood education. Of course, the
Government did away with the “free” in free early childhood education, so it is not
surprising that parents are having to pay more. The Government has failed to keep up
with the targets to increase the number of qualified staff in early childhood education.
Its ide a of expanding provision is to go along to Kidicorp and basically say that the
Government will fund it twice for building the same early childhood centres. This is a
Government that is failing to meet the needs of the future in early childhood education.
In schooling we know what the challenges are. Quality teaching —we should be
backing quality teaching and professional development for teachers. We need a high -
trust, aspirational model for the way we do that. This Government has no trust in
teachers. It sa ys to parents that teachers cannot be trusted. We have got a power -grab
from the Minister of Education, who wants to wrench away control of the entire
teaching profession and put it under her thumb by not even giving teachers any say over
how their own profession is regulated. This is a Government that thinks that bigger class
sizes are the solution to underachievement in the education system. This is a
Government that thinks that charter schools —importing a failed charter school model
from overseas—are the answer to underachievement in our education system. We know
that that is simply not the case. We know that that is not the case. This is a Government,
of course, that thinks that spending up to five times more money on a handful of
students going to chart er schools is a good use of public money, when every other
school in the country is struggling for resources.
We know that they are struggling for resources because donations by parents to New
Zealand’s public schools are now about to top $100 million a y ear. That is a 30 percent
increase in the 5 years that National has been in Government —a 30 percent increase.
The reality is that that is because the overall education budget, when it is adjusted for
population growth and for inflation, has gone backwards in four out of the 6 years that
National has been in office. The money has gone backwards. National has been taking
money out of education.
Yes, the overall amount of money has gone up, but that is because the number of
people in the education system has gone up and because, like everything, the costs go
up. It is called inflation, and it seems to me that this Government struggles with that. To
say that it is spending more money on education than ever before is ridiculous, because
there are actually more p eople in the education system than ever before because the
population has grown, so it stands to reason that more money will be going into the
system. But on a per student basis, it is going backwards. On a per student basis, the
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19093
funding is going backwards  in the education system. It is simply not keeping up with
inflation and with the growing population. Instead, we are seeing the Government trying
to carve up the education system through privatisation, through the introduction of
charter schools and public-private partnerships.
In the meantime, it is ignoring the needs of the future. It is failing to help the
education system and to support the education system to adapt to the needs of the 21 st
century. Instead, it is continuing to refine the education sy stem that we needed in the
last century. We actually need something different now. As Alvin Toffler said, the new
illiterate of the 21 st century will not be those who cannot read and write but those who
cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn. Actually, that is what schools are focused on. They
are focused on giving kids the knowledge and the competencies that they are going to
need to survive in the 21st century, and yet so much Government policy is getting in the
way of that.
The narrowing of the focus of the curriculum has been one of the worst things that
this Government has done in education —narrowing the focus of the curriculum away
from a rich, diverse education down to something that simply is not going to cut it.
When I go and talk to employers, I ask what they want people to leave school with —
what the competencies are that they are looking for. They talk about creativity. They
talk about collaboration. They talk about problem solving. And yet all of those things
are being distracted from by this Government’s very narrow focus —the very narrow
focus of this current Government. And, of course, what have we seen? A litany of
failures in this Government’s education policy: school closures in Christchurch, closing
special education schools around the country, Novopay, and Hekia Parata’s bizarre plan
to increase class sizes, supposedly to improve the quality of education.
There is a better way. There is a better way in all of these areas. Positive, progressive
change in education is what I think New Zealanders are looking for, and I think that is
what they are going to get when they vote for a Labour Government —a Labour -led
Government—at this year’s election. We will put the focus on quality teaching, but not
in the way this National Government wants to, which is to divide the teaching
profession and tell the teaching profession that the Government knows best and try to
tell every teacher in the  country that it knows better how they should be doing their
jobs. We will not do it that way; we are actually going to place some trust in teachers.
We are actually going to say to teachers that we think it is fantastic that they have an
aspirational code of ethics for their profession, rather than a punitive code of conduct
like this Government wants. We are going to say to teachers that actually we trust them
to have a say over how their profession is regulated and governed. We are going to give
teachers a say in how the Teachers Council is composed, unlike under this National
Government, where Hekia Parata wants to hand -pick every single member of the
Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand because she will not trust teachers to have
a say over their own profession.
We are going to say to parents that we recognise the economic pressures that they are
under and we recognise the fact that funding has not kept up with the cost of educating
kids. We will do something about that, unlike this Government, whi ch is saying, in the
words of Bill English, that schools are awash with cash. We know that that is simply not
the case—in fact, funding is not keeping up under this Government. That is something
that the incoming Labour Government will do something about as a matter of priority.
We recognise that education in the 21st century is going to look significantly different
from what it looked like in the 20 th century. That means that schools are going to need
access to new technology. Kids are going to need acces s to new technology. Although
the current Government—and I will give it credit; this is an area where it has done some
good things and we fully support the initiatives that it has put in place in this area, but a
19094 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
lot more needs to be done, and it will be d one under a Labour Government. We will
have some more announcements to make on that very, very soon, as you will see over
the coming couple of days. Investment in education is an investment in the future of the
country. It may sound like a cliché —it has be en said so many times —but this
Government does not seem to acknowledge that. It seems to think that the education
system can continue to scrape by with less and less on a per student basis, in real terms,
every year. It simply cannot. The funding is not ke eping up with the cost of educating
kids. The Government has got its head buried in the sand if it thinks it is. It simply is
not.
So the next Labour Government will invest in quality teaching. We will, in
collaboration with the teaching profession, set v ery high standards for the profession.
We will make sure that we attract the best and brightest into teaching, because we know
how valuable the work of teachers is. We will then place trust in them to get on with it
and to do the job without all of the pun itive measures and sanctions that this
Government is putting in place. We will commit to the free public education system that
New Zealanders have so long been proud of. We will put the “public” and the “free”
back into the free public education that this Government is so determined to dismantle.
We will make sure that schools are supported to deliver an education that is appropriate
for the 21st century. We will ensure that kids get access to the technology that they need
and that it is not a lottery of wh ere they are born and how wealthy their parents are that
determines whether they get access to that technology. Every student needs to have
access to the technology they need to thrive in the 21 st century and the incoming Labour
Government will make sure that they get that.
Education is so important. It is time for positive change and positive investment in
education, and that is exactly what New Zealand is going to get from an incoming
Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak
in this estimates debate. The reason I am very pleased to speak in this debate is I know
that there are many members of this House who care passion ately about education. I
agree with Mr Hipkins that actually this is one of the most important votes in the
country. We all care about young people and want to create the most opportunities
possible for every young New Zealander. The question is how you ge t there. What we
will not take a lecture on, on this side of the Chamber, is around our commitment to that
dream, the investment that we have made, and the commitment to actual life
opportunities and results. What we know will happen in the next 3 months i s that you
will have a party on that side of the Chamber whose basic equation is to tax more and
spend more but that will never once require accountability for the dreams, the futures,
and the opportunities of young New Zealanders.
What we have said throughout the last 5½ years and throughout this period is that
actually we have a responsibility to do more than that. That is about saying every parent
has a right to know how their children are doing in numeracy and literacy. We make n o
apologies for that. That is about saying we are prepared, in the most difficult financial
situation that our country has seen in a generation, to increase the education budget in
every single Budget. We are spending $10.1 billion. We are spending one of the highest
amounts in the OECD. We have increased that significantly because we understand that
we are dealing with the futures of young people, and we can be proud of that additional
investment.
What we have done over this period and what you saw in thi s Budget is our
relentless attempt to try to drive change, particularly for our most disadvantaged,
whether it is the Reading Together programme, which is more money to ensure that
some of our most disadvantaged families have access to greater opportunitie s in terms
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19095
of literary; whether it is $2.5 million for Computers in Homes, which means 1,500
families will have access to being able to learn online; or whether it is the $211 million
that we put in last year on top of another $500 million of investment in  actual modern
infrastructure to enable that equity of access. Our record is incredibly strong, both in
terms of the investment and in terms of the ability to drive change to lift opportunity.
Look at the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 results.
They are up for all young New Zealanders. Look also at the results for Māori and
Pacific students. They are up as well. At the end of the day, what New Zealanders can
know is that not only have we spent more money but actually we have  seen greater
results in NCEA for those students who have not traditionally had those opportunities.
