What we can also see in the area of early childhood education is another $155
million in this Budget. But what is really important is that we have enrolle d more of
those young children who have traditionally started off behind in our education system
into early childhood education than ever before. We have a goal that every child is not
going to have to start 100 metres behind the start line. Our Government  has invested
more than ever before.
In the area of modern learning environments, I have no doubt that what we will see
from the Labour Party in terms of this Budget is a whole lolly scramble. What we will
not see is the ability to hold that accountability and to say that we require more for what
we are going to give in terms of this funding. In the area of modern learning
environments, it is under our Government, actually, that we have seen significant
upgrades right across the country. When you have got 60 percent of your school stock at
more than 40 years old, it has been our Government that has put more classrooms than
ever before in areas of growth. In this Budget alone, there is $284 million. That is 148
more classrooms for areas of growth. It is more new schools and it is more site
acquisitions. We have also committed to areas like the Green Star building programme
to ensure that we have more environmentally sustainable schools.
To get a lecture from the Opposition around Canterbury is actually appall ing. We
have stood beside Canterbury in a very, very difficult situation. Of course it has been a
very hard time for Canterbury, but we have put in over $1 billion to make sure that we
build those schools and for many of those schools to be much better tha n ever before.
Today I announced, on top of the 23 school pools that we are repairing, another 15
pools as well. That is just another example where we are prepared to invest in young
people in Canterbury. These are more modern schools. I also announced $20 0,000 the
other day around digital literacy and connecting a whole lot of young people in
Canterbury.
This is about a Government that has consistently demonstrated increases over every
single Budget that we have been involved in and an overall increase in  the education
budget, which is one of the best in the OECD. This is a Government that has
consistently said that we want more. We particularly want more for our most
disadvantaged because the future of New Zealand —having a much smarter, more
connected cou ntry—relies on us changing the script. We cannot as a country have a
Government filled with people who do not require basic things like standards in
education, and that is what national standards have done. I tell you what: if we are
around as of 20 Septem ber, we are going to continue to invest in areas like digital
literacy and like modern school environments. We are going to continue to invest in
Investing in Educational Success, which, regardless of the fact there is a very healthy
debate about it, is basically about saying that one of the biggest things that we can do to
help change the future of young New Zealanders is to do everything we can to support
the teaching profession, to strengthen quality teaching, and to strengthen governance in
schools.
19096 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
This is a Government that has a vision and has a plan and is committed to investment
to lift standards, to lift achievement, and to ultimately lift the futures and the dreams of
so many young New Zealanders, compared with an alternative party that believes i n
taxing more and spending more for no results and continuing on a very old model. I
believe, when it comes to the election in a couple of months’ time, National has a very
proud record of raising achievement and of helping our most disadvantaged. I am ver y
proud to be an Associate Minister of Education. I want to finish by saying I believe that
the Hon Hekia Parata has an outstanding record in terms of ensuring that young children
are engaged in early childhood education, ensuring that standards are lifted , and
ensuring that we are investing in quality education. These are the things that a great
education system is made of, and we are very proud of that.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora. It is inte resting to follow the Hon Nikki
Kaye, and I think very highly of this Associate Minister of Education. However, she is
wrong on so many points that it is a real disappointment.
I want to address first of all —so that New Zealand hears this —the fact that th e
Minister spoke and actually said that it was the National Government that set standards.
The suggestion is that education in New Zealand has never had any standards. That is
an affront to every teacher who has ever worked in the New Zealand school system ,
which took us to the top of the OECD with regard to our results, and our people are
highly recognised and our education system is so well -recognised that this Government
can sell it. When those statements are made, it is said as if we never had standards  and
as if it took a National Government to put a line in the sand that says: “OK, now your
children can jump over it.”
New Zealanders need to understand that the New Zealand Curriculum had
curriculum bands. Instead of saying that every child on this day,  at this time, after this
year, would jump over this particular line, it treated them like human beings. It treated
them with a 2 -year spread across the academic achievement levels in the New Zealand
Curriculum. It was world-recognised, and this Government put it at risk.
This Government then tried to convince you, New Zealand, that teachers were
untrustworthy. In 2009 this Government and this Prime Minister, John Key, said that
primary school principals lied to parents on report cards and that that was wh y the
Government needed to give them a template that told them exactly where they stood
with reading, writing, and maths. And that was it —no holistic vision and no aspiration
in education—and that lack of aspiration is actually carried out and is proven th rough
the estimates.
So if people want to go and have a look at page 79 of Vote Education, let us have a
look at the aspirations —“What is Intended to be Achieved with this Appropriation” —
for partnership schools. Let us just have a look. These were the sch ools that were going
to be the silver bullet for our most vulnerable. These were the schools that the National
Government wanted to take the credit for lifting achievement for our Māori, our
Pasifika, and our low socio -economic groups. The targets for thes e schools in this
appropriation are that in reading they will have 68 percent of their students at the
standard, 64 percent in maths at the standard, and 60 percent in writing at the standard. I
kept hearing “five out of five”. I am sorry, but I kept heari ng that five out of five were
going to achieve these things. What we have got here is a Government that is quite
happy to have 40 percent fail the standard. It sets it, but it is happy to have 40 percent
fail it.
Now let us have a look at the targets it has put on mainstream schools. In reading it is
81 percent, in maths it is 77 percent, and in writing it is 74 percent. So, apparently,
mainstream schools, which are not funded to the level that partnership schools are under
these appropriations, have got t o achieve higher targets before this Government will
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19097
give them any credit, yet it is funding partnership schools under this Budget at a ratio of
one teacher per nine students. New Zealand, have a listen to it. This is the same
Government that wanted to up your children’s class size not that long ago. It is funding
these partnership schools at a ratio of one teacher to nine students, and it has said in the
legislation that for 5 -year-olds it can be one teacher to 15. This is the Government that
wants you to vote for it later on this year because it says it is strong on education —this
is what it is.
The Associate Minister stood up and said —and National members will stand up
again and say —that more money than ever before has gone into education in New
Zealand, and I am not going to contradict those members. Of course the Government
had to rebuild Christchurch. That is in that money. I mean, what was it going to do—not
build schools down in Christchurch? Do not be ridiculous. Of course there is more
money, because the Christchurch rebuild is in there. What about the $4.5 million rebuild
going on at Mahurangi College —why? Because the buildings are leaky. Who passed
that law? Who passed the law that allowed those materials to be used in our State
schools, so that we have now got to do a complete rebuild?
The Minister talked about the number of buildings that had to be refreshed and
turned into modern learning environments. That money should have been set aside
anyway. There has always been the replacement building fund, so that is not new
money either, New Zealand. Do not let the Government tell you this is new money. But
do ask the Government, New Zealand —have a look through these appropriations—how
much has been spent on the PaCT tool. You do not hear much about t he PaCT tool any
more. It stands for the progressive assessment something or other tool. It is a digital
tool, New Zealand, that has been created through a computer program, so that
teachers—not necessarily qualified and registered teachers —can go on and e nter data
on children.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Thank you for
recognising me and allowing me to take a call.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: You are welcome.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: I knew I would be. The goal of the education system
should be to help all kids reach their potential and to create a fairer society for all, but
unfortunately the Appropriation (2013/14 Supplementary Estimates) Bill fails to deliver
on this issue. It is not about disputing endlessly the amount of money, because, in fact,
more money will always be spent in every Budget on education, otherwise we would be
slipping further back, le t alone standing still. That is just the reality. So there really is
not any point in having that debate about who has spent the most money. That is not the
issue. We do not need to fight over that.
But the estimates have failed to address the elephant in the room that holds back
many of our communities, which is poverty. While we ignore and deny poverty and say
that it is irrelevant to educational achievement, we are always going to have difficulties
with the education system. It does not really matter how  many lime-green squabs and
classrooms with sliding doors you create and call it a modern learning environment if
the children are arriving at school reliant on charity for breakfast because their parents
are not earning enough money. It does not really ma tter if they are sick and there is no
school nurse, because she has been taken away and was only part -time anyway, to work
on the rheumatic fever programme somewhere else. So we have got to acknowledge the
context.
I think it is really important that we r ecognise that education is not in a happy state.
The Government cannot say that Vote Education has solved the issues. I think the
previous speaker, Tracey Martin, when speaking about the targets for charter schools,
was reminding us that an enormous amount  of money is going intro fringe experiments
19098 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
because the Government says that it has this goal of five out of five. But what it fails to
recognise is that five out of five of our children are not getting fed, are not well, and are
not having access to resou rces, and that we have the greatest inequality in this country
that we have had in many, many generations. I am quite ashamed to live in a country
now where I now see older people begging on the streets —that never happened in my
childhood—and children going to school hungry.
The Green Party recently did a tour where we promoted a very positive response,
which is not in the estimates, and that is the community hubs plan. What that is about is
making sure that we provide for kids in school, so there is a fre e lunch, there is a school
nurse for every 400 children in decile 1 to decile 4 schools, and so there is after -school
care and free out -of-school care and recreation programmes available to these kids, so
that they get the things that other children —middle and upper-class children—get as of
right: those extra after -school care and activities that you otherwise have to pay for.
When we toured those mainly decile 1 to 4 schools, it was really interesting to talk to
principals and teachers about the issues.
Some of those schools did not have lime -green squabs and sliding doors, but what
they did have was absolutely dedicated principals and teachers who wanted the best
academic opportunities for their students. They recognised that without the school
having a good relationship with the local community, having food there to feed the kids,
and having an ability for those kids to participate in learning, have a good time, and
have cultural experiences that other kids have as of right, there would not be that five
out of five. So it is fine to talk about all of these wonderful things —and we support
digital literacy and we love lime -green squabs; that is great —but the reality is that we
need to listen to what our decile 1 teachers and principals are telling us about the kids.
The Government has made a strong argument that things like Te Kotahitanga should
be frozen, because they are expensive, apparently, and that building on success is the
new way to bring forward cultural inclusion. Well, actually, Te Kotahitanga ha s been
very successful because, just like school hubs, it put a person in the school to support
the profession to meet the needs of Māori children, in particular. So when we start
talking about really making a difference, it is not going to be about spendi ng money on
constantly revising programmes and getting rid of ones that work. We need to uphold
the fact that we need people in the school system who have the skills, whether it is the
school nurse or the Te Kotahitanga facilitator, or whether it is qualit y, early childhood
education with 100 percent trained teachers. We cannot talk about quality in one breath,
and in the next breath say that we are going to open up early childhood education to
Kidicorp, and we are going to allow charter schools from zero to 8 years.
We have this very odd estimate in Vote Education this time around the Minister of
Education’s new idea, which is that babies aged nothing and children up to the age of 8
should be allowed to be in charter schools. We know that it was the Ministe r’s idea
because we have seen on the report that she received from the ministry what she wrote
in her own handwriting: “This is the idea. Add this to the criteria.” We see these very
odd experimental fringe ideas that come from an international system call ed “the
GERM”. If people are not aware what that is, it is the global education reform
movement, and it is based on the market philosophy that education is the new frontier,
where we can all make money and turn it all into a franchise. This has been attemp ted
with very minimal success in the United States and Britain. These are not the places we
should be using as the models for a modern education system. We need to go back to
the fundamentals, and the fundamentals are not narrowing the curriculum to a narr ow
definition of literacy and numeracy.
The money that will be spent in the estimates on professional development around
national standards will not succeed, because those standards are neither national nor a
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19099
standard. What they have done is reduce childr en’s confidence in themselves and
teachers’ confidence in themselves. If there is one thing we know about learning, it is
that you have got to be confident. We have to be confident that we can do things. If we
are constantly told that we are below standard  or that we are failing our children
because we have taken kids for whom English may be a second language and moved
them up in their ability to learn, to read, to write, to think, to talk, and to participate, but
that does not meet the standard, then is th e teacher a failure? I do not think so. And if
the child has come to school with barriers that, hopefully, no one in this Chamber has
ever faced in terms of poverty, dislocation, transience, possibly no English, all of those
experiences—if those children a re expected to meet a standard and are then called a
failure when they have hugely improved as a result of the efforts of teachers, then we
have missed the bus about what learning is.
Learning is not a tick -the-box mechanistic exercise. We do not need tic k-the-box
exercises. We need to take the New Zealand curriculum, we need to take the cultural
experiences of some of our expert people who are involved in looking at what makes it
work, and we need to invest in that. Yes, it takes money, but there is no gr eater
investment than in our children, and there is no greater investment than in recognising
that children who are hungry and communities that are alienated from education require
our attention in the most profound way. It is not rocket science. There are  people out
there who are growing food in schools, who are teaching people to cook in schools, and
who are building adult and community education back into schools despite the
Government cutting it out of the previous Budget in 2008. We are seeing excellen t
practice going on in our schools and there are people with a lot to tell us. We should be
listening to those people very carefully before making up experiments like the charter
schools for 0 to 8 -year-olds or the limited authority to teach without any pr ofessional
commitments being allowed to be expanded to 3 years, which is what the new
Education Amendment Bill (No 2) will do.
We are disappointed that the estimates for Vote Education do not meet the real need.
We do consider it an underperforming economy when 290,000 children live in poverty.
It does not matter how many statistics we hear in this House about how successful
everything is if our kids are hungry, if they cannot learn, and if our schools are
underfunded. We have to invest in changing that cycle and empowering those kids and
their families to believe that they are entitled to participate in society as well as in all the
things that the privileged have, and that can be done. The Greens have a positive and
modern vision for how that can be done. It was awesome to travel and to get positive
feedback from all of these people who work at the front line, saying “Yes, we want  to
be in that relationship with our communities. We would appreciate your support. We are
creative with our funding. We do not expect the earth, but what we do want is to be able
to build these relationships alongside you.” That is what we believe the sch ool hubs
programme and putting kids at the heart of it means. If children rather than rhetoric are
at the heart of our decision making, we are going to get a different outcome.
The school system does need to be constantly scrutinised. It is important that  we
check ourselves in terms of what we are doing, but we should not be adopting the global
education reform movement and the fringe experiments simply because they offer an
ideological consistency with the idea of education being business and just another
market. Thank you.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I rise to
speak about Vote Education. I think when we look at the amount of money that has
been spent, that is one way of evaluating things. The Opposition has concentrated on
trying to get a smoke -and-mirrors exercise going so that there is perpetual
19100 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
bewilderment, at least on that side of the Chamber, about how much is actually spent
and where that money is spent.
We do not share those confused states. From our perspective, it is pretty
straightforward. We have put a great deal of money into education —$10.1 billion in the
financial year —because we believe that it is the most worthwhile investment we can
make. If we want New Zealand to grow and prosper as a nation, we need to give our
young people every opportunity to get the kind of education that will bring out the very
best in what they are able to achieve as individuals.
Recently I took part in a gif ted and talented children’s political panel, where we
looked at how that group of people is assisted. There are a lot of areas where the
Ministry of Education and this Government are moving towards that are going to
encourage those very talented and very g ifted children to achieve their best. Rolling out
broadband is one thing. The professional development that is put through for the
teachers is very important, not only in English but also in the medium of Māori, and that
is working very well.
Early childhood education—a lot of people have spoken about it and said that really
what we are trying to do is to get that sort of start for as many young people as we
possibly can. Our target was pretty well a straightforward one. We wanted 98 percent of
children ha ving participation in quality early childhood education by 2016. We are
already at 95.7 percent. We are well on track to doing that. What needs to happen with
our very young people is that they are made to feel confident and certain that they can,
with diligence and application, get the best education that they possibly can. So, yes, we
have concentrated on trying to bring up to a standard our poorest performing young
people, because they need that extra assistance. But that must not be at the expense of
gifted and talented children or the great mass of children who are really at a similar
level, with that similar curiosity and excitement.
In my North Shore electorate over the past couple of years I have seen firsthand what
it is like—that sense of excitement as new classrooms are opened up and rolled out, and
as the broadband comes through. These are quality teaching environments and quality
learning environments. Yes, there are sliding doors and, yes, there are lime green
squabs. In fact, the squabs are al l sorts of colours. That does not matter. These are
places that are child friendly and teacher friendly. At Mairangi Bay Primary School, for
example, where I opened a block, which is set above the old classrooms, the teachers
were ecstatic. That is the wor d I would use. They were absolutely convinced that they
had the best possible learning environment for the young people in their school, and
they were right.
Initially, when the designs came out, these same teachers were a little uncertain as to
whether that kind of environment would suit their teaching methods and the children.
They were a little change averse, let us face it. That is not unknown in the teaching
profession, and in other professions as well. But really, when you look at the results and
you look at the outcomes, you look at the broadband roll -out—$700 million is being
spent there—and at digital learning, which has been a very big part of what the Minister
the Hon Nikki Kaye was talking about earlier, what we have had is at the forefront of
where we want to make technology relevant to people’s lives. This has worked in a way
that I think has surprised many, because it has enabled young people to learn at their
own pace, to learn from home.
The education site gifted.tki.org.nz, which is the Mi nistry of Education site, has just
enjoyed an upgrade. There were eight different modules in there for teaching advanced
mathematics, for example, and the children were extraordinarily enthusiastic about that,
and rightly so. They were able, in their own t ime and in their own homes and at their
own pace, to not have the frustrations of perhaps being held back by other children, but
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19101
were able to carve their own path and be stimulated to the level that they need to be so
that they are not bored and frustrated . They are able to share with each other, via the
medium of high technology, their latest thoughts and ideas. I think that has probably
done an enormous amount to relieve that sense of isolation that some of these children
have had because they have been m ade to feel different and special, but not always in a
good way.
I think that the various measures that we have been putting into education have
worked extremely well. It is why this Government has spent so much money —because
we believe that that is the w ay for the future. Yes, we have spent money on
infrastructure and health, but education has been one of our priorities because we are a
Government that cares about families, that cares about children, and that cares about
people. We are not prepared to bor row big and go into a routine where we cannot pay
our debts back in order to fund our education and our other excellent policies. Thank
you.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: It is great to follow on from my
very energetic colleague Maggie Barry, the member for North Shore, and to pick up on
her very positive tone. When listening to some of the members opposite, you would
think that everything is wrong in education, but, in fact, tha t is not my experience at all.
Yesterday I had the pleasure of visiting Melville Primary School in my electorate. I
think that it is just such a bustling, happy, and positive environment. There is a great
principal there, dedicated staff, and young people who are all focused on what they need
to do, and taking advantage of the opportunities they are given.
Just before I talk about some of the specific aspects of the education estimates, I
want to draw attention to a very good presentation that was given in the Grand Hall
during the dinner adjournment, which I suppose crosses over both the justice and the
education sectors. But there is no question that education now is a highly IT -dominated
activity. Young children now are incredibly computer -literate, and, of course, there is
that great maxim now that whenever people of our age get stuck, you need to look for a
21st century kid in order to help you sort things out. But the reason I want to draw
attention to that particular exercise that we had this evening i s that it was all about
cyber-safety and knowing how to use the internet and all the online options safely. A
document that has been put out called Staying Safe Online is one that I would strongly
commend to all parents and to children who are old enough t o be able to make sense of
it. It contains a whole lot of tips, good practical stuff, on how to use the internet safely.
Of course, that is something that is very important in our schools now.
I am sure we are all aware of the fact that some young people have got themselves
into incredible difficulty, and at times very distressing circumstances, when they have
misused the internet. This is a document that has been produced by NetSafe, in
collaboration with Facebook, YouTube, Google, Microsoft, Yahoo! New Z ealand, and
TradeMe. If there are parents who are watching who would like to know how to get it, I
am sure that if you go to the NetSafe website, which is www.netsafe.org.nz, you will
get it from there. It does contain, as I say, a lot of information that is highly valuable. I
want to thank all the presenters tonight for being here in Parliament to educate MPs and
others who were present on this rapidly evolving aspect of our lives.
When listening to some of the members opposite, you would think that educa tion
was chronically underfunded and that everything was going wrong. Let me just point
out to those who are listening that in the next financial year $10.1 billion is allocated to
Vote Education. We have, as a Government, progressively increased the inves tment
right across the board and tied to that significant increases in our expectations of
educational outcomes. I want to acknowledge all of those who are working in the
education sector for the significant achievements that they are getting.
19102 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
I was particularly disappointed to hear Mr Hipkins trying to argue that somehow this
Government has cut funding for early childhood education. Nothing could be further
from the truth. In fact, in the last election campaign I remember going to meetings with
a chart sh owing the huge increase in our investment in early childhood education over
the years of this National Government. I am very proud of that, and I am particularly
proud that tied to the increase in funding was a particular challenge to raise engagement
by Māori and Pasifika families, because they were traditionally the families who were
the most likely to be not engaged in early childhood education.
We all know that those who have a good experience in those pre - primary school
days, and who are ready to le arn, hit school running and take off, whereas the children
who arrive at school having not had that basic education are at a disadvantage from the
outset. All the statistics tell us that they are likely to fall further and further behind. I
want to commend  all those who are working in the early childhood sector for the
incredible successes that they are having at the moment, where we are seeing Māori and
Pasifika levels of achievement and engagement in early childhood education at record
levels, and pretty much up there now with European, Asian, and other population
groups. That has to be good for every one of us.
At the other end of the scale, another initiative that I am really excited about is the
Youth Guarantee scheme. Youth Guarantee is seeing a large  number of young people—
teenagers who are 16, 17, and now even 18 and 19 -year-olds—who have previously
fallen out of the education system, gone through the cracks, and have often been truants
or engaged in activities outside school that are unsatisfactory.  Now they are getting
ahead, with Youth Guarantee. It is a system that is working tremendously, and it is
seeing again a huge increase in opportunities for young people.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Education Review Office agreed to.
Vote Arts, Culture and Heritage agreed to.
Vote Attorney-General agreed to.
Vote Parliamentary Counsel agreed to.
Vote Treaty Negotiations

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.role: Chairperson of the Māori Affairs Committee
items.text: I want, first
of all, to doff my Queensland hat to the honourable Minister Finlayson, who has, over
the last 6 years, shepherded through what can only be seen as, and said to be, some
amazing settlements, some amazing negotiations, by the likes of former members of this
House Rick Barker and Paul Swain, and others as well. I want to thank the Hon Chris
Finlayson for shepherding negotiations through Cabinet, and my thanks also to the
select committee, which has done an enormous amount of work trying to hu rry things
through, but at such a pace that we do not forget how important it is to do that.
I want to make some points. This Government has done more for Treaty settlements
than any other Government. People across the way may frown and they may pull face s,
but that is part of being in the Opposition.

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: That’s how they look.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Yes, that is how they look. But here is this. It was started by
Sir Doug Graham, and an enormous amount of work was done on the first part. Labour
came along and did diddly -squat. Labour did a couple of settlements. But to be able to
do settlements—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It set up most of the stuff that’s happening.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19103

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Yeah, OK. Wel l, it set up some offices —thanks very much.
But when you are doing Treaty settlements, you have to be one -minded, and the one
thing in your mind has to be justice. It has to be getting on with it. This Government has
shown that we have got on with it. It w as about justice. It is about justice. Hundreds of
people have been through the process—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It’s a bipartisan process.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Yeah, I forgot about that —I forgot about that. It is always a
bipartisan process when you are in Opposition. But thanks very much —thanks very
much for your hard work, madam, and ladies and men of the Opposition. But the reality
is if you do not have a plan, nothing is going to come from it. This Minister, this
Government, and the National Party had a plan. They stuck with it and they are sticking
with it.
As we speak, many negotiations are still going on around the country. I am ever
hopeful that Ngāti Hine can see their way through to actually working with what is in
front of them. They will get their cut of the cake, either way. I am sure that Ngāpuhi and
Ngāti Hine, along with so many others, will one day benefit from the negotiations —the
Treaty settlement process.
Treaty settlements are not made to fix the wrongs of society; they ar e about justice.
And when that happens, iwi and people who whakapapa directly to the respective iwi
can look towards the uplifting in terms of the economic and social well -being of those
same people. Six years of hard work by our Minister have made his nam e synonymous
with success in this area, in the Treaty settlement area. I am glad to say that the National
Government has got in behind it and has funded more settlements than ever before
because it wanted to and because there was a plan —and those are the t wo things we
need when we are looking at settlements. Some will say that it is not enough. It is never
enough, and we will never ever have enough money to settle some of the grievances
before our nation. Finally, I say to those who vote against, and abstai n on, Treaty
settlements, namely New Zealand First, that that is an appalling state of affairs.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Tr eaty of Waitangi
Negotiations): I am sure the Committee will indulge me when I, as the Minister for
Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations, simply say how grateful I am to the excellent chair of
the Māori Affairs Committee, the Hon Tau Henare. He and that team in  Māori affairs
have done a wonderful job, and I want to say to him that his best years are ahead of him
and I thank him for his service to this country.
I also want to acknowledge, very briefly, Shane Jones, who has left us, because this
is a bipartisan effort and the contribution of Shane to Treaty settlements, and the advice
he has given me over the years I greatly appreciate, certainly in relation to the Te Hiku
Claims Settlement Bill, which is being introduced to the House. I said to Kelvin Davis,
for w hom I have enormous respect as a person and a parliamentarian, that it is a
pleasure to work with him and it will be a pleasure to work with him on these matters —
unlike, I regret to say, Mr Harawira, who talks big but never delivers. In fact, when it
came to Ngāpuhi, he said to me not so long ago: “I say one thing to you and another
thing to others in my family.” Well, that is the way he wants to operate, but at the end of
the day he does not achieve very much and that is why I think that Kelvin leaves him
for dead.
But this is about bipartisan effort, and I want to say that so much good work has been
done by the chief Crown negotiators. Mr Henare was gracious enough to mention Rick
Barker, former Minister in here, and Paul Swain, who chairs the negotiating  panel and
does a very good job for me. I also want to mention people like John Isles and also John
Wood, because together they have been a formidable team and have enabled us to
address a large number of matters. I must, of course, refer to the Office of Treaty
19104 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
Settlements and the very good work that it does. The proof of the pudding, as they say,
is in the eating. Just a couple of weeks ago, for example, we signed agreements of
principle with the Wairoa and Hastings taiwhenua of Ngāti Kahungunu. I am very  busy
at the present time working with Ron Mark and the team in Ngāti Kahungunu ki
Wairarapa.
We are making very good progress down the East Coast, and what I certainly hope is
that before this House rises on 31 July we will be in a position where we can sign a deed
of settlement with the Whanganui River iwi. That will be a great day for this country
because that is, in fact, 150 years of litigation that went to all the courts of our land and
has been a very long time coming. As I understand it, ratification is going very well, and
it will be a tremendous tribute to Mrs Turia to be able to sign that deed of settlement. I
see Mr Borrows listening intently —and so he should because it is in his takiwā. It will
be great to sign it the day after Mrs Turia says g oodbye to this House after what has
been an extraordinary period of service.
So there is a lot of work to do. Let me emphasise that this Government never said
that there was a deadline of 2014. You cannot have a deadline to resolve these hugely
important matters. It was an aspirational goal. We have done our very best and the
progress that has been made has been phenomenal. Take, for example—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: An aspirational goal.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I hear the sneering of Sue Moroney on the
other side. She could not buy into anything bipartisan if she tried. But Hauraki is an
example of where there are 12 individual iwi and two collective settlements, and with a
bit of luck and a good headwind we sh ould be in a position, I hope, to initial at least 10
of those individual deeds and the two collectives before we get into the campaign
season.
In the spirit of bipartisanship—it is often regarded as a great weakness of mine, but I
try to reach out in a bipartisan way—I have to say that I do appreciate the support of the
Labour Party and other parties in this House so that we could get the work done. I have
nothing but contempt for New Zealand First, which took a shockingly partisan approach
to the Te Urewera—Tūhoe Bill when it was going through the Committee the other day.
Its members were divisive. They had two fundamental problems: they were divisive and
unpleasant, and they were plain wrong. They did not listen to the facts as they were
spelt out to them and instead—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: We stood up for the little guy when you railroaded that through.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON  —like that demented creature over there —
just yelled and screamed.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Social Development

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak in the estimates
debate on Vote Social Development. I want to start at the beginning, which is around
child poverty, because inequal ity is growing in this country and New Zealanders are
very clear about that. The Government members can carp and wail and moan and cry
their crocodile tears about it, as they do, but the reality is that the vast majority of New
Zealanders, when asked wheth er inequality was growing in this country, said yes, it
was. That is because that is what they see day in, day out in their own communities and
they are not going to be fooled by a Government that, first of all, says that inequality is
not growing and, secondly, refuses to actually even measure child poverty.
I think the country feels very let down by the Government when it comes to social
development, because the Government seems completely out of touch with the impact
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19105
of its own policies. I say that becau se the Government has had some deliberate policies
that have grown inequality. Take, for example, its tax cuts right at the height of a global
recession. Who would have thought that tax cuts favouring the wealthy would be the
best thing that a Government could come up with as we were heading into the midst of a
global recession? None the less, that is what the National Government did. Who can be
surprised, then, that inequality is growing? The area where we see that growing
inequality causes New Zealanders the greatest discomfort is when the number of
children living in poverty grows in this country, as it has done under this National
Government.
So here we are in a food -producing nation—a very wealthy society, actually —that
has great resources and a good level of wealth, and 27 percent of our children live in
poverty. Twenty -seven percent of our children —that is more than one in four. More
than one in four of our children live in poverty. John Key may well be relaxed about
that. He may shrug his shoulders, crack a grin, and crack one of his jokes, but on this
side of the Chamber and in the Labour Party we are not relaxed with having 27 percent
of our children in this country living in poverty. We are not OK with that and we are not
going to stand by and just watch that continue to happen.
In terms of the estimates for Vote Social Development, you would think that having
27 percent of our children i n poverty would be an issue that would concern the
Government and that it would have some measure —any measure at all —in its Budget
to address this issue. But there was not one measure, not a single measure in the
estimates, in the Budget, to help address c hild poverty. There was no move to create
jobs. There was no move in the estimates to increase families’ incomes. There was no
move in the Government’s estimates to actually help families out in this regard. So we
saw no measures to address this particular issue.
On this side of the House what we have seen is a Labour Party that is prepared to
lead on addressing this issue. We are not going to pretend that this issue does not exist.
We are not going to put our heads in the sand. We are not going to demonstr ate how out
of touch we are, like that Government does, day in, day out, when it pretends that this is
not going on. People out there in New Zealand see it in their communities and they
know it is indeed going on.
In the Labour Party we have said that we are going to do something about it. We
have a Best Start payment that we have announced. This will be a policy from the
incoming Labour -led Government. What that will do is ensure that all families —
actually, almost all families; families with up to $150,00  coming into the household per
year—with a newborn child will get $60 a week. That will apply to all of those families,
over and above when they are getting paid parental leave as well. So families will get an
entitlement to paid parental leave—and in fact under the Labour Party plan they will get
an extended entitlement to paid parental leave. They will get 26 weeks’ paid parental
leave and then they will get the $60-a-week payment.
But for low and modest -income families it is even better, because that $6 0-a-week
payment will continue until that child’s third birthday. That is a measure that will
reduce child poverty. It will also give some help to those families who are really
struggling on a week to week basis to make ends meet because their power costs and
housing costs are going up but their wages are not going up under this Government. So
that is a very practical solution to a problem that I think is a source of shame for our
country. I feel ashamed that in a country with wealth of the nature that New Zealand
has, we allow 27 percent of our children to live in poverty. That is not OK. John Key is
relaxed about it. We are not.
I want to go on to talk about another area in social development. The Government
seems to be very boastful about getting people off benefits. Well, it would have
19106 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
something to boast about if people were going off benefits and into jobs, but the most
recent quarterly data shows that of all the people who came off benefits in the quarter
ended March 2014, only 36 percent of them went off benefits into work —only 36
percent of them. In other words, 64 percent of them stopped receiving a benefit but they
did not get a job. I am challenging the Government to tell us what is happening with the
rest of those people, because this Government h as actually put in laws whereby, for the
first time in my living history, people who miss an appointment with Work and Income
or for some reason cannot turn up to a seminar —the seminar might be 40 kilometres
away from where they live and there is no public  transport—get cut off the benefit. If
they have dependent children, they get their benefit cut in half. I want to know from the
Minister for Social Development what is happening to those thousands of New
Zealanders who are suffering that fate, because tha t is going to be a big driver of
increasing child poverty in this country.
What I do know is that since the welfare reforms have come into being 4,328 people,
as at the end of March 2014, had failed these obligations and therefore ended up with no
income—no income whatsoever —for 13 weeks. I think the Minister for Social
Development owes the country an explanation about what is happening to those people.
Where are they going? How are they paying the rent? How are they paying their power
bills? Where are they  living? How are they eating? What is happening to those people
who suddenly have no income, no income at all, for 13 weeks and perhaps longer?
The Minister for Social Development, when I asked her about this at the Social
Services Committee, said she did  not want to know. She said that people were not
required to tell her and that she had no interest in knowing. I think that is an appalling
indictment on a Minister who calls herself the Minister for Social Development. The
National Government has changed those laws and so it has a responsibility to know
what is happening to those people. This is another area that is driving inequality in our
country.
The figures that I just quoted do not even tell us the number of people who have
children and who have had their benefits halved under these measures. We do not know
yet what that number is, but I am very concerned about that. The other figure that I am
concerned about is the 64 percent increase between September 2013 and March 2014 in
the number of people who came off a benefit because they went to Australia. Actually, I
do not know that they went to Australia, but I do know that they went overseas. They
left New Zealand. They gave up looking for jobs here in droves, and they cancelled
their benefits because they were going to live somewhere else. Probably they have gone
to Australia to look for work, and there has been a 64 percent increase in the number
doing that.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: It is
my pleasure to take a call in the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill debate in
respect of social welfare. I would like to start by congratulating my friend and colleague
the Hon Paula Bennett on the wonderful work that she has done in her 6 -year tenure as
the Minister for Social Development. It is interesting to look back over previous
Ministers and see the imprint that they have left on our social welfare system and I am
sure that, with hindsight, people will say that Paula Bennett has made a significant
impact in the social sector. It is interesting also to note —to acknowledge, I guess, rather
than note—that there is always a bit of a scrap between left and right in the way you do
social welfare. The left will always say that those of us on the right are mean and stingy
and look after only our rich mates. We will say that those on the left only ever patronise
the poor and do their very best to either ignore them or leave them  poor so that they
have got a reason to keep on voting for a socialist Government.
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19107
I want to talk about a couple of key changes that we made. [ Interruption] I will give
the member calling out just now a quick indication. I was in charge of a piece of
legislation. It was the welfare fraud bill. I offered the opportunity for people to come
and to sit in my office and talk about exactly this piece of legislation, obviously with a
view to be able to gain their support as it came before the House. Jan Logie too k
advantage of that. Tracey Martin took advantage of that. Su’a William Sio took
advantage of that, but Sue Moroney’s opportunity to come coincided with the
Melbourne Cup. She never showed and has never been back to hear about it. We have
just heard a spee ch on how Labour is the only lot who care and apparently we on the
right side of the Chamber do not give a stuff. But there are a couple of initiatives that I
would really like to be able to just elucidate for those people who are listening.
One of them i s around the youth payment. When Labour was in Government, the
independent youth benefit was money that was handed to those people under 18 who
could not get the dole and who for some reason could not live at home, either because
they would not live under the rules of house as they existed at the time or because home
was a dangerous place and it was not good for them to live there. In any event, they
were given a sum of money and that was it. Under this Government, on the initiative of
the Hon Paula Bennett, those people on the youth payment now get their board paid for
them. They get a card with their allowance on that and they get some discretionary
spending. At $6,000 a head they get a budget mentor to walk alongside them, show
them how to spend their money, how to save, and where to put their energies in order to
have a better life. What we know is that under the system that Labour continued with,
about 100 percent of young people on the independent youth benefit who turned 18
went straight on to the dole. What we know now is that only 45 percent of young people
turning 18 and going from the youth payment go on to the dole, because they are going
into education or they are going into work or they are going into training, and that is a
real plus.
Paula Bennett also instituted a similar system for solo mothers under the age of 20; a
similar system where they get their board or rent paid and their electricity paid. They get
their benefit on a card. They have some discretionary income, with the opportunity to be
able to get some more discretionary income by attending up to three courses —they are
able to get an extra allowance for each course as they spend it. That allows them to
spend that money as they wish, and so they should, because good behaviour should be
rewarded. Also, at $6,000 a pop they get a budget mentor, who assists them in learning
how to live, in learning how to budget, in learning how to care for their children. That is
the encouragement.
Under the Labour Government they got the benefit thrown at  them and they walked
away; the Government took no more skin in the game. What we know is that when we
started this policy there were 4,300 solo mums under 20 receiving that benefit. Now, 2
years later, we know that there are 2,600 of those mothers. They a re still having their
babies, so it is not the circumstance of pregnancy or a lack of relationship that finds
them on a benefit. What we do know is that this Government is doing a heck of a lot for
those people who otherwise could easily make up the statis tics of children living in
poverty that the previous speaker was speaking about. I applaud the Minister for that.
I would also like to touch on a number of other things that we are doing within the
social sector and the results that we are having. I talke d earlier about the initiative
around welfare fraud. What we have found over many, many years is that women living
on the domestic purposes benefit are frequently the prey of men who snuggle up next to
them, who provide some comfort for them, who invariabl y take their benefit from them
and use it for other means rather than for the support of the children; or they live like a
leech in a relationship with these women and carry on working, and because of that
19108 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
relationship the domestic purposes beneficiary, the mum, is in breach. The law has only
ever attached criminal responsibility and the debt to the beneficiary, the mum. How fair
can that be? When a relationship goes on for, say, a number of years, what we find is
that, of those people who are found to be c ommitting benefit fraud, the highest dollar
value is attached to people on the domestic purposes benefit. These blokes, if they do
nothing to perpetuate the fraud by making a false statement, say, to the police or to
social welfare, walk away scot-free.
Under this Government, what we set about doing then was to change the law to read
that if somebody has benefited from living on the proceeds of a benefit, then they will
carry not only the criminal responsibility for that act but also the debt. Now we have an
opportunity to charge the male —usually—who was living on the proceeds of benefit
fraud and who knew, should have known, or was reckless as to whether their partner
was a beneficiary. Now they will be prosecuted and will carry the same criminal
responsibility as —it is usually the woman —the beneficiary partner. Also we will be
able to recover the debt —not half the debt; we can recover up to the whole debt from
that male partner. How on earth can a male living in a household like that, where he is
not paying any rent, not paying any power, not contributing to the groceries, or anything
else but using that money for his own purposes, or for both their purposes, be able to
walk away scot-free? One of the things that was raised at that time, of course, was about
a woman in a violent relationship. If she is being extorted to live in this relationship or
to continue applying for a benefit, would this change in the law then put her under a
legal encumbrance? The answer is no, because the courts have found that a wo man
living in a battered -woman relationship is not living in a relationship in the nature of
marriage, so would not be held liable for that offence. That is a really important point to
note.
Members on the other side of the House drew analogies between we lfare fraud and
tax evasion. They said that the Government was putting far too much emphasis on
welfare dependency and none on those who were avoiding paying their taxes. The point
that they overlook is that in a succession of three zero Budgets, this Gove rnment put
aside $200 million for efforts to uncover tax evasion and to get that money in. It has
easily paid for itself. We are proud of the attributes of the Inland Revenue Department
for doing exactly that. Another thing that we have done in this partic ular space is to
share information with the Inland Revenue Department so that we can find out, for
instance, those people who are registered on the dole, the domestic purposes benefit, the
sickness benefit, or the invalid’s benefit, and are also working an d paying tax. The
Inland Revenue Department advises the Ministry of Social Development of those
people who it believes are defrauding the taxpayer, through this mechanism. It is
interesting to note that, since we started, 6,300 people have gone off a benef it because
they were already in work and they had been receiving illegal overpayments.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: The Green Party loves New Zealand, which is why we want
a cleaner, smarter, and fairer New Zealand and a Ministry of Social Development. The
Green Party and its MPs are absolutely passionate about making New Zealand a great
place to grow up in for all of our children. When one in four children live in poverty in
this country, something is going seriously wr ong. The Greens have been calling for
action on child poverty since 1999. We will keep on calling for action and proposing
solutions until we eliminate the problem. But this is not about us; this is about New
Zealand.
Over the last 3 years, along with mos t other New Zealanders in the country, we have
been listening to the Children’s Commissioner, academics, doctors, community
advocates, parents, and children themselves asking us to put children first. We have
been watching the documentaries and the news pr ogrammes, along with the rest of the
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19109
country, and reading the reports from the Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child
Poverty, the thousands of submissions on the green paper, the white paper, and the
Vulnerable Children Bill, as well as the all too n umerous media stories and opinion
pieces calling for us in this House to address inequality and end child poverty. New
Zealand, we will continue to listen and carry your voices for our children into this place
until we create a country where every child thrives.
With the rest of the country we have been seeing the pictures of empty school
lunchboxes, of mouldy houses, of children without shoes or raincoats. We have read
recently about the young mother and her newborn baby who had to live in a car for two
days after they were discharged from hospital, because there was no housing available
for them. Like the rest of the country, I assume, we have fumed at, and at times cried
over, the fact that more than one child a week is dying of poverty -related illness in this
country that we love. At times the stories feel endless and heart -breaking. How much
more it must feel like that for those who are living through it. The cruelty is real. But it
is not the cruelty of an individual; it is the cruelty of a Government that has chosen to
prioritise token efforts over addressing the real problems of poverty -level benefits, low
wages, and substandard housing.
Of course, we are being told that the Government is investing in our people, helping
them into work. Well, last we ek I met with some students and tutors on a Work and
Income mandated course, to find out how that was going for them. The tutor talked to
me about her concern that a mother on her course had had her benefit cut in half for
missing 3 days of the course, whe n it turned out that she had to go with her baby to
hospital after her baby had had a seizure, and she did not have enough money on her
phone to be able to inform anyone of that fact. So their income had been cut in half
while they were stuck in hospital. We heard from a student about how they had
previously had their benefit sanctioned entirely for missing an appointment because
their public transport was running late.
This is happening now in our country, and the sheer reality of being poor means that
there are times when some people cannot afford even to meet the expectations of Work
and Income to be able to get their income support. Everyone in that room of about 20
students and their tutor talked about not being able to afford to heat their house or pu t
proper food on their table. The young ones even talked about not being able to afford
the $40 to buy a blanket to compensate for the lack of heating in their house. So much
for a wraparound service, so much for supporting people, and so much for investment!
It does not have to be this way. It is not even about throwing money at the problem
and leaving people stuck in inequality, as this Government suggests we want to do.
Even at the most basic level it is actually about ensuring people get access to thei r legal
entitlements. Surely, at the absolute minimum that is the job of this Government. Yet
when we have asked the Minister for Social Development, in this House, how she
explains the increasing number of stories that we are hearing from the community of
people being denied their legal entitlements, her response was: “For every one story you
give me, I can give you 10 of people who are getting the entitlements they are eligible
for.”
Well, the basic point is that everyone is entitled to those services, an d it is this
Government’s job to ensure that people are able to get enough money to put food on the
table. That is what we consider a social security system. It is not in any way OK to say:
“Well, these 10 people are getting it, sorry about those ones.” Th at is not doing your
job. That is not providing even the bare minimum of what this country has agreed on,
let alone what is, I believe, a building consensus from academics, from community
organisations, and from people working across our health sector, our  education sector,
and our community sector, who are all saying that there needs to be more. There needs
19110 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
to be a living income for these families, and particularly for our children, because we
know that if we do not invest in those early years of a child’s  life, then we are robbing
them of their potential. That is something that every single person in this country will
have to bear the consequences of.
I really do want to speak just a little bit around the perception that this is too
expensive to do. This is not an issue just about this Government and these estimates; it
is about a framework that was put in place previously that has been consciously
continued by this Government. There has been a decision to prioritise getting these
families into work as the  way out of poverty for these families. I think that we have
missed the fact of the interaction between work and income support —that there is an
interaction between those two things. I would like to point out that the Government is
currently spending more on family in-work tax credits for families working 20 hours a
week than what it is spending on the income support system. The analysis by the Child
Poverty Action Group showed up that somebody coming off the DPB into paid work for
20 hours a week would be getting, on top of their income, a minimum family tax credit
of $22,000 a year, plus the in-work tax credit of $3,000 a year. So that is over $25,000 a
year for that family that is working less than 20 hours a week. What they would get on
the DPB would be $15,000. So the Government is paying a lot more for that group.
The problem with that is —because it is great for people to be able to work if that is
appropriate for their family and they are still able to look after their children —that this
is a system that creates a disincentive for those employers to pay anything more than the
minimum wage. On the minimum wage, somebody who is working the 20 hours a week
would have to work an additional 17 hours before being any better off financially. What
employer is going to pay somebody above the minimum wage if it is not going to give
them anything more in the hand? Basically, those employers are not going to do that.
That does not affect just that one person stuck on the minimum wage; it affects all other
workers i n New Zealand who are trying to get better conditions. So when the
Government tells us that it is all about work being the pathway out of poverty, actually,
what this is doing is entrenching people into poverty. When the Government took away
the training i ncentive allowance for parents to be able to do higher -level study, to be
able to get a chance of getting into that higher -wage bracket of work, we saw the lie of
it.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: I looked at the website of the Ministry of Social
Development and it said that the ministry is there to help people be successful in their
lives. It said that the ministry’s role is to help New Zealanders to be safe, strong, and
independent. My colleague Sue Mor oney—and Jan Logie has also traversed some of
this territory —talked about how inequality and poverty are denying many New
Zealanders the opportunity to be successful in their lives, the core aim of the Ministry of
Social Development.
I want to talk about another issue that limits the ability of people in this country to be
successful in their lives —for them to be safe, strong, and independent —and those are
issues to do with domestic and sexual violence. Issues of sexual and domestic violence
deny many peop le the opportunity to be successful in their lives. There are huge costs
associated with that violence, and there are barriers that are then put in the way of
people actually going about living their lives. Obviously, in extreme circumstances
people lose their lives, so they cannot continue to go on and be successful in their lives.
We have a serious problem in this country. We have a serious problem with the level of
violence that we see against our people, particularly women and children. I just thought
it would be worth noting some of those things.
Last week we had the independent Family Violence Death Review Committee report
come out. It looked at deaths between 2009 and 2012 —so, over a 3 -year period—and
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19111
47 percent of those deaths were family violence deaths. In nearly all of those
circumstances som eone was killed by their partner and there was a known history of
abuse. Thirty -seven children died —37 of our children died —and 77 children were
present when a parent or a sibling died in their home. These people are not going to be
able to live successful lives. Their lives have been cut short by other people’s violence.
Also, the chair of that committee said that —and I think this is just so chilling —the
reviews she read that were the most difficult for her to read were the ones where a
woman is clearly f ighting for her life: “She sees that she is going to die and she is …
actively taking every action she possibly can to save her life. She’s contacting the
police, she’s telling landlords, she’s telling neighbours, she’s telling friends … and we
are not providing her with effective help.” That is just absolutely chilling. And it is not
just domestic violence; one in three women in this country experience intimate partner
violence, sexual or domestic violence, during the course of their lifetime —one in three.
These figures are just horrendous.
So I think we need to be seriously looking at what is happening here and what should
be done. As well as the Family Violence Death Review Committee report last week, the
week before that, I think it was, we had the firs t of the Glenn Inquiry reports —500
interviews with people who have lived in violent situations. There is the loss of life —I
have talked about that —but there are also other costs. There is the loss of people’s
potential. There is the loss of potential for a  child, one of those 77 children who has
witnessed a sibling or a parent being killed by somebody else they potentially love,
another member of their family, and the impact that that has on that child.
There is the loss of their potential and the loss of opportunity for them to go on and
live in this country to their full potential rather than, in fact, going, all too commonly,
into a situation where a cycle of abuse is created. That is a real cost to us as well. For
some it is even a loss of freedom —the freedom to go about their life, to engage with
whom they want to, and to go and do their job or whatever. These are costs. These are
real costs for individuals. Some of them are, as I said, intergenerational. I have been on
the Social Services Committee and have listened to people who have come and talked to
us. Melissa Lee has done a very good job of chairing that committee. This violence is
preventable. This violence is preventable, and the Government has not done enough.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.role: Chairperson of the Social Services Committee
items.text: Following
Carol Beaumont’s speech, I would like to commend her for her passion in her speech
regarding the domestic violence situation in this country and the violence that our
children are facing. I thank the member for participating in the inquiry that the Social
Services Committee has been undertaking.
I am proud to stand on this side of the Chamber, as a member of the National -led
Government under the fantastic leadership of our Prime Minister, John Key. We are a
strong, united caucus behind a strong leader, and we have a Government that has led the
country from recession to sustained growth. We have an economy that has grown by 3.8
percent in the year to the end of March, the third -highest among the world’s developed
economies. It is forecast to reach  4 percent next year, which is a far cry from the
recession we inherited back in 2008.
I was sitting here listening to members opposite talking about some of the social
services and social welfare policies, and I was sort of wondering whether we were
living in the same country or not, because only a net 250 people moved to Australia in
May this year, which is the lowest since the data started in 1996. Under Labour 3,000
New Zealanders a month crossed the Tasman. That was a lot of Kiwis leaving our
shores. In the past year alone, there were more jobs that were created, and if we stick to
the Government’s programme, the average full -time wage is expected to rise to
19112 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
something like $62,000 or $63,000, which is up by about $8,000, in the next 4 years.
This follows a $3,000 increase in the average wage over the past 3 years.
As the economy grows, families will benefit from more jobs and higher wages, and
we are making sure that families will also be among the first to benefit from the extra
Government spending, b ecause family is very important. As members opposite have
also said, families are the core of our nation. Children are the core of our nation. I am
very proud to say that in this Budget we are investing $500 million in a package of
practical support for yo ung families and the vulnerable children who are most in need.
There is $33.4 million extra to support vulnerable children, with eight new children’s
teams to work with at-risk children and families and to support children in care.
I know that some member s talked about having to fix poverty, but child abuse
happens right across society. It does not happen just in poor families; it happens
everywhere. So poverty is not the reason that children are abused. Abuse happened
simply because they were being abused  by abusers. Some children happen to have a
lower socio-economic status and some a higher one. It is right across the board, and I
am appalled that members opposite keep on talking about poverty being the reason for
it.
Earlier, in a different speech —when we were talking about the Vulnerable Children
Bill—I said that poverty cannot be a reason for abusing children. Nothing can be a
reason or an excuse to abuse children. It is just abusers abusing children, full stop.
There is no tolerance for that. I know C arol Beaumont talked about the abuse level. I
cannot believe that she would actually give poverty as an excuse for children being
abused in this country.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: It’s not an excuse but it is a fact.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Your members have actually said that it was an explanation; it was
an excuse. The Government is taking its responsibility to support families very
seriously. We are putting millions of dollars into child protection and services for
vulnerable children and their families.
The other thing that I am very, very pleased about in the work that Paula Bennett has
done—and I would like to applaud the Ministers in the social welfare sector: both the
Hon Paula Bennett and Chester Borrows. One of the things I am most pro ud of as a
member, personally, is the reduction in teen pregnancies that we have seen. From the
policies that we have put through in this Government, we have seen lower rates of
teenagers getting pregnant. I am very positive for the young girls. For them, they will
have a future in education. I am not saying that they would make terrible parents, but
they will now have options. I think that is a fantastic record. There is $155.7 million
more for early childhood education, which has to be celebrated.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I take a call on Vote Social Development.
Recognising that our country’s greatest strength is our people, I draw your attention to
the more than 600,000 New Zealanders over  the age of 65 —almost 15 percent of our
population, and rapidly growing. Someone once said to judge a society on how it treats
its most vulnerable. By that standard, New Zealand is failing its seniors.
Although everyone wants to believe that all New Zeala nders are guaranteed security
in retirement and that the needs of seniors are well catered for, the reality could not be
more different. The inconvenient truth of the matter is that many seniors live in squalor
and despair, feel they are a burden on their families, and tend to withdraw from society
rather than seek help. The consequences are social isolation, malnourishment, and, at
the extreme end, suicide. When we talk about suicide we often refer to the high rate of
young people taking their lives, but t he statistics paint an equally disturbing picture for
our seniors. Last year the Chief Coroner warned that New Zealand men aged 85 or older
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19113
committed suicide at a rate of 31 per 100,000. Words cannot convey the deep sense of
tragedy that is inherent in those figures.
So what can we do about it? First, let us change the culture. Let us challenge the
stereotypes and the prejudices. Older New Zealanders deserve the love and respect of
society as a whole. We should all embrace the seniors in our lives, be they  family
members, neighbours, or friends. These people built our country. They have worked
hard, paid taxes, raised children and grandchildren, and enriched our society in so many
ways.
Second, we need public policy that reflects this —policy that recognise s and values
the contributions that our seniors have made, and policy that encourages seniors to
remain active participants in our society. Life does not end at retirement. Crucially, we
must put an end to political parties using seniors as a political football.
We in the New Zealand Independent Coalition expect cross -party consensus on
superannuation and senior care policy. We are fed up with our seniors being taken for
granted by cynical political leaders who have used them only as votes. The New
Zealand Independent Coalition takes seniors’ concerns seriously and is prepared to walk
the talk. Action is what matters. Over the years there has been no significant increase in
the amount of money in the pockets of older people, and that must change. How can we
expect seniors to live on $276 per week? Many are eating every other day, cannot afford
to go to the doctor, have not had any new clothes in years, and holidays are a thing of
the past.
We are told by Government officials that reasonable living requires $46,000 for a
single person. A senior living on New Zealand superannuation is expected to live on
under $22,000 a year gross. The small things in life are often the ones that bring the
most joy, but many are struggling to afford even those —for example, pets. Pets serve as
an important source of social and emotional support, and yet they are a joy that is
denied for many elderly who simply cannot afford to pay the vet bills or for the food.
The New Zealand Independent Coalition will adopt a policy of vet sub sidies for seniors.
If we are serious about improving the quality of life for senior New Zealanders, then
this is a small but powerful gesture towards doing just that.
We hear the continual cry that New Zealand cannot afford to go any higher in
payments to older people. Those parties degrade our seniors further by stating that they
are a burden that has to be carried, and force them to plead for help from Work and
Income. This intolerable situation cannot be allowed to continue. The New Zealand
Independent Coalition will pursue the implementation of a financial transaction tax
similar to that which has been adopted by 11 countries in the European Union, led by
France and Germany. Revenue from a financial transaction tax of just 0.1 percent would
collect over $6 billion a year from the transactions through the New Zealand banking
system and $3.5 billion in extra revenue from New Zealand’s foreign exchange system.
According to a Reserve Bank survey released today, New Zealand’s foreign
exchange market handled  an average US$12.4 billion per day in April 2013, which is
currently not taxed a single cent. A financial transaction tax on these traders would
produce a significant source of funding that would not only support a living pension and
living wage, but—[Bell rung] Mr Chair?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The member has been allocated one speech
in this debate, and that speech has now taken place. The member does not get a ny more
calls, unless he can negotiate with another party. At this stage, I am calling Alfred
Ngaro.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is an honour to take a call in this estimates debate
around social deve lopment. The best description I have been given about the election
period is that it is an opportunity to bring out the score card. In other words, you go out
19114 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014
to the communities in our cities and in our urban and rural parts up and down the
country and, re ally, it is a chance to actually show the nation what it is that we have
been doing. We know that New Zealanders are looking for a Government that they can
trust, that keeps its promises, and that works together with New Zealanders to make a
difference in their communities.
So for all the talk and all the rhetoric that there is, and for all of the people who are
inflating the stories around the hardship and the difficulties that we know are there in
our communities, when it comes down to it, for all of the  talk, we need to actually get
down to the action. What is it that we have done as a Government to care for those who
are vulnerable who need our support?
I just want to go back to one point. We have often been told that we are beneficiary
bashing and tha t we do not care for those in need. We provide social obligations for
those who are receiving a benefit so they can return to work. I just want to go back to
the Social Security Act 1964 —initiated in 1938 and reformed in 1964. Under section
1B of the princ iples of the Act, it states: “(a) work in paid employment offers the best
opportunity for people to achieve social and economic well -being: [and] (b) the priority
for people of working age should be to find and retain work:”—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Where are the jobs?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: And, Mr Clark, it says: “(c) people … should be assisted to
prepare for work in the future and develop employment-focused skills:”.
This is really clear about the fact that we know that people who can work should
work. This is about social obligations. These welfare reforms that we have had have not
gone away from the key principles —yes, and they were established in 1964. In fact, in
1938, Michael Joseph Savage and others set up these reforms. They were  about caring
for people. Here is what it says: work provides the best opportunities. That is what we
have done. So when we talk about social obligations, those who can work should work.
It is really simple. Most New Zealanders get it, right? Those opportunities are there.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Where are the jobs? When will you get back to Labour levels of
employment?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Mr Clark keeps on going on about the jobs. In fact, he keeps
banging on around that. The problem is he actually does not want to hear the statistics
and the facts. I am going to give Mr Clark a few statistics so he can go away. I have a
few little takeaway points for you, Mr Clark, and here they are: an extra 84,000 jobs
were created in the year to March , and Treasury forecasts 172,000 being created over
4½ years. There you go—84,000 jobs. The cost of living increases are low, and inflation
