was just 1.5 percent—Mr Clark will get this—in the year to March, well below average
weekly wage increases of 3.2 pe rcent. So what we are saying to Mr Clark, to others,
and, most important, to the Kiwis who are out there listening is that this is a
Government that has delivered. When it needed to do the things that are important to
care for the nation, that is what it has done. Average wage increases—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. The time has come for me to report progress.
Progress reported.
Report adopted.
The House adjourned at 9.56 p.m.

TUESDAY, 1 JULY 2014 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.

VISITORS 
Philippines—Paolo Benigno Aquino IV, Senate 
Mr SPEAKER : I am sure that members would wish to welcome Senator Paolo 
Benigno Aquino IV from the 16 th Congress of the Republic of the Philippines, who is 
present in the gallery. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Freshwater Management—Water Quality 
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Dr Russel Norman: Does he stand by his statement in relation to the Ruataniwha 
Dam that “there’s quite a bit of debate about the science …”; if so, is the debate that he 
is referring to being generated by other scientists or is the debate being generated by 
Federated Farmers? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. 
Dr Russel Norman : Well, with regard to debating the science, does he agree with 
the statements by Associate Professor Russell Death that “Mor e pollutants, lower water 
quality, it’s not rocket science.”, or by Professor David Hamilton that “  ‘business as 
usual’ will not get us over the line …” on water quality, or is it that he wishes to dispute 
the statements of Dr Mike Joy that the “Impacts on  fresh water from dairying have 
definitely got worse …” in the last 3 years? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, some of those statements have an element of truth in 
them, but there is a range of particular views from the scientific community, and we will 
see how the thing plays out. 
Dr Russel Norman : Well, with regard to the range of views, when he said on the 
BBC’s HARDtalk programme 3 years ago that he could find another scientist to state 
that intensive agriculture is not polluting our rivers, how is that going, and can he tell us 
the names of these other scientists? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well. 
Dr Russel Norman: Can he tell us the names of those other scientists? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: There would be a range of people who would indicate that you 
can actually increase agriculture and do it in an environmentally balanced way. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Prime Minister agree with the Otago Regional 
Council, which stated tha t his Government’s water -quality rules misapply the science 
and would result in water bodies that are not only unsafe for swimming or for letting 
your dog swim in but are potentially toxic and unsafe for stock to drink from? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. 
Dr Russel Norman : Is the reason that his Government is repeatedly rejecting the 
scientific evidence when it comes to Māui’s dolphins, polluted rivers, or climate change 
that the scientific evidence conflicts with his economic agenda of more oil, more cows, 
and more motorways? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In answer to the last part of the question, no. 
19030 Questions for Oral Answer 1 Jul 2014 
 
State-owned Assets, Sales—Purpose and Use of Proceeds 
2. JOHN HAYES (National —Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance : What 
progress is the Government making in allocating proceeds from its share offer 
programme to pay for new public assets through the Future Investment Fund? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government continues to make 
good progress in investing almost $4.7 billion from its share offer programme into new 
public assets. We are able to invest this money without having to borr ow more from 
overseas lenders. At the weekend the Prime Minister and Minister Brownlee confirmed 
that $212 million from the Future Investment Fund will be invested in 14 important 
regional State highway projects around New Zealand. That is on top of the $3 60 million 
that we have already proposed for regional roads across New Zealand. This investment 
will continue to build on the Government’s extensive investment in vital infrastructure, 
which includes ultra -fast broadband, schools, hospitals, roads, and rai l, and more of it 
will be financed from the Future Investment Fund. 
John Hayes: How will the latest investment in regional roads meet the objectives set 
for using capital raised from the Government’s share offer programme? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : This investment follows through on the logic of the sales, 
where the Government sold shares to investors, the investors passed cash to the 
Government, and now we have the opportunity to invest that cash. As the Prime 
Minister said at the we ekend, the investment in regional roads is a perfect example of 
money from the share floats being invested for the benefit of New Zealanders, the 
economy, and their families. The 14 projects are spread across the country from Otago 
to Northland, from the West Coast to the East Coast. 
John Hayes : What other investments in new public assets has the Government 
confirmed using proceeds from the share offer programme? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As the House is now familiar with, there is $4.7 billion of 
proceeds from the share offer programme. In Budget 2014 the Government confirmed a 
further $1 billion of new investment. This included $200 million for health, including 
$67 million for the new Grey Base Hospital on the West Coast. This too k health 
spending from the Future Investment Fund to $684 million. It also allocated $172 
million to education, including the upgrade and replacement of schools in Canterbury. 
KiwiRail received another $198 million. All up, the $1 billion allocated from th e fund 
in Budget 2014 brought the total allocated to almost $3 billion, which left nearly $1.7 
billion in the fund for new public assets over the next couple of years without having to 
borrow more money. 
John Hayes : What reports has he seen su pporting the Government’s approach to 
investing proceeds from the share offer programme in new public assets? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I have seen reports from an unlikely source: an alternative 
budget that was issued in the last week or two. Th e reports indicate that this alternative

introduced and the 2 -year safety strategy under the previous transport Minister, Steven 
Joyce, was implemented, the effect was nearly immediate.  
Last year, I am pleased to report, we had the lowest road toll in this country since 
1950. If one uses the measure of vehicle kilometres travelled, it would have been one -
sixth of the road toll of 6 3 years ago. So we are making progress, but I think it is 
important to reflect on what happens next. The 2 -year action plan has an engineering 
aspect to it, recognising that human beings, as we are, will make mistakes on the road,

roads is as good as we can afford and that drivers purchase vehicles that are as safe as 
we can afford.

transport systems—which are not just things of the future but are available today, in our

control that will slow a car down automatically if the car in front is slowing down. I am 
about to make some announcements around electronic stability control, or ESC, to 
ensure that over the next few years it becomes mandatory for all cars to have it.

served us very well historically. Institutions like the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research and the old MAF, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, 
contributed a great deal to the creation and the success of the pastoral industry. We have

cannot and will not build a rich and prosperous economy by trying to increase the

movement, and it is based on the market philosophy that education is the new frontier, 
where we can all make money and turn it all into a franchise. This has been attemp ted 
with very minimal success in the United States and Britain. These are not the places we 
should be using as the models for a modern education system. We need to go back to 
the fundamentals, and the fundamentals are not narrowing the curriculum to a narr ow 
definition of literacy and numeracy.  
The money that will be spent in the estimates on professional development around 
national standards will not succeed, because those standards are neither national nor a 
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19099 
 
standard. What they have done is reduce childr en’s confidence in themselves and 
teachers’ confidence in themselves. If there is one thing we know about learning, it is 
that you have got to be confident. We have to be confident that we can do things. If we 
are constantly told that we are below standard  or that we are failing our children 
because we have taken kids for whom English may be a second language and moved 
them up in their ability to learn, to read, to write, to think, to talk, and to participate, but 
that does not meet the standard, then is th e teacher a failure? I do not think so. And if 
the child has come to school with barriers that, hopefully, no one in this Chamber has 
ever faced in terms of poverty, dislocation, transience, possibly no English, all of those 
experiences—if those children a re expected to meet a standard and are then called a 
failure when they have hugely improved as a result of the efforts of teachers, then we 
have missed the bus about what learning is.  
Learning is not a tick -the-box mechanistic exercise. We do not need tic k-the-box 
exercises. We need to take the New Zealand curriculum, we need to take the cultural 
experiences of some of our expert people who are involved in looking at what makes it 
work, and we need to invest in that. Yes, it takes money, but there is no gr eater 
investment than in our children, and there is no greater investment than in recognising 
that children who are hungry and communities that are alienated from education require 
our attention in the most profound way. It is not rocket science. There are  people out 
there who are growing food in schools, who are teaching people to cook in schools, and 
who are building adult and community education back into schools despite the 
Government cutting it out of the previous Budget in 2008. We are seeing excellen t 
practice going on in our schools and there are people with a lot to tell us. We should be 
listening to those people very carefully before making up experiments like the charter 
schools for 0 to 8 -year-olds or the limited authority to teach without any pr ofessional 
commitments being allowed to be expanded to 3 years, which is what the new 
Education Amendment Bill (No 2) will do. 
We are disappointed that the estimates for Vote Education do not meet the real need. 
We do consider it an underperforming economy when 290,000 children live in poverty. 
It does not matter how many statistics we hear in this House about how successful 
everything is if our kids are hungry, if they cannot learn, and if our schools are 
underfunded. We have to invest in changing that cycle and empowering those kids and 
their families to believe that they are entitled to participate in society as well as in all the 
things that the privileged have, and that can be done. The Greens have a positive and 
modern vision for how that can be done. It was awesome to travel and to get positive 
feedback from all of these people who work at the front line, saying “Yes, we want  to 
be in that relationship with our communities. We would appreciate your support. We are 
creative with our funding. We do not expect the earth, but what we do want is to be able 
to build these relationships alongside you.” That is what we believe the sch ool hubs 
programme and putting kids at the heart of it means. If children rather than rhetoric are 
at the heart of our decision making, we are going to get a different outcome.  
The school system does need to be constantly scrutinised. It is important that  we 
check ourselves in terms of what we are doing, but we should not be adopting the global 
education reform movement and the fringe experiments simply because they offer an 
ideological consistency with the idea of education being business and just another  
market. Thank you.

debate on Vote Social Development. I want to start at the beginning, which is around

very clear about that. The Government members can carp and wail and moan and cry 
their crocodile tears about it, as they do, but the reality is that the vast majority of New 
Zealanders, when asked wheth er inequality was growing in this country, said yes, it 
was. That is because that is what they see day in, day out in their own communities and

not growing and, secondly, refuses to actually even measure child poverty. 
I think the country feels very let down by the Government when it comes to social 
development, because the Government seems completely out of touch with the impact 
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19105 
 
of its own policies. I say that becau se the Government has had some deliberate policies 
that have grown inequality. Take, for example, its tax cuts right at the height of a global 
recession. Who would have thought that tax cuts favouring the wealthy would be the 
best thing that a Government could come up with as we were heading into the midst of a 
global recession? None the less, that is what the National Government did. Who can be

inequality causes New Zealanders the greatest discomfort is when the number of 
children living in poverty grows in this country, as it has done under this National

has great resources and a good level of wealth, and 27 percent of our children live in 
poverty. Twenty -seven percent of our children —that is more than one in four. More 
than one in four of our children live in poverty. John Key may well be relaxed about 
that. He may shrug his shoulders, crack a grin, and crack one of his jokes, but on this 
side of the Chamber and in the Labour Party we are not relaxed with having 27 percent 
of our children in this country living in poverty. We are not OK with that and we are not 
going to stand by and just watch that continue to happen.  
In terms of the estimates for Vote Social Development, you would think that having 
27 percent of our children i n poverty would be an issue that would concern the 
Government and that it would have some measure —any measure at all —in its Budget 
to address this issue. But there was not one measure, not a single measure in the 
estimates, in the Budget, to help address c hild poverty. There was no move to create 
jobs. There was no move in the estimates to increase families’ incomes. There was no 
move in the Government’s estimates to actually help families out in this regard. So we

On this side of the House what we have seen is a Labour Party that is prepared to 
lead on addressing this issue. We are not going to pretend that this issue does not exist. 
We are not going to put our heads in the sand. We are not going to demonstr ate how out 
of touch we are, like that Government does, day in, day out, when it pretends that this is 
not going on. People out there in New Zealand see it in their communities and they 
know it is indeed going on.  
In the Labour Party we have said that we are going to do something about it. We 
have a Best Start payment that we have announced. This will be a policy from the 
incoming Labour -led Government. What that will do is ensure that all families —
actually, almost all families; families with up to $150,00  coming into the household per 
year—with a newborn child will get $60 a week. That will apply to all of those families, 
over and above when they are getting paid parental leave as well. So families will get an 
entitlement to paid parental leave—and in fact under the Labour Party plan they will get 
an extended entitlement to paid parental leave. They will get 26 weeks’ paid parental 
leave and then they will get the $60-a-week payment.  
But for low and modest -income families it is even better, because that $6 0-a-week 
payment will continue until that child’s third birthday. That is a measure that will 
reduce child poverty. It will also give some help to those families who are really 
struggling on a week to week basis to make ends meet because their power costs and 
housing costs are going up but their wages are not going up under this Government. So 
that is a very practical solution to a problem that I think is a source of shame for our 
country. I feel ashamed that in a country with wealth of the nature that New Zealand 
has, we allow 27 percent of our children to live in poverty. That is not OK. John Key is 
relaxed about it. We are not.  
I want to go on to talk about another area in social development. The Government 
seems to be very boastful about getting people off benefits. Well, it would have

something to boast about if people were going off benefits and into jobs, but the most

One of them i s around the youth payment. When Labour was in Government, the 
independent youth benefit was money that was handed to those people under 18 who 
could not get the dole and who for some reason could not live at home, either because 
they would not live under the rules of house as they existed at the time or because home 
was a dangerous place and it was not good for them to live there. In any event, they 
were given a sum of money and that was it. Under this Government, on the initiative of 
the Hon Paula Bennett, those people on the youth payment now get their board paid for 
them. They get a card with their allowance on that and they get some discretionary 
spending. At $6,000 a head they get a budget mentor to walk alongside them, show 
them how to spend their money, how to save, and where to put their energies in order to 
have a better life. What we know is that under the system that Labour continued with, 
about 100 percent of young people on the independent youth benefit who turned 18 
went straight on to the dole. What we know now is that only 45 percent of young people 
turning 18 and going from the youth payment go on to the dole, because they are going 
into education or they are going into work or they are going into training, and that is a 
real plus. 
Paula Bennett also instituted a similar system for solo mothers under the age of 20; a 
similar system where they get their board or rent paid and their electricity paid. They get 
their benefit on a card. They have some discretionary income, with the opportunity to be 
able to get some more discretionary income by attending up to three courses —they are 
able to get an extra allowance for each course as they spend it. That allows them to 
spend that money as they wish, and so they should, because good behaviour should be 
rewarded. Also, at $6,000 a pop they get a budget mentor, who assists them in learning 
how to live, in learning how to budget, in learning how to care for their children. That is 
the encouragement. 
Under the Labour Government they got the benefit thrown at  them and they walked 
away; the Government took no more skin in the game. What we know is that when we 
started this policy there were 4,300 solo mums under 20 receiving that benefit. Now, 2 
years later, we know that there are 2,600 of those mothers. They a re still having their 
babies, so it is not the circumstance of pregnancy or a lack of relationship that finds 
them on a benefit. What we do know is that this Government is doing a heck of a lot for 
those people who otherwise could easily make up the statis tics of children living in 
poverty that the previous speaker was speaking about. I applaud the Minister for that.  
I would also like to touch on a number of other things that we are doing within the 
social sector and the results that we are having. I talke d earlier about the initiative 
around welfare fraud. What we have found over many, many years is that women living 
on the domestic purposes benefit are frequently the prey of men who snuggle up next to 
them, who provide some comfort for them, who invariabl y take their benefit from them 
and use it for other means rather than for the support of the children; or they live like a 
leech in a relationship with these women and carry on working, and because of that 
19108 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014 
 
relationship the domestic purposes beneficiary, the mum, is in breach. The law has only 
ever attached criminal responsibility and the debt to the beneficiary, the mum. How fair 
can that be? When a relationship goes on for, say, a number of years, what we find is 
that, of those people who are found to be c ommitting benefit fraud, the highest dollar 
value is attached to people on the domestic purposes benefit. These blokes, if they do 
nothing to perpetuate the fraud by making a false statement, say, to the police or to 
social welfare, walk away scot-free.  
Under this Government, what we set about doing then was to change the law to read 
that if somebody has benefited from living on the proceeds of a benefit, then they will 
carry not only the criminal responsibility for that act but also the debt. Now we have an 
opportunity to charge the male —usually—who was living on the proceeds of benefit 
fraud and who knew, should have known, or was reckless as to whether their partner 
was a beneficiary. Now they will be prosecuted and will carry the same criminal 
responsibility as —it is usually the woman —the beneficiary partner. Also we will be 
able to recover the debt —not half the debt; we can recover up to the whole debt from 
that male partner. How on earth can a male living in a household like that, where he is 
not paying any rent, not paying any power, not contributing to the groceries, or anything 
else but using that money for his own purposes, or for both their purposes, be able to 
walk away scot-free? One of the things that was raised at that time, of course, was about 
a woman in a violent relationship. If she is being extorted to live in this relationship or 
to continue applying for a benefit, would this change in the law then put her under a 
legal encumbrance? The answer is no, because the courts have found that a wo man 
living in a battered -woman relationship is not living in a relationship in the nature of 
marriage, so would not be held liable for that offence. That is a really important point to 
note.  
Members on the other side of the House drew analogies between we lfare fraud and 
tax evasion. They said that the Government was putting far too much emphasis on 
welfare dependency and none on those who were avoiding paying their taxes. The point 
that they overlook is that in a succession of three zero Budgets, this Gove rnment put 
aside $200 million for efforts to uncover tax evasion and to get that money in. It has 
easily paid for itself. We are proud of the attributes of the Inland Revenue Department 
for doing exactly that. Another thing that we have done in this partic ular space is to 
share information with the Inland Revenue Department so that we can find out, for 
instance, those people who are registered on the dole, the domestic purposes benefit, the 
sickness benefit, or the invalid’s benefit, and are also working an d paying tax. The 
Inland Revenue Department advises the Ministry of Social Development of those 
people who it believes are defrauding the taxpayer, through this mechanism. It is 
interesting to note that, since we started, 6,300 people have gone off a benef it because 
they were already in work and they had been receiving illegal overpayments. 
JAN LOGIE (Green): The Green Party loves New Zealand, which is why we want 
a cleaner, smarter, and fairer New Zealand and a Ministry of Social Development. The 
Green Party and its MPs are absolutely passionate about making New Zealand a great 
place to grow up in for all of our children. When one in four children live in poverty in 
this country, something is going seriously wr ong. The Greens have been calling for 
action on child poverty since 1999. We will keep on calling for action and proposing 
solutions until we eliminate the problem. But this is not about us; this is about New 
Zealand.  
Over the last 3 years, along with mos t other New Zealanders in the country, we have 
been listening to the Children’s Commissioner, academics, doctors, community 
advocates, parents, and children themselves asking us to put children first. We have 
been watching the documentaries and the news pr ogrammes, along with the rest of the 
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19109 
 
country, and reading the reports from the Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child 
Poverty, the thousands of submissions on the green paper, the white paper, and the 
Vulnerable Children Bill, as well as the all too n umerous media stories and opinion 
pieces calling for us in this House to address inequality and end child poverty. New 
Zealand, we will continue to listen and carry your voices for our children into this place 
until we create a country where every child thrives.  
With the rest of the country we have been seeing the pictures of empty school 
lunchboxes, of mouldy houses, of children without shoes or raincoats. We have read 
recently about the young mother and her newborn baby who had to live in a car for two 
days after they were discharged from hospital, because there was no housing available 
for them. Like the rest of the country, I assume, we have fumed at, and at times cried 
over, the fact that more than one child a week is dying of poverty -related illness in this 
country that we love. At times the stories feel endless and heart -breaking. How much 
more it must feel like that for those who are living through it. The cruelty is real. But it 
is not the cruelty of an individual; it is the cruelty of a Government that has chosen to 
prioritise token efforts over addressing the real problems of poverty -level benefits, low 
wages, and substandard housing.  
Of course, we are being told that the Government is investing in our people, helping 
them into work. Well, last we ek I met with some students and tutors on a Work and 
Income mandated course, to find out how that was going for them. The tutor talked to 
me about her concern that a mother on her course had had her benefit cut in half for 
missing 3 days of the course, whe n it turned out that she had to go with her baby to 
hospital after her baby had had a seizure, and she did not have enough money on her 
phone to be able to inform anyone of that fact. So their income had been cut in half 
while they were stuck in hospital. We heard from a student about how they had 
previously had their benefit sanctioned entirely for missing an appointment because 
their public transport was running late.  
This is happening now in our country, and the sheer reality of being poor means that 
there are times when some people cannot afford even to meet the expectations of Work 
and Income to be able to get their income support. Everyone in that room of about 20 
students and their tutor talked about not being able to afford to heat their house or pu t 
proper food on their table. The young ones even talked about not being able to afford 
the $40 to buy a blanket to compensate for the lack of heating in their house. So much 
for a wraparound service, so much for supporting people, and so much for investment!  
It does not have to be this way. It is not even about throwing money at the problem 
and leaving people stuck in inequality, as this Government suggests we want to do. 
Even at the most basic level it is actually about ensuring people get access to thei r legal 
entitlements. Surely, at the absolute minimum that is the job of this Government. Yet 
when we have asked the Minister for Social Development, in this House, how she 
explains the increasing number of stories that we are hearing from the community of  
people being denied their legal entitlements, her response was: “For every one story you 
give me, I can give you 10 of people who are getting the entitlements they are eligible 
for.” 
Well, the basic point is that everyone is entitled to those services, an d it is this 
Government’s job to ensure that people are able to get enough money to put food on the 
table. That is what we consider a social security system. It is not in any way OK to say: 
“Well, these 10 people are getting it, sorry about those ones.” Th at is not doing your 
job. That is not providing even the bare minimum of what this country has agreed on, 
let alone what is, I believe, a building consensus from academics, from community 
organisations, and from people working across our health sector, our  education sector, 
and our community sector, who are all saying that there needs to be more. There needs 
19110 Estimates Debate 1 Jul 2014 
 
to be a living income for these families, and particularly for our children, because we 
know that if we do not invest in those early years of a child’s  life, then we are robbing 
them of their potential. That is something that every single person in this country will 
have to bear the consequences of.  
I really do want to speak just a little bit around the perception that this is too 
expensive to do. This is not an issue just about this Government and these estimates; it 
is about a framework that was put in place previously that has been consciously 
continued by this Government. There has been a decision to prioritise getting these 
families into work as the  way out of poverty for these families. I think that we have 
missed the fact of the interaction between work and income support —that there is an 
interaction between those two things. I would like to point out that the Government is 
currently spending more on family in-work tax credits for families working 20 hours a 
week than what it is spending on the income support system. The analysis by the Child 
Poverty Action Group showed up that somebody coming off the DPB into paid work for 
20 hours a week would be getting, on top of their income, a minimum family tax credit 
of $22,000 a year, plus the in-work tax credit of $3,000 a year. So that is over $25,000 a 
year for that family that is working less than 20 hours a week. What they would get on 
the DPB would be $15,000. So the Government is paying a lot more for that group.  
The problem with that is —because it is great for people to be able to work if that is 
appropriate for their family and they are still able to look after their children —that this 
is a system that creates a disincentive for those employers to pay anything more than the 
minimum wage. On the minimum wage, somebody who is working the 20 hours a week 
would have to work an additional 17 hours before being any better off financially. What 
employer is going to pay somebody above the minimum wage if it is not going to give 
them anything more in the hand? Basically, those employers are not going to do that. 
That does not affect just that one person stuck on the minimum wage; it affects all other 
workers i n New Zealand who are trying to get better conditions. So when the 
Government tells us that it is all about work being the pathway out of poverty, actually, 
what this is doing is entrenching people into poverty. When the Government took away 
the training i ncentive allowance for parents to be able to do higher -level study, to be 
able to get a chance of getting into that higher -wage bracket of work, we saw the lie of 
it. 
CAROL BEAUMONT (Labour): I looked at the website of the Ministry of Social 
Development and it said that the ministry is there to help people be successful in their 
lives. It said that the ministry’s role is to help New Zealanders to be safe, strong, and 
independent. My colleague Sue Mor oney—and Jan Logie has also traversed some of 
this territory —talked about how inequality and poverty are denying many New 
Zealanders the opportunity to be successful in their lives, the core aim of the Ministry of 
Social Development.  
I want to talk about another issue that limits the ability of people in this country to be 
successful in their lives —for them to be safe, strong, and independent —and those are 
issues to do with domestic and sexual violence. Issues of sexual and domestic violence 
deny many peop le the opportunity to be successful in their lives. There are huge costs 
associated with that violence, and there are barriers that are then put in the way of 
people actually going about living their lives. Obviously, in extreme circumstances 
people lose their lives, so they cannot continue to go on and be successful in their lives. 
We have a serious problem in this country. We have a serious problem with the level of 
violence that we see against our people, particularly women and children. I just thought 
it would be worth noting some of those things.  
Last week we had the independent Family Violence Death Review Committee report 
come out. It looked at deaths between 2009 and 2012 —so, over a 3 -year period—and 
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19111 
 
47 percent of those deaths were family violence deaths. In nearly all of those 
circumstances som eone was killed by their partner and there was a known history of 
abuse. Thirty -seven children died —37 of our children died —and 77 children were 
present when a parent or a sibling died in their home. These people are not going to be 
able to live successful lives. Their lives have been cut short by other people’s violence.  
Also, the chair of that committee said that —and I think this is just so chilling —the 
reviews she read that were the most difficult for her to read were the ones where a 
woman is clearly f ighting for her life: “She sees that she is going to die and she is … 
actively taking every action she possibly can to save her life. She’s contacting the 
police, she’s telling landlords, she’s telling neighbours, she’s telling friends … and we 
are not providing her with effective help.” That is just absolutely chilling. And it is not 
just domestic violence; one in three women in this country experience intimate partner 
violence, sexual or domestic violence, during the course of their lifetime —one in three. 
These figures are just horrendous.  
So I think we need to be seriously looking at what is happening here and what should 
be done. As well as the Family Violence Death Review Committee report last week, the 
week before that, I think it was, we had the firs t of the Glenn Inquiry reports —500 
interviews with people who have lived in violent situations. There is the loss of life —I 
have talked about that —but there are also other costs. There is the loss of people’s 
potential. There is the loss of potential for a  child, one of those 77 children who has 
witnessed a sibling or a parent being killed by somebody else they potentially love, 
another member of their family, and the impact that that has on that child.  
There is the loss of their potential and the loss of opportunity for them to go on and 
live in this country to their full potential rather than, in fact, going, all too commonly, 
into a situation where a cycle of abuse is created. That is a real cost to us as well. For 
some it is even a loss of freedom —the freedom to go about their life, to engage with 
whom they want to, and to go and do their job or whatever. These are costs. These are 
real costs for individuals. Some of them are, as I said, intergenerational. I have been on 
the Social Services Committee and have listened to people who have come and talked to 
us. Melissa Lee has done a very good job of chairing that committee. This violence is 
preventable. This violence is preventable, and the Government has not done enough. 
MELISSA LEE (Chairperson of the Social Services Committee) : Following 
Carol Beaumont’s speech, I would like to commend her for her passion in her speech 
regarding the domestic violence situation in this country and the violence that our 
children are facing. I thank the member for participating in the inquiry that the Social

I am proud to stand on this side of the Chamber, as a member of the National -led 
Government under the fantastic leadership of our Prime Minister, John Key. We are a 
strong, united caucus behind a strong leader, and we have a Government that has led the 
country from recession to sustained growth. We have an economy that has grown by 3.8 
percent in the year to the end of March, the third -highest among the world’s developed 
economies. It is forecast to reach  4 percent next year, which is a far cry from the 
recession we inherited back in 2008.  
I was sitting here listening to members opposite talking about some of the social 
services and social welfare policies, and I was sort of wondering whether we were 
living in the same country or not, because only a net 250 people moved to Australia in 
May this year, which is the lowest since the data started in 1996. Under Labour 3,000 
New Zealanders a month crossed the Tasman. That was a lot of Kiwis leaving our 
shores. In the past year alone, there were more jobs that were created, and if we stick to 
the Government’s programme, the average full -time wage is expected to rise to

something like $62,000 or $63,000, which is up by about $8,000, in the next 4 years. 
This follows a $3,000 increase in the average wage over the past 3 years.  
As the economy grows, families will benefit from more jobs and higher wages, and 
we are making sure that families will also be among the first to benefit from the extra 
Government spending, b ecause family is very important. As members opposite have 
also said, families are the core of our nation. Children are the core of our nation. I am

practical support for yo ung families and the vulnerable children who are most in need. 
There is $33.4 million extra to support vulnerable children, with eight new children’s

I know that some member s talked about having to fix poverty, but child abuse

simply because they were being abused  by abusers. Some children happen to have a

am appalled that members opposite keep on talking about poverty being the reason for 
it. 
Earlier, in a different speech —when we were talking about the Vulnerable Children 
Bill—I said that poverty cannot be a reason for abusing children. Nothing can be a

There is no tolerance for that. I know C arol Beaumont talked about the abuse level. I 
cannot believe that she would actually give poverty as an excuse for children being 
abused in this country.  
Carol Beaumont: It’s not an excuse but it is a fact.  
MELISSA LEE: Your members have actually said that it was an explanation; it was 
an excuse. The Government is taking its responsibility to support families very 
seriously. We are putting millions of dollars into child protection and services for 
vulnerable children and their families.  
The other thing that I am very, very pleased about in the work that Paula Bennett has 
done—and I would like to applaud the Ministers in the social welfare sector: both the 
Hon Paula Bennett and Chester Borrows. One of the things I am most pro ud of as a 
member, personally, is the reduction in teen pregnancies that we have seen. From the 
policies that we have put through in this Government, we have seen lower rates of 
teenagers getting pregnant. I am very positive for the young girls. For them, they will

BRENDAN HORAN (Independent) : I take a call on Vote Social Development. 
Recognising that our country’s greatest strength is our people, I draw your attention to 
the more than 600,000 New Zealanders over  the age of 65 —almost 15 percent of our 
population, and rapidly growing. Someone once said to judge a society on how it treats 
its most vulnerable. By that standard, New Zealand is failing its seniors.  
Although everyone wants to believe that all New Zeala nders are guaranteed security 
in retirement and that the needs of seniors are well catered for, the reality could not be 
more different. The inconvenient truth of the matter is that many seniors live in squalor 
and despair, feel they are a burden on their families, and tend to withdraw from society 
rather than seek help. The consequences are social isolation, malnourishment, and, at 
the extreme end, suicide. When we talk about suicide we often refer to the high rate of 
young people taking their lives, but t he statistics paint an equally disturbing picture for 
our seniors. Last year the Chief Coroner warned that New Zealand men aged 85 or older 
1 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19113 
 
committed suicide at a rate of 31 per 100,000. Words cannot convey the deep sense of 
tragedy that is inherent in those figures.  
So what can we do about it? First, let us change the culture. Let us challenge the 
stereotypes and the prejudices. Older New Zealanders deserve the love and respect of 
society as a whole. We should all embrace the seniors in our lives, be they  family 
members, neighbours, or friends. These people built our country. They have worked 
hard, paid taxes, raised children and grandchildren, and enriched our society in so many 
ways.  
Second, we need public policy that reflects this —policy that recognise s and values 
the contributions that our seniors have made, and policy that encourages seniors to 
remain active participants in our society. Life does not end at retirement. Crucially, we 
must put an end to political parties using seniors as a political football.  
We in the New Zealand Independent Coalition expect cross -party consensus on 
superannuation and senior care policy. We are fed up with our seniors being taken for 
granted by cynical political leaders who have used them only as votes. The New 
Zealand Independent Coalition takes seniors’ concerns seriously and is prepared to walk 
the talk. Action is what matters. Over the years there has been no significant increase in 
the amount of money in the pockets of older people, and that must change. How can we  
expect seniors to live on $276 per week? Many are eating every other day, cannot afford 
to go to the doctor, have not had any new clothes in years, and holidays are a thing of 
the past.  
We are told by Government officials that reasonable living requires $46,000 for a 
single person. A senior living on New Zealand superannuation is expected to live on 
under $22,000 a year gross. The small things in life are often the ones that bring the 
most joy, but many are struggling to afford even those —for example, pets. Pets serve as 
an important source of social and emotional support, and yet they are a joy that is 
denied for many elderly who simply cannot afford to pay the vet bills or for the food. 
The New Zealand Independent Coalition will adopt a policy of vet sub sidies for seniors. 
If we are serious about improving the quality of life for senior New Zealanders, then 
this is a small but powerful gesture towards doing just that.  
We hear the continual cry that New Zealand cannot afford to go any higher in 
payments to older people. Those parties degrade our seniors further by stating that they 
are a burden that has to be carried, and force them to plead for help from Work and 
Income. This intolerable situation cannot be allowed to continue. The New Zealand 
Independent Coalition will pursue the implementation of a financial transaction tax 
similar to that which has been adopted by 11 countries in the European Union, led by 
France and Germany. Revenue from a financial transaction tax of just 0.1 percent would 
collect over $6 billion a year from the transactions through the New Zealand banking 
system and $3.5 billion in extra revenue from New Zealand’s foreign exchange system.  
According to a Reserve Bank survey released today, New Zealand’s foreign 
exchange market handled  an average US$12.4 billion per day in April 2013, which is 
currently not taxed a single cent. A financial transaction tax on these traders would 
produce a significant source of funding that would not only support a living pension and 
living wage, but—[Bell rung] Mr Chair?
